How this curriculum works.back: Six kinds: **read the document**, **compare two accounts**, **check the number**, **place a source**, **trace a thing to its origin**, **follow it live**. None of it is needed to understand the lesson.

Anything that can change with an election, a reshuffle or a court date is written as a **bold, dated** snapshot. The teaching around it never depends on the snapshot being current — so when it goes stale, the stale part is the one with a date on it.

The schools, and what each one is for.front: The five schools of South African historiography
The schools, and what each one is for.back: **Settler** (Theal) · **Liberal** (Macmillan, de Kiewiet, Thompson) · **Afrikaner nationalist** (Preller, van Jaarsveld) · **Revisionist / radical** (Wolpe, Legassick, Bundy) · **Social history / Africanist** (the Wits History Workshop, van Onselen). Plus a still-forming post-1994 turn.
**Irrational** — a deviation from a trajectory toward a liberal order, and economically self-harming. Driver: ideas and policy. Weakness: if it was irrational, who was it for?

**Functional, not irrational** — it produced the cheap labour the mines needed. Wolpe's claim: the reserves subsidised wages by bearing the cost of reproducing labour. Weakness: functionalism explains everything and so explains nothing.

The four big disagreements.front: The four big disagreements in this subject
The four big disagreements.back: 1. Was apartheid a **continuation of segregation or a break**? 2. Did it fall to **resistance, economic failure, or the end of the Cold War**? 3. Was the settlement a **victory or a compromise** that left economic power untouched? 4. Is the post-1994 state's failure **corruption or design**?

Establish what a source is before readin.back: **About** — an account, assessed for accuracy. **Of** — evidence of its own author's thinking, which cannot be wrong in the same way. An Afrikaner nationalist history of the Trek is a poor source *about* the Trek and an excellent source *of* Afrikaner nationalism.

Establish what a source is before readin.front: The five questions to place a source
Establish what a source is before readin.back: Who wrote it and **when** · what **tradition** · what is it trying to **establish** · what must it **leave out** · is it a source *about* or a source *of*. The test that you have placed it: you can predict how it will handle a chapter you have not read.

A commission is not a court.front: What a commission of inquiry can and cannot do
A commission is not a court.back: **Can**: subpoena, take evidence on oath, **find**, recommend, refer. **Cannot**: convict, sentence, order compensation, make law. Its findings are **reviewable**. "Zondo found him guilty" is not a thing that can happen.
The statute commissions of inquiry operate under, together with **s84(2)(f)** of the Constitution, which lets the President appoint them.

A commission is not a court.front: Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995
A commission is not a court.back: Established the **Truth and Reconciliation Commission**, and gave it the power that made it more than a commission: its Amnesty Committee could **extinguish criminal and civil liability** for a disclosed act.

A commission is not a court.front: Court, commission, Public Protector — the three-way test
A commission is not a court.back: **Court**: decided, with precedent and consequence. **Commission**: found, on the evidence it heard, reviewable, no consequence of its own. **Public Protector**: directed — **binding unless set aside on review** (*EFF v Speaker*, 2016).

**Five parts, January to June 2022.** Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture, chaired by Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo, appointed 2018 after the Public Protector's *State of Capture* report recommended it. It **referred** to the NPA; it did not charge.
**Volumes 1–5 in 1998; volumes 6–7 in 2003**, after the Amnesty Committee finished. All seven are free in full.

How to read a judgment.back: The reasoning a decision **needed**. Binding on lower courts.
Said in passing, not needed for the outcome. **Persuasive, not binding** — and quoting it as settled law is the commonest error in public argument about judgments.
The **Constitutional Court**, in a neutral citation — e.g. *[2002] ZACC 15*. ZASCA is the Supreme Court of Appeal. Neutral citations are stable and free to look up.

How to read a judgment.front: The order to read a judgment in
How to read a judgment.back: **The order first** — it is what was actually decided. Then the first few paragraphs, where the court states the question. Then the reasoning. Then the separate judgments, because a dissent is often where the next decade's argument comes from.

How to read a statistic.back: A single number, 0 to 1, summarising how unequally something is distributed. South Africa's is **about 0.63** — among the highest measured. **It depends on what you measure**: income before tax, income after tax and transfers, or consumption, and the three differ meaningfully.

How to read a statistic.front: The five questions to ask of any figure
How to read a statistic.back: Who **produced** it · what exactly is being **counted** · over what **period** and against what **baseline** · is it a **level or a rate** · what is the **denominator**. The definition, not the arithmetic, is almost always where the misuse is.

The two unemployment rates.back: The whole difference is the **search requirement**. Official (strict) requires having **actively looked for work in the last four weeks**; expanded does not, and so includes **discouraged work-seekers**. The official definition is the ILO standard used in international comparison.

**Official 33.6%**, **expanded 43.8%**, labour underutilisation 46.3%. 8.5m unemployed, 16.7m employed. Youth (15–34) 47.4%; women 37.5% vs men 30.3%. *Go and get the current figure — the structure of the gap is the durable fact.*
**Employed ÷ working-age population.** Immune to the strict-versus-expanded dispute, which makes it the best single number for how much of the country is working. Published in every QLFS.
**Quarterly Labour Force Survey** — StatsSA's household survey, the source of both unemployment rates, the absorption rate and the participation rate.

The Gazette, where the law actually appe.front: When does a South African Act become law?
The Gazette, where the law actually appe.back: Parliament passes it → the President **assents** → it is **published in the Gazette** (now it is an Act) → it **commences**, either on publication or **on a date fixed by proclamation**. An Act can be signed and not in force, sometimes for years. Check commencement before saying something is law.

The Gazette, where the law actually appe.front: Act, regulation, policy — which is law?
The Gazette, where the law actually appe.back: **Act**: made by Parliament. **Regulation**: made by a **minister** under an Act, and changeable by that minister — where the operative detail lives. **Policy, framework, plan, White Paper**: **not law at all**. The NDP is not law.

The official journal of record. **Nothing is law until it appears there.** Acts, proclamations, regulations, notices — including every apartheid group-area proclamation and removal notice. Open Gazettes makes the scanned originals searchable, free.

The words that carry an argument.back: **Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment Act 53 of 2003**: a generic term meaning **Africans, Coloureds and Indians**. So in any discussion of BEE, employment equity or procurement, the broad meaning is the legal one — and mixing it with the narrow everyday sense produces a lot of confused argument about BEE statistics.

**Non-racial**: race is not a legitimate political category at all — the Congress tradition's position, and the Constitution's. **Multiracial**: races exist and should be represented. Not synonyms; the distinction was fought over for decades.

Three names for the same territories. **"Homeland" accepts the premise** that they were the national homes of separate peoples; **"bantustan" rejects it**; "self-governing territory" and "Bantu area" are the state's own terms, so using them tells you who is speaking.

What would change your mind.front: The three kinds of claim, and what settles each
What would change your mind.back: **Factual** — evidence, straightforwardly. **Causal** — evidence, with difficulty. **Evaluative** — not by evidence at all. Most arguments about South Africa mix all three in one sentence, and separating them is most of the work.

What would change your mind.front: The test of whether stage 1 worked
What would change your mind.back: Can you state the position you **disagree** with, in its strongest form, well enough that someone who holds it would recognise it as their own?

The Bantu-speaking farmers: when, from w.back: The earliest known **Bantu-speaking farming settlement** in what is now South Africa, in Limpopo near Tzaneen — **about 1,370 years before 1652**. With Broederstroom (c. 500 CE) and the KwaZulu-Natal coastal sites (c. 400 CE).

The Bantu-speaking farmers: when, from w.front: Why pre-colonial farming settlement stopped where it did
The Bantu-speaking farmers: when, from w.back: **Sorghum and millet are summer-rainfall crops.** The east and north have summer rainfall and were settled from the early centuries CE; the **south-western Cape has winter rainfall** and was not. The boundary ran roughly to the **Great Fish River** — which is where the colonial frontier later met them, over a century after the Dutch landed.

The Bantu-speaking farmers: when, from w.front: What click consonants in isiZulu and isiXhosa prove
The Bantu-speaking farmers: when, from w.back: **Sustained, intimate contact** with Khoe and San speakers over generations — intermarriage and bilingual households. Other Bantu languages overwhelmingly lack clicks. Borrowing on that scale is not what conquest leaves behind.

Iron, cattle and grain.back: Not primarily food. **Bridewealth** (*lobola*, *bogadi*), **clientage** (*mafisa*, *sisa* — a rich man placed cattle with a poor one, who owed loyalty), tribute, store of value, and the judicial medium for fines. **A chief's power was the number of people who owed him** — which is why colonial conquest worked by seizing herds.

Huffman's model: a **central cattle byre**, senior male burials in it, grain stored in the residential zone, houses by seniority, a court at the centre — read as patrilineal, cattle-owning, male-dominated society. **The pattern is a finding; the social interpretation is a hypothesis**, criticised for reading the ethnographic present backwards.

Mapungubwe, and the states of the Limpop.back: A **state** in the Limpopo–Shashe confluence, c. **1220–1290 CE**. Elite on the hill, commoners below — the first clear **class separation** in the region's archaeology. Gold and ivory out, **Chinese celadon and Persian pottery in**, via Indian Ocean trade. Excavated from 1933; UNESCO World Heritage 2003.

Excavated from a Mapungubwe hill burial in **1933** — wood covered in gold foil, with over two kilograms of other gold objects. Little was made of it for decades: a sophisticated African state with gold and international trade did not suit a government whose schools taught an empty interior. Now the **Order of Mapungubwe** is South Africa's highest honour.

On the Mpumalanga escarpment, c. **1500–1820**: **hundreds of square kilometres of terraced fields**, stone-walled homesteads and cattle tracks. Intensive, labour-organised agriculture with generations of capital investment in the land.

Great Zimbabwe, and why it is in this cu.back: A stone city in modern Zimbabwe, c. **1270–1450 CE**, up to **18,000** people, dry-stone walls to eleven metres. Successor to Mapungubwe in the same trading system, and the **Zimbabwe tradition extends into South Africa** — Thulamela, Dzata. The country and its flag's bird are named from it.

Attributed to Phoenicians, Sheba, anyone but Africans. **Randall-MacIver (1905) and decisively Caton-Thompson (1929) settled the African medieval origin** and no competent archaeologist contested it after. From the 1960s **Rhodesia required that the consensus not be stated as fact** — displays altered, archaeologists pressured out. A manufactured controversy, not a live one.

The Highveld towns.back: A Tswana stone-walled town near present-day Zeerust, c. 1750–1823. The missionary **John Campbell visited in 1820 and estimated 16,000–20,000 people** — comparable to Cape Town at the time. **He published it**, and it was ignored for a century and a half.

The court and assembly place at the centre of a Tswana ward and town, where a chief heard matters in public. A durable institution, not an archaeological curiosity — it persists in modified form in traditional councils today.

The Mfecane: what is agreed.front: The states formed in the Mfecane period
The Mfecane: what is agreed.back: **Zulu** (Shaka, c. 1816–28) · **Lesotho** (Moshoeshoe, from 1824, on Thaba Bosiu) · **Ndebele** (Mzilikazi, moving north to present Zimbabwe) · **Swazi** (Sobhuza) · **Gaza** (Soshangane, southern Mozambique) · **Kololo** (Sebetwane). These are the political map the colonial state later dealt with.

Zulu **age-regiments**, drawn from across the kingdom rather than from a lineage — which concentrated military and political power in the king. Whether Shaka invented them or expanded an existing institution is argued; that they were consolidated under him is not.

**Mfecane** — isiZulu/isiXhosa, "the crushing". **Difaqane/Lifaqane** — Sesotho, the Highveld's word. **"The Wars of Shaka"** names a cause in its title, which is the thing being argued about. The term *Mfecane* entered historical writing carrying the Shaka-centred explanation, which is why its use is part of the dispute.

The Mfecane as alibi: the debate.back: Julian Cobbing's argument that the Shaka-centred account **served as an alibi for settler land seizure** — a self-destroyed interior means land was found, not taken. Also: the sources are settlers', traders' and missionaries'; **Dithakong (1823) was a raid misreported**; the real drivers were **Delagoa Bay slaving and Cape labour raiding**.

The Mfecane as alibi: the debate.front: What the Mfecane debate settled, and what it did not
The Mfecane as alibi: the debate.back: **Accepted**: the concept served settler interests; the depopulated-interior claim is false; the sources must be read critically; Dithakong was misreported. **Not accepted**: that Shaka's role was essentially invented, or that the upheaval was wholly externally driven. A revision can win on method and lose its strongest substantive claim.

The Mfecane as alibi: the debate.front: The current multi-causal account of the Mfecane
The Mfecane as alibi: the debate.back: **Ivory and slave trade via Delagoa Bay** · **Cape labour and cattle raiding** · **drought (the Madlathule famine)** · **the maize transition** — higher yields, then catastrophic drought vulnerability · internal political competition · **Zulu state formation, as one driver among several**. No protagonist, regional variation, and a worse story that fits the evidence better.

The \"empty land\" claim, built and dism.front: The five components of the "empty land" claim
The \"empty land\" claim, built and dism.back: 1. The interior was empty. 2. Simultaneous arrival. 3. The Cape was unoccupied. 4. African self-destruction depopulated the interior. 5. **Therefore neither has a prior claim.** Each of 1–4 fails; 5 is a non-sequitur that would not follow even if they held.

The \"empty land\" claim, built and dism.front: The honest residue of the "empty land" claim
The \"empty land\" claim, built and dism.back: Settlement was **uneven** and followed rainfall, soil and water. **Boundaries were not lines** — a real difficulty for later restitution. Populations **moved**; 1830's map was not 1750's. **Parts of the Highveld genuinely were empty in the 1830s.** None of it supports the claim; all of it bears on the land arguments in stages 9 and 12.

Rock art, and reading a record with no w.front: Why the eland dominates San rock art
Rock art, and reading a record with no w.back: It is painted far out of proportion to its share of the diet — so the art is **not a hunting record**. Read against the **ǀXam testimony**, the eland is the animal of greatest ritual potency, associated with rain, healing and the trance dance. Two independent kinds of evidence corroborating each other is what lifts the interpretation above speculation.

A rock art panel cut from a farm in the Eastern Cape in **1918** and taken to the South African Museum. A figure from it is on the **national coat of arms** (2000), whose motto **!ke e: ǀxarra ǁke** is in **ǀXam — a language with no living speakers**.

Ordinance 50, and the pattern it starts.back: Cape measure, won by missionary lobbying (John Philip): **abolished pass requirements** for Khoekhoe and free persons of colour, **ended compulsory child apprenticeship**, and **allowed them to hold land**. Legal equality in movement, contract and property — a century before anything comparable elsewhere in the country.

**A legal disability is removed, and an economically equivalent, formally race-neutral mechanism is substituted.** Pass laws (1828) → **criminal breach of contract (1841)**. Slavery (1834) → apprenticeship, then masters and servants law. The statutory colour bar → job reservation. Watch for it throughout stages 3 to 5.

From the 1841 Cape Ordinance: **made breach of a labour contract a criminal offence**, so an employer's remedy was the police and a worker who left could be imprisoned. Repeatedly amended and extended, and **on the South African statute book until 1974**.

The eastern frontier: a hundred years of.front: How the frontier wars were actually won
The eastern frontier: a hundred years of.back: Not by battles. **Cattle seizure** (cattle were authority, so taking herds destroyed a chief's following), **crop and homestead burning**, **forced relocation**, playing chiefdoms against each other, settler buffer populations, and roads and forts into the Amathole. **The destruction of an economy.**

Xhosa prophet and war leader who attacked Grahamstown in **1819**, gave himself up to end the war, was imprisoned on Robben Island and drowned escaping in 1820. **Grahamstown was renamed Makhanda in 2018** — the town named after the colonel who cleared the Zuurveld now carries the name of the man who attacked it.

The cattle-killing, 1856-57.back: **Nongqawuse**'s prophecy: kill the cattle and destroy the grain, and the dead will rise and the invaders be swept away. Roughly **400,000 cattle killed**, **40,000 dead of starvation**, **150,000 left** the territory. Xhosa independent power ended.

**Lungsickness, from 1854, had already killed perhaps two-thirds of Xhosa herds** — so the claim that the cattle were contaminated was literally true. Plus a century of military defeat, millenarian precedent (Nxele, 1819), and a religious framework in which cattle linked the living to the ancestors. Peires, *The Dead Will Arise*.

Governor **Grey exploited the cattle-killing famine systematically** — relief only in exchange for labour, chiefdoms dismantled, land to settlers — and said so in his own despatches. **That is a separate claim from having caused it**, and the evidence supports the first and not the second. *Who benefited* is a powerful question, not an answer.

The Great Trek: what it was, and what it.back: Pretorius's laager of about **470 trekkers** against several thousand Zulu: roughly **3,000 Zulu dead, three trekkers wounded**. A technological outcome — wagons, cannon and massed musketry against close-order attack — which the nationalist account read as providential.

**Dingane's Day** → **Day of the Vow** (*Geloftedag*) → since 1995 the **Day of Reconciliation**. Whether a vow was made in 1838 in the remembered terms is genuinely uncertain; the full form became fixed through later promotion, Preller's in particular. The **Ncome Museum** stands across the river from the Blood River memorial.

The Great Trek: what it was, and what it.front: How the Great Trek was made into a founding
The Great Trek: what it was, and what it.back: **Gustav Preller** from the 1900s — Retief's biography, the Vow, the first Afrikaans films. Then the **1938 centenary**, an ox-wagon re-enactment drawing enormous crowds, **a decade before the National Party won power**. The **Voortrekker Monument** opened in 1949. Nationalism built deliberately, by identifiable people, in the twentieth century.

Natal, the Zulu kingdom, and annexation.back: From 1845: govern Africans through **recognised chiefs**, administering **"native law"**, in **locations**, under a **separate legal system**, with the governor as **Supreme Chief**. Cheap, and **the administrative template for the 1927 Native Administration Act, the Bantu Authorities Act and the homelands**. Indirect rule, invented before segregation had a name.

A British column of roughly **1,800 destroyed** — the worst defeat inflicted on a British army by an African force. And strategically it changed nothing: the Zulu could not replace their losses and Britain could. **Ulundi, 4 July 1879**, broke the army; Zululand was then **partitioned into thirteen chiefdoms chosen to be weak**, and annexed in 1887.

Required, among other things, that the **amabutho be disbanded within thirty days** — a demand to dissolve the state, designed to be refused. Frere and Shepstone wanted the kingdom gone as an obstacle to confederation.

The Boer republics.front: The Sand River and Bloemfontein Conventions
The Boer republics.back: **1852** — Britain recognises the **Transvaal (ZAR)**. **1854** — Britain recognises the **Orange Free State**. Not generosity but **retrenchment**: the interior was expensive to govern. Both secured that slavery would not be permitted and said nothing about the African majority.

The Boer republics.front: Why the ZAR could not subdue its own claimed territory
The Boer republics.back: It was bankrupt and militarily weak. **The Pedi defeated it in 1876**; only British forces broke Sekhukhune, in 1879. **The Venda were not subdued until 1898.** Tswana chiefdoms sought British protection instead — which is how Bechuanaland became a protectorate rather than Transvaal land.

Diamonds, 1867.back: **Migrant labour · the closed compound (1885) · body searching · the pass system · a racial division of labour · monopsony recruiting · industrial amalgamation.** Nearly every institution of South African labour control, worked out on the diamond fields and transferred wholesale to the goldfields.

Diamonds, 1867.front: The closed compound's stated reason and real function
Diamonds, 1867.back: Stated: preventing **illicit diamond buying** — a real problem specific to diamonds. Actual function: **immobilised the workforce, excluded families, prevented organisation, and made the wage a single man's wage.** It transferred to gold, where a worker cannot pocket the ore, and lasted a century.

White diggers, squeezed from above by amalgamation, secured protection by **having black competitors excluded by law** rather than by being protected from capital. Recurs in 1907, in the 1922 Rand Revolt, in the civilised labour policy, and in job reservation. **The central dynamic of South African political economy.**

Gold, 1886.front: Why the fixed gold price shaped a century
Gold, 1886.back: Under the gold standard **gold had a set price**, so a mine could not raise its price to cover rising costs. It could only **cut costs** or mine richer ore. **The largest controllable cost was unskilled wages** — so the whole structure of the industry pointed at holding down the cost of black labour. Not prejudice: arithmetic.

A wage must normally cover reproducing the worker and the next generation. **If the family subsists on reserve land, the employer need not pay for that** — so the reserves **subsidised** mine wages. Conclusion: the reserves were a **component of the wage structure**, which is why the state maintained them and why total dispossession was never policy.

**Roughly no higher in 1970 than in 1911.** Sixty years of industrialisation and rising productivity, with black real wages flat — the outcome of monopsony, pass law and a regional labour supply. The single most quoted number in South African economic history.

The mining labour system.back: The **Witwatersrand Native Labour Association (1900)** and **Native Recruiting Corporation (1912)** — single recruiting agencies for the whole gold industry, **with agreed maximum wages**. Monopsony institutionalised: a single buyer facing many sellers sets the price.

A portion of a migrant's wage held back and paid on arrival home. **It guaranteed the return**, kept the system circular, and transferred part of the wage into the rural economy that the wage did not have to cover. Wolpe's mechanism, administered.

About **63,000 indentured Chinese workers** imported after the war, when African workers declined pre-war wages. **"Chinese slavery" became an issue in Britain's 1906 election** and contributed to the Liberal landslide; repatriation was complete by 1910.

The compound, the pass and the colour ba.front: Natives (Abolition of Passes and Co-ordination of Documents) Act, 1952
The compound, the pass and the colour ba.back: **It extended the pass system to women and made a single document — the reference book — compulsory nationally.** Named for the abolition of passes because it replaced several documents with one. Deliberate drafting, and the best illustration in South African law of how a title can carry an argument.

**1911 Mines and Works Act** regulations reserved certificates of competency for whites. **1923: a court struck them down.** **1926: Parliament re-enacted the bar explicitly**, under the Pact government elected on that platform. Discrimination as legislative choice, not administrative drift.

The compound, the pass and the colour ba.front: Who the colour bar was for
The compound, the pass and the colour ba.back: **Not the mine owners** — they wanted the cheapest competent labour and fought to dilute skilled work. **White labour won it against capital, by political means.** So apartheid's labour order has two logics: the migrant/reserve system was functional **for capital**; the colour bar was functional **for white workers** and costly to capital.

The Cape franchise, and the non-racial e.back: Adult men with **property worth £25 or wages of £50 a year** — **no racial bar in the law**. By 1909 African and Coloured voters were **about 15% of the Cape electorate** and held the balance in several eastern districts.

The Cape franchise, and the non-racial e.front: How the Cape franchise was narrowed without mentioning race
The Cape franchise, and the non-racial e.back: **1887**: land held under **communal tenure excluded** from the property qualification — about 20,000 African voters gone. **1892**: qualification raised to £75 plus a **literacy test**. **1894 Glen Grey Act**: individual title granted in a form **drafted not to qualify a man to vote**. The right preserved, the qualification adjusted until it was empty.

The Cape franchise could be altered only by **two-thirds of both Houses sitting together**. It held 26 years: **African voters removed in 1936** when the United and National Parties combined; **Coloured voters in 1951–56** after the government enlarged the Senate and reconstituted the Appellate Division. **A procedural safeguard will not stop a determined parliament** — which is why 1996 chose a justiciable Bill of Rights instead.

Rhodes, the Chartered Company and the Ra.back: Rhodes's "Bill for Africa": **individual title, one allotment per man** (so sons were landless), **the allotments excluded from the franchise qualification**, a **labour tax** of ten shillings on men who had not worked outside the district for three months, and **district councils**. A blueprint for producing migrant labourers — and the ancestor of the homeland administrations.

Every consequence ran against its intention. **Kruger's position strengthened; the republics concluded a military alliance (1897); the Transvaal re-armed with Mausers and Creusot guns; the Afrikaner Bond's alliance with Rhodes ended; Chamberlain was implicated and the inquiry read as a cover-up.** It armed the enemy four years before the war.

The road to war.front: Why the uitlander franchise could not be conceded
The road to war.back: The Boer electorate was perhaps **30,000 men** and the uitlander male adult population on the Rand was comparable and growing. **A five-year franchise would hand the republic to a population largely in the mining companies' employ** — companies that had just attempted a coup. Kruger offered seven years, then five with conditions; both were rejected.

The road to war.front: Who caused the South African War
The road to war.back: **Milner and Chamberlain deliberately engineered it** — strongly supported by Milner's own correspondence about wanting to "work up to a crisis", and the dominant view. Kruger's intransigence was real but was about a demand that would have ended the republic. "The mining capitalists drove it" is more complicated: the industry was divided.

The guerrilla phase, the farms and the c.back: **About 110,000–160,000 white internees, roughly 28,000 deaths, of whom about 22,000 were children.** Separately, **about 115,000 black internees with at least 14,000–20,000 recorded deaths**, and poorer records. Deaths from disease and neglect after farm burning removed the population's means of living — not a programme of killing, which is a different and still serious charge.

The British woman who visited the camps in 1901, documented conditions and published — producing a political storm, the **Fawcett Commission**, and reforms that cut mortality in the war's last months. **A national figure in South Africa and largely forgotten in Britain.** She did not visit the black camps.

**About 8,000 blockhouses** linked by some **6,000 km of barbed wire**; **drives** sweeping commandos against the wire; **scorched earth** — farms burned, crops destroyed, stock killed; and **concentration camps**, which followed directly, because the families off the burned farms had to go somewhere.

Vereeniging, and the peace that excluded.front: Article 8 of the Peace of Vereeniging
Vereeniging, and the peace that excluded.back: **The question of an African franchise was deferred until after self-government in the new colonies** — that is, assigned to a white electorate certain to refuse it. Not a prohibition: **a procedure with a predictable outcome.** Britain had partly justified the war by the republics' racial order, and settled it by guaranteeing that order.

**White unity was bought with African exclusion.** The price of reconciling Boer and Briton was that the victors would not impose the Cape's franchise on the vanquished. Stated in Article 8, executed in the South Africa Act.

Reconstruction, Milner, and anglicisatio.back: The **South African Native Affairs Commission** under Lagden. Recommended **territorial separation of land purchase**, **a separate political roll**, a common national policy, and chiefly administration of the reserves. **The blueprint for the 1913 Land Act and the 1936 Representation of Natives Act** — drafted under British Crown colony rule, 43 years before the National Party took power.

English-medium state schooling provoked the **CNO** (*Christelike Nasionale Onderwys*) private Dutch schools, funded from the Netherlands — and the schools fight made **language the central symbol of Afrikaner identity** and pushed the move from Dutch to **Afrikaans**. Milner wanted to dissolve Afrikaner identity and gave it a cause, a grievance and an institution.

African and Coloured politics before Uni.back: **The first African political organisation in South Africa**, at Port Elizabeth. With Jabavu's ***Imvo Zabantsundu*** (1884), the South African Native Congress (1898), the **APO** under Abdurahman (1902) and the colonial congresses, it means organised African and Coloured politics ran for **thirty years before 1912**.

**The first national African political gathering**, at Bloemfontein, opposing the draft South Africa Act. Its London delegation — **led by W. P. Schreiner, a former Cape premier**, with Jabavu, Rubusana and Abdurahman — was received and **the Act passed unamended**.

Convened by **Pixley ka Isaka Seme** at Bloemfontein; **John Dube** first president, **Sol Plaatje** first secretary-general. A **federation of existing bodies**, not a founding from nothing. Its first great campaign was against the 1913 Natives Land Act, documented in Plaatje's ***Native Life in South Africa*** (1916).

The National Convention and Union, 1910.back: **Unitary, not federal** · the franchise left as each province had it, **the Cape's entrenched and quarantined** · **a colour bar on membership of Parliament** ("British subjects of European descent") · **two official languages, entrenched** · **three capitals** · a Senate with nominated members · provision to incorporate the territories, never exercised. **33 delegates, all white men.**

The National Convention and Union, 1910.front: Why the unitary choice of 1910 mattered most
The National Convention and Union, 1910.back: **A sovereign parliament with no justiciable bill of rights meant a bare majority could do anything** — which is how every segregation and apartheid statute passed, and why no court could stop them. The 1996 Constitution answers the opposite on every point.

Union came into being **eight years to the day after the Peace of Vereeniging**. The date was chosen. First Prime Minister **Louis Botha**, with Smuts and Hertzog in cabinet; Hertzog left in 1912 and founded the **National Party in 1914**.

What 1910 settled, and what it deferred.front: What Union deferred, and when each came due
What 1910 settled, and what it deferred.back: **African franchise → 1936.** **Coloured franchise → 1951–56.** **Land → 1913.** **Urban residence → 1923.** **The colour bar → 1911/1926.** **The republic → 1961.** **Citizenship → 1970.** **The High Commission Territories → never.** **The whole settlement → 1990–96.** Every one is a cheque written in 1910.

What 1910 settled, and what it deferred.front: The evidence for continuity, from stage 3
What 1910 settled, and what it deferred.back: Pass, compound and colour bar built by an industry before 1900 · **SANAC's 1905 blueprint, under British rule** · the 1910 sovereign parliament with no judicial check · **Article 8 of Vereeniging** · the Cape franchise narrowed by the Cape's own parliament in 1887 and 1892 · indirect rule invented in Natal in the 1840s. **So the first big disagreement cannot be settled by pointing at 1948.**

The Natives Land Act, 1913.back: **Africans could not buy or lease land outside the scheduled areas — about 7.3% of the country** — and **sharecropping and labour tenancy were prohibited** (the Free State clause), which caused immediate mass eviction. It did not initially apply in the Cape, because land ownership was an entrenched franchise qualification there.

**The restitution cut-off.** The Restitution of Land Rights Act 1994 allows claims for dispossession **after** this date — so everything before it, including all of conquest and all Khoe and San dispossession, falls outside the programme. Chosen for administrability: records exist after it and largely do not before.

Plaatje, and the campaign against the Ac.back: **Sol Plaatje's** record of the 1913 Act's evictions, gathered on a bicycle through the winter of 1913 — family by family, place by place. Primary for the Act's effects, and a polemic written to move British opinion. Both are true. **Free on South African History Online.**

**Self-government meant Britain would not intervene.** The 1909 delegation had failed to amend the Act; the 1914 one failed to get Britain to disallow a Union statute at all. **After 1914 there was no external authority to appeal to**, and it took thirty years to find an alternative.

The Natives (Urban Areas) Act, 1923.back: *The native should only be allowed to enter urban areas... when he is willing to enter and to minister to the needs of the white man, and should depart therefrom when he ceases so to minister.* **The temporary sojourner doctrine** — the city as white creation, presence by permission, justified only by employment. It governed urban policy from 1923 to the 1980s.

The 1923 Act required African townships to be **financed from African rents and municipal beer-hall profits**, not from general rates. So locations were **under-serviced by design**, the beer hall became a political target into the 1970s, and South African municipal finance inherited a structure where the service obligations and the rateable value are in different places.

The 1922 Rand Revolt.front: "Workers of the world, unite and fight for a white South Africa"
The 1922 Rand Revolt.back: The 1922 Rand Revolt's slogan. **Not a confusion** — the exact statement of a militant labour movement whose material interest was the statutory protection of white jobs against cheaper black competition. Smuts suppressed the rising with **20,000 troops, artillery and aircraft; about 200 died; four strikers were hanged** — and he lost the 1924 election.

The 1922 Rand Revolt.front: What 1922 proves about capital and apartheid
The 1922 Rand Revolt.back: **The Chamber of Mines was trying to employ black workers in semi-skilled jobs, and white workers rose against it.** So the two logics differ: the **migrant/reserve system was functional for capital**; the **colour bar was won by white labour against capital, by political means**. Any account in which capital and apartheid are identical fails here.

The Pact government, and civilised labou.back: The state and its agencies to employ **"civilised" (white) labour at "civilised" rates**. The Railways, Post Office and public works replaced African workers with whites at several times the wage — **a state-funded solution to the poor white problem**, paid for by displacement.

The Pact government, and civilised labou.front: The 1925 Wage Act as a colour bar
The Pact government, and civilised labou.back: Racially neutral on its face — it set minimum wages by occupation. **Its effect was to price black workers out of jobs white workers wanted**: at an equal "civilised" wage an employer prefers the white worker. A minimum wage used as an exclusion — **the most sophisticated form of the substitution pattern**.

The Pact government, and civilised labou.front: The 1924 Industrial Conciliation Act's definition of "employee"
The Pact government, and civilised labou.back: **It excluded pass-bearing Africans** — so African workers could not register a union, could not bargain lawfully, and their strikes were criminal. **This lasted until 1979** (the Wiehahn reforms): fifty-five years in which the majority of the industrial workforce had no legal collective voice.

The Native Administration Act, 1927.back: **The Governor-General declared "Supreme Chief" of all Africans**, with power to **legislate for the reserves by proclamation**, **depose chiefs**, and **order whole communities to move** — the legal machinery behind the forced removals. Plus a separate court system and codified "native law".

**An offence to utter words with intent to promote hostility between Africans and Europeans.** Almost any political statement about racial injustice could be charged; truth was no defence. Used for decades against the ICU, the Communist Party and the ANC — **the ancestor of apartheid's security legislation.**

The Native Administration Act, 1927.front: What the 1927 Act did to chiefs
The Native Administration Act, 1927.back: It made chiefly office a **state appointment**: authority from the state rather than from lineage and followers, **accountable upward**, paid a stipend, and removable for resisting. It created the deepest division in twentieth-century African politics, and the 1950s rural revolts were largely revolts against state-appointed chiefs.

The poor white problem.back: Funded by the **Carnegie Corporation of New York**: found roughly **300,000 "very poor" whites out of about 1.8 million** — one in six — and framed it as a **structural** problem requiring state action. **In 1984 the Second Carnegie Inquiry studied black poverty**, same funder, and its recommendations were not acted on by that state.

**Mass poverty in a population of two million was largely ended within thirty years by deliberate policy** — education, state employment, housing, health, protected wages. It is evidence that poverty of that scale is not intractable. **And it was for one group, substantially funded by the exclusion of another.** Both are the same fact.

Afrikaner nationalism: the institutions.front: The six institutional pillars of Afrikaner nationalism
Afrikaner nationalism: the institutions.back: **Culture and language** (CNO schools, Afrikaans official 1925, the **1933 Afrikaans Bible**, the FAK, the 1938 centenary) · **the churches** · **the Broederbond** (1918) · **capital** — *volkskapitalisme*: Sanlam, Volkskas, the 1939 economic congress, the **Reddingsdaadbond** · **labour** · **the party**. Built deliberately, over four decades.

A mass savings and mutual-aid movement — **small contributions from many, channelled into Afrikaner enterprise**. The mechanism by which a poor population accumulated capital it could not accumulate individually. Federale Volksbeleggings and Rembrandt came out of the same movement.

Afrikaner nationalism: the institutions.front: Why Afrikaner nationalism is the model case
Afrikaner nationalism: the institutions.back: It is **the best-documented case of a national identity being deliberately constructed** — a language standardised and given a Bible, a history made into a founding, a theology, a capital base from pooled savings, a party and a civil service. **And the grievance was real**, which is why it worked. The same method applies to any identity: who built this, when, with what institutions, against what.

The ICU, and the first mass movement.back: **Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union**, founded 1919 by **Clements Kadalie** — the first mass African organisation, peaking around **100,000 members** in the mid-1920s, **with a rural reach** among farm workers and labour tenants that nothing before or since matched. Collapsed by 1930.

**No shop-floor base** (a farm workers' union has no plant and no strike that does not end in eviction) · no financial discipline · state and farmer repression · the 1927–28 split · and decisively **the 1924 legal exclusion of Africans from the definition of "employee"**. It was not out-competed; it was **legislated out of existence as a union**.

The Communist Party and the Native Repub.back: Comintern directive: *an independent native South African republic as a stage towards a workers' and peasants' republic, with full protection and equal rights for all national minorities.* Three moves: the primary contradiction is **national**, not simply class; so the struggle has **two stages**, liberation then socialism; and whites are a national minority.

**The Congress Alliance · the SACP working inside the ANC from 1953 · the National Democratic Revolution as the ANC's own framework · and the live post-1994 argument about when the second stage begins.** Reading "the NDR", "the motive forces" and "the balance of forces" in a current ANC document is reading the 1928 thesis's descendants.

The Communist Party and the Native Repub.front: Why the CPSA mattered beyond its size
The Communist Party and the Native Repub.back: **It was the only political organisation in the country with white, African, Coloured and Indian members on equal terms** — so much of the Congress Alliance's cross-racial machinery was built by communists. Plus union organisers after the ICU's collapse, discipline, theory, and later Soviet training and arms.

Women's politics, and the anti-pass camp.back: **The first sustained civil disobedience campaign in South African history, run by women — and it won.** Refusal to carry passes, marches and imprisonment rather than fines, in Bloemfontein and other Free State towns; **Charlotte Maxeke** among its leaders. The requirement was suspended. Forty-three years before the 1956 march.

**The vote for white women only** — which roughly **doubled the white electorate**. With the 1931 removal of the Cape property and literacy qualification for white men, it **cut the Cape's black voters' share of the electorate roughly in half**, five years before they were removed from the common roll. A real advance for one group, used as an instrument of dilution.

Women's politics, and the anti-pass camp.front: When women became full ANC members
Women's politics, and the anti-pass camp.back: **1943** — thirty-one years after the organisation was founded. Before that, auxiliary membership without voting rights, which is why the **Bantu Women's League (1918)** existed. The ANC Women's League followed in 1948, FEDSAW in 1954, and the Women's Charter in 1955.

Fusion, 1934.front: Why Fusion was the precondition for removing the African franchise
Fusion, 1934.back: The Cape franchise was entrenched: **two-thirds of both Houses sitting together**. Hertzog's bills failed for want of it through the 1920s. **Fusion in 1934 merged the National and South African Parties and supplied the majority** — and the 1936 Act then passed **169 votes to 11**. A procedural safeguard is only as strong as the legislature's unwillingness to meet it.

The 1936 Acts: the franchise.back: African voters removed from the **Cape common roll** and put on a separate roll electing **three white MPs**, with four white senators, and the advisory **Natives Representative Council**. Passed at a joint sitting **169 to 11** — by the Fusion government, with the National Party in opposition voting for it, **twelve years before 1948**.

The 1936 Acts: the franchise.front: "We have been talking to a toy telephone"
The 1936 Acts: the franchise.back: **Paul Mosaka**, on the **Natives Representative Council**, which adjourned in protest when the 1946 mineworkers' strike was broken and never effectively met again. **A participation mechanism with no power is more corrosive of faith in a system than exclusion**, because it produces evidence. The test for any council: can anything it says oblige anybody to do anything?

The 1936 Acts: the land.front: Native Trust and Land Act 18 of 1936
The 1936 Acts: the land.back: **Where the 13% comes from.** Added "released areas" to the 1913 schedule, targeting about **13.6%** for roughly two-thirds of the population — **a target never fully delivered**. And Chapter IV tightened labour tenancy, causing a further wave of evictions.

**Political rights in the common system traded for more land.** The Representation of Natives Act took the vote; the Native Trust and Land Act promised the land. **The first was delivered in full and the second was not** — and even full delivery could not have supported the population, as the state's own commissions said.

African politics between the wars.back: Drafted under **Alfred Xuma** in response to the **Atlantic Charter**, asking for its principles to be applied in South Africa: universal franchise, equality before the law, land, education, freedom of movement. **The ancestor of the Freedom Charter and, at a distance, the 1996 Bill of Rights.** It was ignored.

The Non-European Unity Movement (1943) and the All African Convention tradition: **refuse to participate in any segregated institution** — no Natives Representative Council, no advisory boards, no separate rolls — with the **boycott** as principal weapon and unity of all the oppressed. Strongest among Cape Coloured teachers and intellectuals; never built a mass base; **largely written out of the ANC-centred account.**

**Anton Lembede** (first president, died 1947 aged 33), **A. P. Mda**, **Sisulu**, **Tambo**, **Mandela**. Diagnosis: deputations had failed for thirty years and the ANC was a club without members. Produced the **1949 Programme of Action** — boycott, strike, civil disobedience. Its Africanist wing broke away in 1959 as the **PAC**.

The war, and the Afrikaner split.back: The Assembly votes **80 to 67 for war**. **Hertzog, the Prime Minister, had argued for neutrality and resigned**; Smuts became Prime Minister. The Fusion government broke on the question five years after it was formed, and the vote cut across the merged party.

Afrikaner paramilitary and cultural movement from 1939, under **Hans van Rensburg** from 1941; its *Stormjaers* carried out **sabotage**, and the state responded with **internment without trial**. **Among those interned was B. J. Vorster — Prime Minister from 1966 to 1978.** Malan's National Party kept its distance, which is politically important.

Wartime urbanisation and the squatters.back: In **1944** Mpanza led thousands of sub-tenants out of overcrowded Orlando onto vacant municipal land. The state **could not remove them** and had to lay out serviced sites instead — which became **Soweto**. *Sofasonke*: "we shall all die together".

**Manufacturing — which overtook mining and agriculture during the war — needed the labour.** The pass system was not repealed; enforcement was reduced. Which demonstrates what it was for: **when labour was wanted in cities the controls eased, and when it was not they tightened.**

**1940 and 1943–44**: tens of thousands walked nine miles each way to work for weeks rather than pay a raised fare — **and won, twice**. The clearest demonstration of the period that mass action worked where deputation did not, and the Youth League was watching.

The 1946 mineworkers' strike.back: **60,000–70,000 out** on the gold mines from **12 August 1946**, demanding **ten shillings a day**, organised by the AMWU under **J. B. Marks**. Broken in four days by police baton charges and shooting — **nine official deaths, probably more**; men driven back underground at gunpoint. The union was destroyed and its leaders prosecuted.

The 1946 mineworkers' strike.front: What 1946 closed, and what it opened
The 1946 mineworkers' strike.back: **Both routes closed in the same week**: industrial action without legal standing was crushed by force, and the **Natives Representative Council adjourned in protest** and never functioned again. **The Programme of Action followed in December 1949** — so the change of method was not simply a response to 1948. The new government made it urgent; it did not make it necessary.

Fagan and Sauer: the two reports.back: **Fagan (1948)**: African urbanisation is **permanent and irreversible**, total segregation is impossible, influx control has not worked and will not — so accept a settled urban population and relax control. **Sauer (1947)**: total separation is the goal, Africans belong in the reserves, urban Africans are temporary, migrant labour only. **Same evidence, opposite answers**, and the 1948 election was between them.

**The state was told, in advance, by its own commission, that the policy could not work — and proceeded for thirty-eight years, then conceded it by abolishing influx control in 1986.** The liberal tradition's best evidence. The reply: it did not reverse urbanisation, but **it did control the terms of labour, suppress wages and prevent organisation**, successfully, until the 1970s. "It failed" needs the question "at what?"

1948: how it was won.back: **NP 70 + Afrikaner Party 9 = 79 seats** against **UP 65 + Labour 6 = 71** — on about **41% of the vote against 53%**. **Smuts lost his own seat.** Delivered substantially by **rural weighting** (constituencies loadable by up to 15%) and by the NP–AP electoral pact. Nobody expected it.

1948: how it was won.front: Three claims about 1948 to keep apart
1948: how it was won.back: **"White South Africa voted for apartheid in 1948"** — false as stated; a majority voted against the governing parties. **"Apartheid was imposed by a minority"** — true of 1948, and **not** of what followed: the NP's support grew at every election to 1977. **"1948 began segregation"** — false; the whole of stage 4 refutes it.

1948: how it was won.front: Continuity or break at 1948 — stage 4's answer
1948: how it was won.back: **Continuity in the architecture, break in the ambition.** Every major mechanism existed before 1948 — the land Acts, the Urban Areas Act, the 1927 Act, the pass system, the colour bar, the exclusion from labour law, the franchise removal of 1936. **What was new was the attempt to make it total, systematic and permanent, and to reverse urbanisation rather than regulate it** — which needed coercion on a scale the segregation state had not used, and which failed.

What apartheid was: the four pillars.back: **1. Classification** (Population Registration Act 1950 — everything else needs it). **2. Separation of space** (Group Areas, removals, passes, the homelands). **3. Separate and unequal institutions** (Bantu Education, the universities, job reservation). **4. Suppression of opposition** (Suppression of Communism, detention, the security state).

**Petty**: segregated amenities, signage, social separation — internationally notorious, and **dismantled from the late 1970s**. **Grand**: territorial and political separation — Group Areas, removals, the homelands, citizenship — **maintained to the end**. Foreign observers consistently misread concessions on the first as reform of the second.

Population Registration, and classificat.back: **The foundational statute** — a national register of race, with an identity number, in three primary categories (White, Coloured, Native). **Every other apartheid law depends on knowing who is what**, which is why it came first and was repealed last, in 1991.

**Appearance**, **general acceptance** (what the community treated you as — habits, speech, schooling, associations), and **descent**. The **pencil test was never statutory** — administrative practice, which is in some ways worse. And the state published annual **reclassification** figures, which is a statistical admission that the categories corresponded to nothing findable.

**South African Chinese were classified Coloured; Japanese businessmen were treated in practice as "honorary whites"** — because Japan bought South African minerals. **The categories bent for commerce and for nothing else**, which tells you what they were.

The Group Areas Act.back: **Investigation → proclamation in the Gazette → everyone of another group becomes a "disqualified person" → permits → expropriation at a state valuation → removal → redevelopment.** The hearings were real and did not matter; the valuations were low; and permits **hollowed a community out over years** before the bulldozers came. That was the design.

The Group Areas Act.front: Why the Group Areas map is still the country's
The Group Areas Act.back: It fixed where the townships are (far out, behind a buffer), where the industrial land is, where the transport runs, and **where the rates base is**. Repealed in 1991 — and **the city it built is still there**, which is why South African commuting is among the world's most expensive as a share of income, and why state housing on cheap peripheral land reproduces the pattern.

Forced removals: the method and the numb.back: The number usually given for people **forcibly removed between 1960 and 1983** — from the **Surplus People Project**, a five-volume independent survey of 1983–85. **An estimate with a method, not an official count**; the state published no total.

**Group Areas** removals · **"black spot"** removals (African **freehold land with registered title**) · **homeland consolidation** · **farm removals** (the largest and least documented, under the 1936 Act's Chapter IV) · **urban relocation** under influx control.

Dimbaza, Limehill, Sada, Ilinge, Thornhill, Botshabelo — **marginal land, no services, and no economy**, populated disproportionately by **women, children and the old** because the men were migrants. **Infant mortality among the highest recorded anywhere.** *Last Grave at Dimbaza* (1973) filmed it clandestinely.

Suppression of Communism, and the securi.back: To include **any doctrine or scheme aiming at political, industrial, social or economic change by the promotion of disturbance or disorder** — which catches any campaign, strike, boycott or march. **No Marxism required.** The state could then truthfully say those it banned had been named under the Communism Act.

Imposed by **ministerial signature, no trial, renewable**. Typically: no attending any **gathering** — defined to include being with **more than one other person** — no entering listed places, no leaving a district, **no being quoted**, no holding office. A person socially erased without trial.

**1963: 90 days. 1965: 180 days. 1967: Terrorism Act section 6 — indefinite, incommunicado, with no court able to pronounce on the detention or order release.** Each step moved power from the courts to the executive, and section 6 is the provision under which people died.

The pass system at its height.back: **(a)** born and permanently resident in the area · **(b)** **ten years with one employer** or fifteen years' lawful residence · **(c)** wife, unmarried daughter or **son under eighteen** of a qualifier · **(d)** a labour-bureau permit. So a dismissal in year nine destroyed a decade; a widow could lose her right; **and a township-born man had to qualify in his own right at eighteen or be endorsed out.**

The order of magnitude usually given for **arrests for pass offences** over the system's life, running at **hundreds of thousands a year** at its height. The most intensively enforced body of law in South African history — and **abolished by the apartheid state itself in 1986**, on the grounds that it had not worked.

Bantu Education.back: *There is no place for him in the European community above the level of certain forms of labour… What is the use of teaching the Bantu child mathematics when it cannot use it in practice?* **In the Senate, in Hansard** — the responsible minister's own statement of the policy's purpose.

**Enrolment rose enormously** — from under a million in 1953 to several million by the mid-1970s — **while quality and content were deliberately limited**, at roughly **ten to one** per-capita spending. The policy's quantitative success produced a large, literate, urban generation with nowhere to go — **and that generation made 1976.**

The universities, and higher education.front: The irony of the 1959 Extension of University Education Act
The universities, and higher education.back: It barred black students from the open universities and built **ethnic colleges** to produce a compliant professional class. Instead the colleges **concentrated politically conscious black students with no white students and petty authoritarian administration — and produced SASO and Black Consciousness.** Fort Hare, which had educated Mandela, Tambo, Sobukwe, Mugabe, Nyerere and Kaunda, became a Xhosa college under state control.

Bantu Authorities, and the homelands beg.back: **South Africa contains many nations; each has a right to self-determination in its own homeland; therefore there is no racial discrimination, only the separate development of distinct peoples** — and the white nation's claim to 87% of the land follows from its being one nation among several. The state's own argument, made internationally for thirty years, and the reason "separate development" replaced "apartheid" in official language.

**1853–1936**: Cape common roll, qualified, non-racial. **1936–1960**: three white MPs on a separate roll. **1960–1994**: **none** — the three seats abolished by the 1959 Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act, traded against homeland self-government.

Tomlinson, and the viability question.back: The state's own commission on whether the reserves could work. **Found they could support only about half to two-thirds of their existing population**, and recommended **about £104 million over ten years**, land consolidation, **white capital inside the reserves**, and viable farms with a landless majority. **Verwoerd refused the funding, the capital and the farming class** — and proceeded with the policy.

**Cost** · white capital inside the reserves **would create white interests there** · a landless reserve class **would have to go to the cities**, which the policy existed to prevent · and **viable reserves would not supply migrant labour**. Ideology, labour economics and the fiscus all pointed the same way, so the refusal was overdetermined.

The Coloured vote and the constitutional.back: The court struck the Act down (*Harris*, 1952); the government created a **High Court of Parliament** and that was struck down too; so it **enlarged the Senate from 48 to 89** and **the Appeal Court from 5 to 11**, got its two-thirds in 1956, and the enlarged court upheld it in 1957. **Every step was lawful.**

The Coloured vote and the constitutional.front: The lesson the 1996 Constitution learned from the 1950s
The Coloured vote and the constitutional.back: **A procedural entrenchment cannot restrain a government willing to change the procedure.** Hence: **the Constitution supreme, not Parliament** · a **justiciable** Bill of Rights · a court that can **strike down legislation** · amendment thresholds of 66⅔% and 75% plus provincial concurrence · and a **Judicial Service Commission** with a prescribed composition.

The Defiance Campaign, 1952.back: Launched **26 June 1952** — timed against the **tercentenary of Van Riebeeck's landing** — jointly by the ANC and the South African Indian Congress. **About 8,500 volunteers arrested** for deliberate, public, non-violent breach of six laws. **ANC membership went from about 7,000 to around 100,000.**

The Defiance Campaign, 1952.front: Why filling the jails stopped working
The Defiance Campaign, 1952.back: The **Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1953** raised the penalty for protesting against a law to **three years and a whipping**. Filling the jails depends on the penalty being bearable; **the apartheid state removed its limits by statute within a year.**

The Freedom Charter, 1955.back: *The mineral wealth beneath the soil, the banks and monopoly industry shall be transferred to the ownership of the people as a whole.* **A nationalisation clause** — cited by the left as abandoned after 1994, by the right as proof of socialist intent, and **it is the EFF's founding position**. It is **not** in the 1996 Constitution; section 25 protects property instead.

The Freedom Charter, 1955.front: How the Freedom Charter was drafted
The Freedom Charter, 1955.back: **"Freedom volunteers" collected demands** — around ten thousand submissions on scraps of paper, at meetings, in townships and on farms — which a committee worked into a document, adopted clause by clause at **Kliptown, 25–26 June 1955**, by about 3,000 delegates. **The police surrounded the gathering on the second day and took the names**, which is how the Treason Trial's evidence was gathered.

The Freedom Charter, 1955.front: The Charter against the 1996 Bill of Rights
The Freedom Charter, 1955.back: **Eight of ten clauses substantially delivered** — franchise, equality, housing, education, labour rights, assembly. **Two not**: the **nationalisation** clause, and the land clause's "shared among those who work it" (section 25 provides restitution, redistribution and tenure reform, with compensation). **That table is stage 1's third disagreement, and both sides are reading the same document.**

The Treason Trial.back: **156 arrested** in December 1956 — 105 African, 23 white, 21 Indian, 7 Coloured — charged with **high treason**, with the **Freedom Charter as the principal evidence**. **All acquitted**, 29 March 1961: the court found the state had failed to prove that the ANC had a policy of violence or was communist.

The Treason Trial.front: What the Treason Trial's failure taught the state
The Treason Trial.back: **That the courts were unreliable — so it stopped using them.** 1962: sabotage with reversed onus and minimum sentences. 1963: 90-day detention. 1967: section 6, indefinite, no court access. **A state that cannot convict its opponents in four years finds a procedure that does not require conviction.**

The PAC split, and 1959.front: Robert Sobukwe's definition of an African
The PAC split, and 1959.back: **Anyone who owes loyalty only to Africa and accepts majority rule** — more open than "Africa for the Africans" sounds, though the practice was more exclusive than the formulation. The PAC was founded on **6 April 1959 — Van Riebeeck's day.**

The PAC split, and 1959.front: The Africanist objection to the Freedom Charter
The PAC split, and 1959.back: **"All national groups shall have equal rights" concedes that South Africa contains distinct national groups** — which is apartheid's own separate-development premise. Plus: the Congress of Democrats as a white organisation inside the Alliance, and the Alliance's organisation into **separate racial congresses**, which institutionalised race while denying it.

Sharpeville, and the turn to armed strug.back: Police fired on a PAC anti-pass crowd at the police station: **69 killed** (8 women, 10 children), **over 180 wounded**, and **most of the dead were shot in the back** — which disposes of the self-defence account. **State of emergency 30 March, about 18,000 detained; the ANC and PAC banned 8 April.** Now the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

**16 December 1961 — the Day of the Vow**, Blood River's anniversary. **Sabotage, not terrorism**: installations chosen to avoid loss of life. **MK was constituted separately from the ANC** so that Luthuli's non-violent position was formally preserved — which let him accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo days before the first attacks.

**Militarily, very little** — MK never threatened the state's security. **Politically and symbolically, a great deal**: it established that the movement would not acquiesce, gave international supporters a cause, and brought Soviet and OAU backing that built the exile organisation. **So the "resistance won" account must rest on the mass movements of the 1970s and 1980s, not on MK's operations.**

Rivonia, and the silent decade.front: Mandela's statement from the dock, 20 April 1964
Rivonia, and the silent decade.back: *I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination… It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.* **Four hours, mostly explanation rather than appeal**, delivered on a charge that carried the death penalty.

Rivonia, and the silent decade.front: Why Rivonia was charged as sabotage, not treason
Rivonia, and the silent decade.back: **The Treason Trial's lesson.** The 1962 sabotage law carried the **death penalty**, **reversed the onus of proof**, and was far easier to prove. The state had learned.

**No significant organised internal opposition**: the ANC and PAC banned, leadership imprisoned or exiled, MK broken, *Poqo* broken, no legal African unions, the press constrained. What filled it: **exile politics under Tambo, Robben Island as the movement's university, the fastest economic growth in the country's history, and then Black Consciousness from 1968.**

Citizenship, 1970.back: **Every African South African assigned citizenship of a homeland**, whether or not they had ever been there — and **on that homeland's "independence" they ceased to be South African**. The four TBVC independences **denationalised about eight million people.** Fully reversed only in 1993–94.

*If our policy is taken to its full logical conclusion… there will be not one black man with South African citizenship.* **The responsible minister, in Hansard** — the policy's destination, stated by the government. It is why the "break at 1948" reading has force: no segregation government before 1948 proposed to denationalise the majority.

Citizenship, 1970.front: How denationalisation solved the demographic problem
Citizenship, 1970.back: **By redefining the denominator.** Counted as it was, the population was about 70% African; **excluding homeland citizens, there was a white plurality.** Official South African statistics of the late 1970s and 1980s **excluded TBVC citizens** — so any 1980s per-capita figure needs checking for which population it covers.

The 1960s boom, and the ceiling.front: Why the 1960s boom happened, and what ended it
The 1960s boom, and the ceiling.back: **Growth of 5.5–6% a year** — among the world's fastest — on political stability achieved by repression (**investment returned after 1963, once the state had visibly won**), cheap controlled labour, import substitution, foreign capital, state investment and gold. **It ended on the skills ceiling**: industrial growth needed skilled workers, and the colour bar, job reservation and Bantu Education forbade producing them.

The 1960s boom, and the ceiling.front: When apartheid's labour policy stopped being functional
The 1960s boom, and the ceiling.back: **Mining, to the 1940s: functional** — cheap unskilled migrant labour was exactly what was needed. **Manufacturing, from the 1960s: dysfunctional** — the skills the economy needed were the ones the policy forbade. **The liberal and revisionist traditions are describing different economies**, and the transition is in the 1960s.

The gold price was **freed in 1971** with the end of Bretton Woods and rose from $35 an ounce to several hundred by 1980 — **which postponed the reckoning by most of a decade and funded Total Strategy's military build-up**. Its decline through the 1980s is part of why that decade was terminal.

Black Consciousness, and Biko.back: **All those who are by law or tradition politically, economically and socially discriminated against and who identify themselves as a unit in the struggle** — so it **includes African, Coloured and Indian** and **excludes collaborators**. A **political** category, not a racial one. "Non-white" was rejected, because it defines people by what they are not.

**The deepest injury was to the mind** — *the most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed*. So psychological liberation is **prior** to political liberation, and **it can begin immediately, without an organisation the state can ban.** Which is why it could grow in a decade when organised politics was impossible.

Detained 18 August under section 6; **severe head injuries** in interrogation; **driven about 1,100 km to Pretoria, naked, in the back of a Land Rover**; died on a cell floor, aged 30. **The inquest found no one responsible.** In 1997 five security policemen admitted involvement to the TRC and **amnesty was refused — and they were never prosecuted.**

The Durban strikes, 1973.back: **About 100,000 workers out across 150+ factories** in three months, **with no union and deliberately no identifiable leaders** — because named leaders meant prosecutions, African unions having no legal standing. **Employers conceded wage increases**, and the independent union movement dates from here.

The Durban strikes, 1973.front: The 1973 strikes as the control experiment
The Durban strikes, 1973.back: **Real black wages were roughly flat from 1911 to 1970 and rose substantially from 1973.** What changed was not the market — it had been tight before — but **the workers' capacity to act**. Which establishes that the sixty flat years were produced by the suppression of organisation.

Soweto, 1976.back: Between 10,000 and 20,000 Soweto school students marched against the **Afrikaans-medium directive**; police opened fire; **Hastings Ndlovu and Hector Pieterson** among the first killed. **Sam Nzima's photograph** went worldwide. The **Cillié Commission's official toll for the uprising was 575, of whom 134 were under eighteen** — generally regarded as an undercount.

Soweto, 1976.front: Why 1976 mattered more than its casualty figure
Soweto, 1976.back: **Thousands of young people left the country and joined MK** — and the exile movement, decapitated in 1964 with no internal base, **acquired a generation**. The MK and underground of the 1980s, and much of the post-1994 leadership, is the class of '76. **And the townships were never administratively governed again.**

The security state: detention, torture,.back: **The documented number of people who died in security detention between 1963 and 1990.** The official explanations recur — fell down stairs, slipped in the shower, jumped from a window, hanged himself — and **in virtually every case before 1990 the inquest found no one responsible.** Timol's finding was reversed in 2017; Aggett's inquest reopened in 2019–20.

**Adriaan Vlok, Minister of Law and Order, told the TRC that he ordered the bombing of the South African Council of Churches' headquarters on PW Botha's instruction.** Not an allegation — an admission on the record.

The security state: detention, torture,.front: Why the apartheid-era record is unusually good
The security state: detention, torture,.back: **The TRC's amnesty mechanism required full disclosure in exchange for amnesty** — so perpetrators described their own acts. Plus De Kock's trial, reopened inquests and declassified documents. **And almost nobody was prosecuted**: roughly 300 TRC referrals produced very few prosecutions, which is stage 11's parallel with Zondo.

Wiehahn and Riekert, 1979.front: Wiehahn, and why the co-option failed
Wiehahn and Riekert, 1979.back: **1979: African unions recognised and job reservation abolished** — the state expecting registration to mean regulation, bureaucratisation and the separation of industrial from political. Instead legal standing gave the unions **open organisation, enforceable recognition agreements, stop-order dues, protected shop stewards and the Industrial Court**. Membership went from tens of thousands to over a million; **COSATU adopted the Freedom Charter in 1987.**

**Ease controls on urban Africans with section 10 rights; tighten them on everyone else** — creating a black urban middle class with something to lose. It failed because **the township was not divided that way**: the 1984 rent increases fell on insiders, and the revolt they started was township-wide.

**An authoritarian state reforming under pressure frequently gives its opponents the organisational capacity they lacked.** The concession that relieves an economic constraint can create a political one.

Total Strategy, and PW Botha.back: **"Total onslaught" met by a "total strategy"** — and the doctrine's one accurate insight was **80% political, 20% military**, which is why Total Strategy included real reform. Institutionally: the **State Security Council elevated above cabinet** and the **National Security Management System**, a parallel state of Joint Management Centres.

Major reform had been briefed to foreign governments and bankers. **Botha was defiant instead.** The rand collapsed, **foreign banks refused to roll over short-term loans, and South Africa declared a debt standstill in late August** — cut off from international capital markets for the rest of the decade. **The economic turning point of apartheid**, and more important than the formal sanctions.

Sustained SADF operations in **Angola**, support for **RENAMO in Mozambique**, raids on Lesotho, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana and Swaziland. **It killed very large numbers and wrecked two economies for a generation** — a Commonwealth study put the cost to the frontline states in the tens of billions of dollars. Usually a footnote in South African accounts.

The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the.back: **178 white, 85 Coloured, 45 Indian members; Africans excluded entirely.** The white chamber outnumbered the other two combined in any joint sitting, by construction. **"Own affairs"** covered education, housing and welfare; **"general affairs"** — including African affairs — were decided jointly. **1984 turnout: about 31% Coloured, 20% Indian.**

Launched **20 August 1983** at Mitchells Plain to oppose the tricameral constitution: **a front of around 400 and later 600+ affiliates**, each keeping its own identity — **very hard to ban**. Charterist, and effectively the ANC's internal expression. *"UDF unites, apartheid divides."*

The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the.front: Why the Black Local Authorities revolted
The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the.back: The 1982 Act created township councils with **no rateable tax base** (the 1923 Act's financing rule, and the Group Areas city), so **their only possible policy was raising rents** — in communities that regarded them as collaborators and voted at 10–20%. **The Vaal Triangle rent increases of 3 September 1984 began six years of revolt.**

The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the.front: What the TRC found about the ANC and the UDF
The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the.back: **Responsible for gross human rights violations** — including the killing of suspected collaborators and **necklacing** — which the ANC accepted a share of. Street committees were in places genuine local self-government under pressure, and in places the people's courts became arbitrary and violent. **An account of the 1980s that omits it is not honest.**

States of emergency, 1985-1989.back: **20 July 1985** in 36 districts; **12 June 1986 nationwide**, renewed annually to 1990. **About 25,000 detained in the first year** of the 1986 emergency, including thousands of children. Security forces indemnified; rule by proclamation; **and reporting of "unrest" and filming of security action banned — which ended television coverage.**

**The state could not be overthrown** (MK never came close) · **the townships could not be governed** (administration had collapsed; emergency rule is not government) · **the economy could not grow** (no credit, falling gold, capital flight, skills ceiling) · **the movement could not win** militarily · **and could not be defeated**, because every repression produced recruits. **Both sides' best alternative to agreement had become worse than agreement.**

A Commonwealth mission exploring a negotiated settlement was **in the country when the SADF raided Harare, Lusaka and Gaborone on 19 May 1986**, ending the mission. The clearest evidence of the securocrats' ascendancy.

Why it ended: the four accounts.front: Why apartheid ended — the four accounts
Why it ended: the four accounts.back: **Internal resistance** (ungovernable townships, a million-strong union movement) · **economic failure** (the 1985 debt standstill, falling gold, sanctions, the skills ceiling) · **the end of the Cold War** (the Wall fell in November 1989; de Klerk spoke in February 1990) · **an elite decision** (secret talks from 1985–87; negotiate from strength and secure property, pensions and the civil service).

Why it ended: the four accounts.front: The composite account of why apartheid ended
Why it ended: the four accounts.back: **A stalemate made negotiation necessary; economic failure made it urgent; the Cold War's end made it safe; and the National Party chose the timing to negotiate from strength.** Each account supplies one element and none is sufficient alone — and note that the accounts rank differently on explaining the **timing** and the **necessity**.

Why it ended: the four accounts.front: Why the "why it ended" question is political
