Why it ended: the four accounts.back: **If resistance won**, the settlement was a victory earned. **If the economy failed**, it was a managed handover and the economic order was never defeated. **If the Cold War ended it**, South Africans were least the authors of their own liberation. **If the elite chose it**, the terms were set by the outgoing power — the strongest form of the "compromise" case.

2 February 1990.back: De Klerk's speech: **the ANC, PAC, SACP and 33 other organisations unbanned**, political prisoners released, restrictions lifted on 374 people, the death penalty suspended, and a commitment to **negotiate a new constitution**. **Mandela released nine days later.** It did **not** concede majority rule — de Klerk's position was "power-sharing".

**Political deaths 1990–94: about 14,000** — **more than in the whole preceding decade** of insurrection and emergency. More people were killed during the negotiations than during the states of emergency.

Why de Klerk did it.front: The National Party's eight negotiating objectives
Why de Klerk did it.back: **Property rights ✔ · civil service security and pensions ✔ · amnesty (partly) · a market economy and Reserve Bank independence ✔ · federalism (partly) · no prosecutions ✔ in practice · group rights and minority vetoes ✘ · power-sharing ✔ for five years only.** Six of eight broadly — and the two that failed are the two that would have preserved the party.

**Group rights, proposed by the architects of group classification, could not be presented as minority protection**; every foreign government backed one person one vote; and **the ANC did not need to concede** — its alternative was bad and the NP's was worse. Recognising groups was apartheid's own premise, so the ANC could not concede it without conceding fifty years of argument.

Mandela's release, and the first talks.back: **The ANC suspended the armed struggle**, in exchange for progress on prisoners, exiles and security legislation. Contested internally as surrendering leverage before anything was secured. **The consequence: when the violence rose, the ANC had given up its only coercive instrument and had mass action left.**

**Exile** (Tambo in Lusaka, who had a stroke in 1989), **prison** (Mandela), and **internal** (the UDF and the mass movement). Plus no branches, no offices and no membership rolls in South Africa after thirty years. **The UDF was dissolved in 1991** and absorbed — a decision argued about ever since.

The violence, and the third force.front: What was established about the "third force"
The violence, and the third force.back: **Police secretly funded Inkatha** ("Inkathagate", 1991) · **the SADF trained an Inkatha paramilitary force in the Caprivi** (Operation Marion, 1986) · **the Goldstone Commission found police and SADF involvement** · **the Steyn Report (Dec 1992) led to 23 senior officers being dismissed or retired** · and the TRC found the state accountable. **Networks within the security forces, not a single body under central command.**

The violence, and the third force.front: The three elements of the transition violence
The violence, and the third force.back: **A real political conflict** (ANC/UDF against Inkatha) · **a real ethnic and institutional dimension** (rural KwaZulu authority, the single-sex migrant hostels inside settled townships) · **and state covert action that armed and amplified it.** Any version with fewer than three elements is incomplete. **The TRC found both the state and the ANC responsible for gross violations in this period.**

CODESA, Boipatong and the breakdown.back: **The percentage required to adopt the final constitution: the ANC wanted two-thirds, the government 75%.** A 75% threshold gives a party with 26% of the seats a **veto over the constitution** — group rights by a procedural route. Both sides understood it exactly, and CODESA II broke up over it in May 1992.

CODESA, Boipatong and the breakdown.front: Why the breakdown improved the settlement
CODESA, Boipatong and the breakdown.back: CODESA's nineteen-party consensus format had stalled. **Boipatong and Bisho forced a bilateral channel — Ramaphosa and Meyer — which could trade across issues**, and the Record of Understanding followed. The cost: **it marginalised the IFP**, which allied with the white right.

The sunset clauses.back: *We are not dealing with a defeated enemy.* **The SACP general secretary's 1992 article** proposed: **a government of national unity for a fixed period · regional government · amnesty · and job security and pensions for existing civil servants.** Adopted by the ANC NEC in November 1992 and became the interim constitution's framework.

**With a sunset: power-sharing in the GNU** — and it expired. **Without: property rights, Reserve Bank independence, the apartheid debt, civil service jobs and pensions, and amnesty.** **The political concessions expired and the economic and administrative ones did not** — which is the sharpest observation in the third disagreement.

The right wing, and Chris Hani.back: A former **Chief of the SADF** leading the Afrikaner Volksfront, who claimed to be able to mobilise tens of thousands of trained men. After the **Bophuthatswana debacle** — AWB men shooting at civilians and three killed on camera — **he broke with the AWB and registered the Freedom Front days before the deadline**, taking his constituency into the election. **That is why there was no Afrikaner insurgency.**

**SACP general secretary and former MK chief of staff**, the most popular ANC figure after Mandela among township youth, shot by **Janusz Waluś** with **Clive Derby-Lewis**, a Conservative Party MP. **Mandela's televised address held the country.** And **the ANC used the crisis to force an election date** — 27 April 1994, announced that June.

The Multi-Party Negotiating Forum.back: The MPNF's decision rule: **not unanimity and not a defined majority, but a chairs' judgement that enough weight supported a proposal** — which in practice meant **if the ANC and the NP agreed, there was sufficient consensus**. The objection: two parties decide. The defence: unanimity hands a veto to the least willing, and the Freedom Alliance opposed the central question.

The interim constitution, agreed by an **unelected multi-party forum** and then **passed by the tricameral apartheid Parliament** in December 1993 — **so the old Parliament legislated itself out of existence.** That legal continuity meant contracts, debts, property titles and judgments survived, which is the third disagreement in constitutional form.

The interim constitution.back: **Nine provinces** (replacing four provinces and ten homelands) · **a justiciable Bill of Rights and a Constitutional Court** · **the GNU** (20+ seats for cabinet posts, 80+ for a deputy president, five years) · **the Constitutional Assembly** (both houses sitting together, two years, two-thirds, bound by 34 principles and certified by the Court) · **section 236's civil service guarantee**.

*…there is a need for understanding but not for vengeance, a need for reparation but not for retaliation, a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation.* And then: **amnesty shall be granted for acts associated with political objectives, with Parliament to legislate the mechanism.** **It does not grant amnesty — it requires a mechanism**, which left "conditional or blanket" to a Parliament the ANC would control.

The thirty-four principles.front: Why the Constitutional Principles were the key invention
The thirty-four principles.back: **The content decided by an elected assembly** (satisfying the democratic claim) **within limits agreed before the election by all parties** (satisfying the minorities) **and a court enforcing the limits** (so the guarantee is justiciable). No comparable mechanism had been used anywhere.

**The powers and functions of the provinces in the final constitution shall not be "substantially less than or substantially inferior to" those in the interim constitution** — the federalists' central guarantee, and **the principle the Constitutional Court used to refuse certification on 6 September 1996.**

**A court told a democratically elected constitutional assembly that its constitution did not comply and had to be redone** — on provincial powers (Principle XVIII), the amendment procedure, local government, the lockout asymmetry and the independence of the Public Protector and Auditor-General. **The Assembly complied.** Certified 4 December; signed at **Sharpeville on 10 December 1996**.

The TEC, and the run-up.back: From December 1993: a **multi-party body sitting alongside the government** that **could block action prejudicing free political activity or a free and fair election**, with sub-councils on **law and order, defence, foreign affairs, finance, regional government and intelligence**. It appointed administrators when Bophuthatswana and Ciskei collapsed.

The TEC, and the run-up.front: How the 1994 election ran without a voters' roll
The TEC, and the run-up.back: **None had ever existed for the majority** — so no registration. **Anyone with an identity document could vote at any station**, with **indelible ink on the thumb** as the safeguard against double voting. About **80 million ballots printed** and 200,000 staff recruited in a few months. Which is why it ran over several days.

**The December 1993 IMF facility** (about $850m, with policy commitments) and **the GATT Uruguay Round tariff commitments** — both agreed by **the outgoing government**, binding the incoming one, with the ANC informed through the TEC rather than deciding.

The last crises, and the IFP's entry.back: The IFP was not contesting the election until **eight days before it**, after **Kissinger and Carrington's mediation failed** and **Washington Okumu's succeeded** — in exchange for constitutional recognition of the Zulu monarchy and further consideration of provincial powers. **The ballots were already printed, so IFP stickers were affixed to eighty million of them by hand.**

Bombs in central Johannesburg (nine killed), Germiston and at the airport in the election's final week — **about 31 killed in total**. **It failed completely**: turnout was not reduced, and **the perpetrators were identified, tried and convicted**, which broke the AWB as an organisation.

ANC security guards at the party's headquarters fired on an IFP march, **killing eight there** and more elsewhere that day. **Mandela said publicly that he had authorised the defence of Shell House.** Contested, investigated by Goldstone, and **no successful prosecution**. The incident most often raised against the ANC's conduct in the transition.

27 April 1994.back: **ANC 62.65% (252 seats) · NP 20.39% (82) · IFP 10.54% (43) · FF 2.17% (9) · DP 1.73% (7) · PAC 1.25% (5) · ACDP 0.45% (2).** About **19.7 million votes, roughly 86% turnout.** The ANC won seven provinces; **the NP won the Western Cape and the IFP KwaZulu-Natal.**

**The threshold for adopting the final constitution was two-thirds — 66.7%.** The ANC fell about four points short, **so it could not write the constitution alone** and the NP and IFP had real leverage in the Constitutional Assembly. **The arithmetic legitimated the constitutional process**, which was luck.

**Widely regarded as unreliable** — stations inaccessible, the count disputed, and the figures ultimately **agreed politically as much as established**. All parties accepted it because a contested provincial count was judged more dangerous than an imperfect one. An uncomfortable fact about the founding election, and not a hidden one.

The Government of National Unity.back: **Mandela president; Mbeki and de Klerk deputy presidents; cabinet ANC 18, NP 6, IFP 3** — with **no formal veto**, which the NP had wanted. **The NP announced its withdrawal on 9 May 1996, the day after the final constitution was adopted** without power-sharing, and left on 30 June. **The IFP stayed in cabinet until 2004.**

The Government of National Unity.front: Who held Finance in the first democratic government
The Government of National Unity.back: **Derek Keys**, the outgoing government's finance minister, **stayed on** — then **Chris Liebenberg**, a banker — and only in **1996 Trevor Manuel**, the first ANC finance minister. For the first two years of democracy the ministry was run by people from the old order or from banking.

**RDP**: redistribution driving growth; developed with COSATU and the civics; an office in the Presidency — **closed in March 1996**. **GEAR**, June 1996: growth enabling redistribution, deficit reduction, developed substantially in confidence and presented as **non-negotiable**. **Two months after the final constitution was adopted.**

The Constitutional Assembly.back: **The National Assembly and Senate sitting together — 490 members**, chaired by **Ramaphosa** with **Leon Wessels** deputy, two years, and **about two million public submissions**. Adopted **8 May 1996 by 421 to 2 with 10 abstentions** — **the IFP had withdrawn in early 1995 and did not return**, so the final constitution was written without the party governing KwaZulu-Natal.

The Constitutional Assembly.front: What each feature of the 1996 Constitution prevents
The Constitutional Assembly.back: **Constitutional supremacy** — parliamentary sovereignty produced apartheid. **A justiciable Bill of Rights** — entrenched clauses did not hold in the 1950s. **A Judicial Service Commission** — the Appeal Court was packed in 1955. **Chapter 9 institutions** — nothing had held the executive to account. **Socio-economic rights** — the dispossession was material. **Section 25's land mandate** — 1913 and 1936.

The economic settlement.front: Where the economic settlement was decided
The economic settlement.back: **Negotiated with the NP**: property rights, Reserve Bank independence, civil service guarantees. **Inherited or pre-committed by the outgoing government**: the apartheid debt, the Uruguay Round tariffs, the December 1993 IMF terms. **The ANC's own, after 1990**: abandoning nationalisation, shelving MERG, adopting GEAR. **So "outnegotiated at Kempton Park" is not quite right.**

**The Reserve Bank's primary object is to protect the value of the currency… and it must perform its functions independently.** Monetary policy removed from elected control, constitutionally. The SARB is also **one of very few central banks with private shareholders**. Nationalising it and amending its mandate are standing ANC resolutions never implemented.

The economic settlement.front: The odious-debt argument, and the answer
The economic settlement.back: **That debt incurred by an illegitimate regime to suppress its own population should not bind its victims** — argued by Jubilee South Africa. **The answer: most creditors were South African pension funds and insurers**, so repudiation would have destroyed the savings of the workers and civil servants the new government represented. Both are true.

The TRC: design and mandate.back: **Full disclosure** · the act **associated with a political objective** · and **proportionality**. So the bargain is **truth for amnesty**, individually and conditionally — **not the blanket amnesty the security establishment had expected.** It is why the apartheid-era record is as detailed as it is.

The TRC: design and mandate.front: The TRC's mandate, and its limit
The TRC: design and mandate.back: **"Gross violations of human rights" — killing, abduction, torture, severe ill-treatment — between 1 March 1960 and 10 May 1994, by all sides.** **Not covered: the ordinary operation of apartheid** — removals, pass laws, Bantu Education, Group Areas, the migrant system. **The commission acknowledged this about itself**: most of apartheid's harm was lawful and administrative, so a commission investigating murder will not find the Group Areas Act.

The TRC: design and mandate.front: AZAPO v President of the RSA (1996)
The TRC: design and mandate.back: **The families of Biko, Mxenge and Ribeiro challenged the amnesty** as depriving them of the right to have a dispute settled by a court. **The Constitutional Court upheld it**: the postamble authorised amnesty, and without it the truth would not emerge. **The Court told Biko's family they could not sue or prosecute, because the country needed the truth more.**

The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d.back: **About 21,000 victim statements; about 2,000 public testimonies. 7,112 amnesty applications; 849 granted — about 12%; over 5,000 refused.** Report volumes 1–5 in 1998, 6–7 in 2003. **The 12% grant rate corrects the impression that it traded blanket amnesty for truth.**

The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d.front: Both parties tried to censor the TRC report
The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d.back: **The ANC went to court in October 1998 to stop publication of the findings against it — and lost.** **De Klerk obtained an interdict that removed a passage about him.** One failed and one partly succeeded, and the report was published with the ANC findings in. The best short evidence of the commission's independence.

The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d.front: The TRC's two failures, and whose they were
The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d.back: **Reparations**: recommended about R21,700 a year for six years per victim (~R3bn); **the government paid a once-off R30,000 to about 16,000 people, from 2003** — roughly a sixth, once. **Prosecutions**: about **300 referrals, very few prosecutions**. **Both were decisions by the democratic government, not by the commission** — and the bargain upheld in *AZAPO* was that victims gave up legal claims for truth **and reparation**.

What was traded.back: **The "victory" case is about the constitutional settlement and is largely right about it** — franchise, Bill of Rights, constitutional supremacy, group rights defeated, power-sharing expired, no civil war. **The "compromise" case is about the economic trajectory and is largely right about that** — property, debt, the Reserve Bank, tariffs, pensions, amnesty, GEAR. **They are not arguing about the same thing.**

What was traded.front: What can and cannot be settled about the transition
What was traded.back: **Checkable**: what was on the table (the CODESA and MPNF records, the O'Malley interviews taken as it happened), the state's real condition in 1992, what the ANC asked for and was refused, whether nationalisation was abandoned under pressure or by persuasion. **Not checkable**: whether a different course would have produced capital flight. **The terms are establishable; the alternative is not.**

How to read a constitution.back: **The state must respect, protect, promote and fulfil the rights in the Bill of Rights.** **Respect** — do not infringe. **Protect** — prevent others from infringing. **Promote** — create the conditions. **Fulfil** — take positive steps to deliver. Which is why South African rights law reaches private conduct and requires state action.

Interpretation: a court **must** promote the values underlying an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom; **must consider international law**; **may consider foreign law**. And **39(2)**: every court interpreting legislation or developing the common law must promote the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.

The founding provisions.back: **(a) Human dignity, the achievement of equality, the advancement of human rights and freedoms. (b) Non-racialism and non-sexism. (c) Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law. (d) Universal adult suffrage, a national common voters roll, regular elections and a multi-party system.** Every clause is a specific repudiation of stages 3 to 5.

The founding provisions.front: Why section 1 is harder to amend than the Bill of Rights
The founding provisions.back: **Section 1 needs 75% of the National Assembly plus six of nine provinces; the Bill of Rights needs two-thirds plus six provinces.** A government that could amend the supremacy clause could then do anything — so the values and constitutional supremacy are protected above the specific rights. **No party has ever had 75%.**

Since the **Eighteenth Amendment, signed 19 July 2023**, which added **South African Sign Language** to the eleven. Section 6 also requires the state to promote the **Khoi, Nama and San** languages — which has been very thinly honoured.

Supremacy, and what it changed.back: *This Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic; **law or conduct** inconsistent with it is invalid, and the obligations imposed by it must be fulfilled.* **"Conduct"** is the word that makes it bite on administration — a president's decision, a minister's appointment, a parliamentary procedure.

**"All constitutional obligations must be performed diligently and without delay."** The sleeper provision — used to compel the state to act on appointments not made, reports not filed and decisions not taken, and the textual basis for much of the litigation that has substituted for administration.

Supremacy, and what it changed.front: Litigation as a substitute for government
Supremacy, and what it changed.back: South Africa has **strong constitutional law and a weak state** — so civil society sues the state to compel what it has already undertaken: textbooks, antiretrovirals, emergency housing, sanitation. **Read as success**, the mechanism works. **Read as failure**, a state that must be sued to supply textbooks is not functioning, and courts are a poor way to run a schools system.

Equality — section 9.back: **A measure that genuinely satisfies 9(2) is not "discrimination" to be excused — it is part of equality itself.** *Minister of Finance v Van Heerden* (2004). The test: does it **target persons disadvantaged by unfair discrimination**, is it **designed to protect or advance them**, and does it **promote the achievement of equality**. So the constitutional objection to BEE does not run — though policy objections may.

**1.** Is there differentiation with a rational connection to a legitimate purpose? **2.** Does it amount to discrimination — **automatically if on a listed ground**; otherwise only if based on attributes that can impair dignity. **3.** Is it unfair — **presumed unfair on a listed ground** (s9(5)). **4.** If unfair, can it be justified under **section 36**?

Dignity, life, and the person.back: The injury of apartheid was **classification, humiliation, the pass, the removal, the bench** — not principally a restriction of liberty. A liberty-centred constitution would struggle to name that; a dignity-centred one names it exactly. **Following the German Basic Law**, and it is why South African rights law is comfortable with positive obligations.

The Constitutional Court's first major judgment: **the death penalty abolished**, on the rights to life and dignity and the prohibition on cruel punishment. **Public opinion strongly favoured it, then and now** — and the Court held that the question is what the Constitution requires, not what the majority wants. The founding judgment of South African constitutionalism.

Section 12(1)(c) — freedom from violence **"from either public or private sources"** — used to develop the common law of delict so that **the state could be liable for failing to protect a woman from a known dangerous man**. The constitutional root of the state's obligations on gender-based violence.

Expression, and its limits.front: Section 16(2) is an exclusion, not a limitation
Expression, and its limits.back: The right **"does not extend to"** propaganda for war, **incitement of *imminent* violence**, or advocacy of hatred based on **race, ethnicity, gender or religion** that **constitutes incitement to cause harm**. So there is **nothing to justify under section 36** — the speech is simply outside the right, which makes the definitions decisive. Note: **not sexual orientation, not disability.**

**The "hurtful" limb of PEPUDA section 10 struck down as overbroad**; the rest upheld and reformulated. So **hate speech requires harm or incitement to harm, or the promotion of hatred — not merely being hurtful.** PEPUDA may prohibit more than s16(2) excludes, as a justified section 36 limitation.

Assembly, association, and political rig.back: **Criminalising the convening of a gathering without notice held unconstitutional.** The notice obligation under the Regulation of Gatherings Act remains; the criminal offence does not. The Court noted that **the people most likely to protest without a lawyer's notice are those with least access to one.**

**It does not specify an electoral system.** The Constitution requires free, fair, regular elections, a national common voters roll and results that are in general proportional — **but closed national party lists are a statutory choice, not a constitutional requirement**, chosen in 1994 for an election with no voters' roll. It could be changed by ordinary legislation.

The Electoral Act was **unconstitutional in requiring candidates to stand only through parties** — so **independent candidates** must be able to contest the National Assembly and provincial legislatures. Produced the **Electoral Amendment Act of 2023**, used in 2024 with negligible success, because the seat allocation makes an independent's path very hard.

Property — section 25.back: Compensation must be **just and equitable**, reflecting an equitable balance, having regard to: **(a) current use · (b) the history of acquisition and use · (c) market value · (d) the extent of direct state investment and subsidy · (e) the purpose of the expropriation.** **Market value is one of five factors, not the measure.** So both "without compensation" and "at market value" depart from the text.

Property — section 25.front: The land reform half of section 25
Property — section 25.back: **25(5)** redistribution — the state must take reasonable measures to enable equitable access to land. **25(6)** tenure security for those whose tenure is insecure from past racial laws. **25(7)** restitution for dispossession **after 19 June 1913**. **25(8)** no provision of the section may impede land, water and related reform. **25(9)** Parliament must enact the tenure legislation.

Property — section 25.front: What the Constitutional Court has not decided about section 25
Property — section 25.back: **It has never decided a section 25(3) compensation case.** Land Claims Court decisions have held that just and equitable compensation can be below market value. So **the most consequential question in South African property law is open** — which is what the failed 2021 amendment would have settled.

The Expropriation Act, and the failed am.back: Signed **23 January 2025**, replacing the apartheid-era 1975 Act. **Section 12(3) permits nil compensation in narrow specified circumstances**, limited to land expropriated **in the public interest** — abandoned land, land held purely for speculation, land where the state already holds an interest. **As of 14 October 2026 it has not been brought into force** — no commencement proclamation. *Check before relying on it.*

The Expropriation Act, and the failed am.front: Why the section 25 amendment failed, December 2021
The Expropriation Act, and the failed am.back: **204 votes of the 267 needed.** The DA and others voted against because it went too far; **the EFF voted against because it did not go far enough** — it wanted **state custodianship of all land**. The amendment failed because its opponents on both sides outnumbered its supporters.

The Expropriation Act, and the failed am.front: The fact that reframes the land argument
The Expropriation Act, and the failed am.back: **The state has had the power to expropriate for land reform since 1994** — sections 25(2) and 25(4)(a) — **and has essentially not used it.** Land has been acquired overwhelmingly by purchase on a willing-buyer basis. So whether the constraint has been the Constitution or the state's own capacity and choices is a live question, and the record points substantially at the second.

Housing — section 26.back: A programme must be **comprehensive, coherent and co-ordinated**; **balanced and flexible**, with **short, medium and long-term** provision; allocate responsibilities and resources clearly; **not exclude a significant segment of society**; and **respond to those in desperate need**. The state's housing programme failed on the last: it had nothing for a family evicted today.

**Minimum core**: the right has a minimum content the state must deliver immediately, with courts determining it. **Reasonableness**: the state must have a reasonable programme, which courts review. **The Court chose reasonableness in *Grootboom*** — citing its lack of information and institutional competence, and the text's "available resources" and "progressive realisation". **Irene Grootboom died in 2008 without a house.**

**A city must provide temporary accommodation to those it evicts, and cannot plead a budget it failed to plan for.** A city that knows evictions happen and budgets nothing for them has not acted reasonably — which converted a planning failure into a legal obligation.

Health, food, water, social security.back: The state's restriction of **nevirapine** to two pilot sites per province was **unreasonable** under section 27; it was ordered to remove the restrictions and facilitate the drug's use throughout the public health system. **The programme that followed is now the largest antiretroviral programme in the world** — and the delay's excess mortality runs into the hundreds of thousands.

**Soobramoney (1997)**: dialysis rationing upheld — s27(3) covers a sudden catastrophe, not ongoing treatment. **TAC (2002)**: the state lost; mandatory relief granted. **Mazibuko (2009)**: the Court **would not quantify "sufficient water"** — determining a numerical entitlement is a legislative and executive function. The three mark reasonableness review's reach and its limits.

Health, food, water, social security.front: Khosa v Minister of Social Development (2004)
Health, food, water, social security.back: Restricting social grants to citizens, **excluding permanent residents, was unconstitutional** — section 27(1)(c) says **"everyone"**. The reference point for every argument about non-citizens' access to services: where the text says everyone, citizenship is not a permissible filter without justification.

Children, and education.front: Why basic education is the strongest socio-economic right
Children, and education.back: **Section 29(1)(a) carries no "available resources" and no "progressive realisation"** — unlike 29(1)(b) for further education, and unlike sections 26 and 27. ***Juma Musjid* (2011)** confirmed it is **immediately realisable and unqualified** — which is the basis of the textbook, furniture, infrastructure and sanitation litigation.

**"A child's best interests are of paramount importance in every matter concerning the child."** "Paramount" treated as a strong word — it applies in custody, **in sentencing a primary caregiver** (*S v M*, 2007), in eviction, in immigration and in schooling.

**Michael Komape, aged five, drowned in a school pit latrine in Limpopo in 2014.** Years of litigation on liability, damages and the state's obligations followed. **Eradicating school pit latrines has been declared government policy for a decade and is still incomplete.**

Language, culture and community.front: How group rights were refused while group life was protected
Language, culture and community.back: **Sections 30 and 31 confer rights on *persons*, not communities** — "everyone", "persons belonging to". **No community has standing as such, a veto, a reserved seat or a territorial claim.** Membership is "of their choice" — the inverse of the Population Registration Act. And both sections may not be exercised inconsistently with the Bill of Rights.

**Official**: the colonial codification of the 1920s, fixed, and systematically more patriarchal than the practice it recorded. **Living**: the community's actual current practice, which develops. ***Bhe* (2004)** struck down codified male primogeniture; ***Shilubana* (2008)** held that **a community's own decision to develop its custom is valid** — which is the answer to the charge that constitutionalism overrides African law.

Information, and administrative justice.back: Administrative action must be **lawful** (within the power conferred, used for its purpose), **reasonable** (rationally connected, not so unreasonable no reasonable decision-maker could reach it), and **procedurally fair** (notice, a hearing, an unbiased decision-maker, reasons). Plus **33(2)**: written reasons on request where rights are adversely affected.

Information, and administrative justice.front: PAJA against the principle of legality
Information, and administrative justice.back: **PAJA** governs **administrative action** — with a 180-day limit and listed grounds. **The principle of legality**, derived from the rule of law in section 1, governs **all exercises of public power that are not administrative action** — executive and policy decisions, a president's appointments. Its core requirement is **rationality**, and the state capture litigation runs almost entirely on it.

The **public interest override**: disclosure must be granted despite a refusal ground if the record reveals **a substantial contravention of the law or an imminent and serious public safety or environmental risk**, and the public interest in disclosure clearly outweighs the harm. The provision investigative journalism relies on.

Courts, and the rights of the accused.back: An arrested person must be **brought before a court as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 48 hours after the arrest.** Against stage 5: 90-day detention, 180-day detention, and section 6 of the Terrorism Act's indefinite incommunicado detention with no court able to pronounce on it.

Evidence obtained in violation of a right **must be excluded if its admission would render the trial unfair or otherwise be detrimental to the administration of justice.** **Not automatic exclusion** — the court weighs it, which is deliberately more flexible than the American rule.

The limitation clause — section 36.back: **(a) the nature of the right · (b) the importance of the purpose of the limitation · (c) the nature and extent of the limitation · (d) the relation between the limitation and its purpose · (e) less restrictive means.** Reasonable and justifiable **in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom** — and the factors are not exhaustive.

The limitation clause — section 36.front: "Only in terms of law of general application"
The limitation clause — section 36.back: The threshold requirement, and it does more work than the five factors. **A statute, regulation, by-law or the common law qualifies. A policy, circular, instruction, practice or discretionary decision does not** — so a right infringed by one of those **cannot be saved by section 36 at all.** Which is why much litigation against the state succeeds without reaching the weighing.

States of emergency — section 37.back: **Only by Act of Parliament**, only when **the life of the nation is threatened**, **prospective only**, **21 days** then a National Assembly extension, **60% for subsequent extensions**, **any competent court may review the declaration**, **no indemnity for unlawful acts**, and **a Table of Non-Derogable Rights** — with **dignity and life absolutely non-derogable**.

States of emergency — section 37.front: Why section 37 has never been used
States of emergency — section 37.back: **The Covid lockdowns of 2020–22 ran under the Disaster Management Act, not section 37** — declared **by a minister** on 15 March 2020, extended **monthly by ministerial notice** for more than two years, with **no parliamentary approval requirement and no non-derogable rights table**. The most extensive restriction of rights in democratic South Africa was imposed under a statute with fewer safeguards than the emergency clause.

Enforcement, standing and remedies.back: **"Anyone acting in the public interest"** may approach a court alleging a rights infringement. **Most legal systems require a personal interest; South Africa does not for constitutional cases** — which is why its public interest litigation sector exists, and why a constitutional defect does not go unchallenged merely because its victims cannot litigate.

In constitutional litigation against the state, **a private litigant who loses should not ordinarily pay the state's costs.** Without it the ordinary loser-pays rule would make public interest litigation prohibitively risky. **With section 38(d), it is why the sector exists.**

A court **must** declare invalid law or conduct inconsistent with the Constitution, and **may make any order that is just and equitable** — including **limiting retrospectivity** and **suspending the invalidity** to let the legislature fix the defect. The developed remedies: severance, **reading-in**, reading-down, mandatory orders, **structural interdicts** (do it, and report back), constitutional damages, and personal costs orders against officials.

Three spheres, and co-operative governme.back: Section 40: national, provincial and local government are **"distinctive, interdependent and interrelated" spheres**. The word was chosen to avoid hierarchy — **a municipality is not a creature of the province; its powers come from the Constitution.**

**Schedule 4 (concurrent)** holds the real work — health, education, housing, welfare, agriculture, transport. **Schedule 5 (exclusive provincial)** is short and minor — liquor licences, provincial roads, abattoirs, provincial museums. **So a province is largely an implementing agency with legislative powers it rarely uses**, spending enormous budgets. Whether nine are worth their cost is a live argument.

**Section 100**: the national executive may intervene in a province failing an executive obligation, including by assuming responsibility for it. **Section 139**: a province may intervene in a municipality, including by **dissolving the council and appointing an administrator** — used on dozens of municipalities, and the record is that it rarely fixes them.

The courts, and Chapter 9.back: **The Chief Justice and Deputy Chief Justice**: the President appoints **after consulting** the JSC and party leaders — not binding. **All other judges**: the President appoints **on the advice of** the JSC — binding. So the Chief Justice's appointment is substantially the President's choice.

**23 members**: the Chief Justice, the SCA President, a Judge President, the Minister of Justice, two advocates, two attorneys, one law teacher, **six National Assembly members (at least three from opposition parties)**, four NCOP delegates, and **four presidential designees**. A politically appointed majority, by design — answering the 1955 court-packing, so appointments are neither the executive's alone nor the judiciary's.

**The Public Protector · the South African Human Rights Commission · the Commission for Cultural, Religious and Linguistic Communities · the Commission for Gender Equality · the Auditor-General · the Electoral Commission** (plus ICASA under section 192). Independent, **"without fear, favour or prejudice"**, no interference permitted, accountable to the National Assembly. **60% of the Assembly is needed to appoint the Public Protector and the Auditor-General.**

Amending the Constitution.back: **Section 1 or section 74 itself: 75% of the National Assembly plus six of nine provinces. The Bill of Rights: two-thirds plus six provinces. Anything else: two-thirds** (plus six provinces if it affects the NCOP, provincial boundaries, powers or institutions). **Section 74(4)** bars omnibus amendments; **30 days' publication** is required before introduction.

**Is there an unamendable core?** The text says no — section 74 provides a procedure for amending anything, including section 1. **India has a basic structure doctrine; Germany has a textual eternity clause; South Africa is undecided.** In *Premier of KwaZulu-Natal v President* (1996) the Court observed **in passing** that an amendment abolishing the Bill of Rights or dismantling the democratic state might raise questions it would have to consider. **Untested — and the practical protection has been arithmetic.**

Enacted 2002–03 to let MPs and councillors **change parties without losing their seats**; **upheld** in *UDM v President* (2002); widely regarded as corrosive under a closed-list system, where a seat belongs to the party; **repealed in 2008**. Both the enactment and the repeal were self-interested.

The National Prosecuting Authority.back: **179(4): national legislation must ensure the prosecuting authority exercises its functions without fear, favour or prejudice.** **179(6): the Cabinet member responsible for justice must exercise final responsibility over the prosecuting authority.** The courts read (6) as responsibility for the institution rather than for individual decisions — but **the drafting is the source of twenty years of argument.** And **the NDPP is appointed by the President alone** — no commission, no parliamentary approval.

**NDPP 2005–2009.** Obtained an **arrest warrant for Jackie Selebi**, the National Police Commissioner and president of Interpol; **suspended within days**; the **Ginwala inquiry found him fit for office**; **dismissed anyway.** Selebi was later convicted of corruption. **The clearest single episode of prosecutorial independence being overridden.**

Held **Nxasana's removal by a large settlement was invalid** — an NDPP cannot be bought out; **consequently Abrahams's appointment was invalid**, the vacancy having been created unlawfully; and **sections 12(4) and 12(6) of the NPA Act — indefinite suspension of an NDPP without pay — unconstitutional.** The last is the structural finding: **an NDPP who can be suspended indefinitely without pay is not independent.**

The **Directorate of Special Operations**, 1999–2009, **inside the NPA** — prosecutors and investigators together on organised crime and corruption, with high conviction rates, investigating the arms deal and Selebi. **The ANC's 2007 Polokwane conference resolved to dissolve it; legislation disbanded it in 2009**, replaced by the **Hawks** inside the police. **A party conference resolution became law in eighteen months.**

Held **the Constitution requires an adequately independent anti-corruption entity** — derived from the state's obligations and international agreements — and **the Hawks as legislated lacked adequate independence**, so the legislation was invalid. ***Helen Suzman Foundation v President* (2014)** struck down further provisions. **One of the Court's most creative judgments, and not yet fully satisfied.**

**The TRC referred about 300 cases** (stage 6) — almost no prosecutions. **Zondo referred a large volume** (2022) — few prosecutions, slowly. **The arms deal: no successful prosecution of a South African official.** The principal reason is the NPA's own record: **six NDPPs in twenty-one years, two appointments set aside by courts, one dismissed after acting against a police commissioner, one paid to leave.** An institution whose leadership is contested for twenty years does not build the capacity to prosecute complex financial crime.

The police, and the Hawks.front: Section 205(3) — the objects of the police
The police, and the Hawks.back: **"To prevent, combat and investigate crime, to maintain public order, to protect and secure the inhabitants of the Republic and their property, and to uphold and enforce the law."** Section 206: **a Cabinet member is responsible for policing** and determines national policy; provinces have oversight. Section 207: **the National Commissioner is appointed by the President** — as with the NDPP, no commission and no parliamentary process.

The police, and the Hawks.front: Why the police problem is not the number of police
The police, and the Hawks.back: **South Africa has a large police service by international comparison** — roughly 180,000–190,000 members. **The deficit is investigative capacity**: low murder detection and conviction rates, detective case loads far above any reasonable workload, **DNA backlogs running to hundreds of thousands of cases** in the 2020s, lost experienced detectives, and **crime intelligence repeatedly compromised.** The consequence is **impunity** — for ordinary crime, political violence and corruption alike.

The **Independent Police Investigative Directorate** (IPID Act, 2011) must investigate deaths in police custody, deaths from police action, torture, rape by police and police corruption. ***McBride v Minister of Police* (2016)**: the provisions letting the minister suspend and remove the IPID head were **unconstitutional** — the same reasoning as the NDPP's. **An oversight body whose head the overseen minister can remove is not independent.**

**16 August 2012: police shot dead 34 striking mineworkers** at Lonmin's platinum operations in the North West; ten people, including two police and two security guards, had been killed the preceding week. **The Farlam Commission (2015)** found the operation **defective and dangerous**, the plan unlawful in material respects, and that **the police misled the commission and altered documents.** The National Commissioner was found unfit. **No police officer has been convicted of the killings.**

The **Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation**, created 2009, sits **inside the police** rather than in the NPA. ***Glenister*'s* objection: an anti-corruption unit inside an institution it may have to investigate, reporting to a commissioner appointed by the President, is not insulated. Its independence was litigated twice (2011, 2014); **its record on capture-era cases is weak**, which is why **IDAC was given its own investigators in 2024** — partially restoring the Scorpions' model.

Intelligence.back: **199(6): "No member of any security service may obey a manifestly illegal order."** **199(7): the security services may not prejudice a legitimate political party interest, nor further, in a partisan manner, any interest of a political party.** Both clauses are **written against stage 5's security state.** Section 210 requires **civilian monitoring by an inspector appointed by the President and approved by two-thirds of the National Assembly.**

Chaired by **Sydney Mufamadi**, on the State Security Agency. Found **a "doctrinal shift" — the SSA had been repurposed from protecting the constitutional order to serving factional political ends**; parallel structures outside the lawful command chain; **large volumes of unaccounted cash**; operations directed at domestic political actors; **degraded core capability**; and failed oversight. **As serious a finding as can be made about an intelligence service in a constitutional democracy.**

Intelligence.front: The 2009 SSA merger, and the 2024 split
Intelligence.back: **2009: the State Security Agency was created by proclamation**, merging the domestic NIA and the foreign SASS — removing a separation that had existed since 1994 and doing it without legislation debated in public. **The General Intelligence Laws Amendment Act (2024)** gives effect to the review panel's central recommendation: **splitting the SSA back into separate domestic and foreign services**, strengthening the Inspector-General and tightening vetting. **Implementation in progress as of 14 October 2026.**

Intelligence.front: Why intelligence oversight has no backstop
Intelligence.back: Secrecy is necessary, and **secrecy defeats oversight** — the overseers must be trusted with what they cannot disclose. So oversight rests entirely on **the Inspector-General and a committee meeting in closed session**, and **if they are captured or incapable there is nothing behind them.** South Africa's were under-resourced and under-informed for a decade. **Almost everything publicly known about SA intelligence since 1994 comes from commissions and journalism, not from the oversight architecture.**

SARS.front: Why SARS is the case study
SARS.back: **The one South African institution whose rise, destruction and partial recovery are all documented, measurable and within twenty-five years.** Built 1997–2009 under **Pravin Gordhan** — e-filing, risk-based audit, a Large Business Centre, specialist enforcement, collection above target for a decade, and **a compliance culture, the asset that takes longest to build.** Dismantled 2014–2018. Rebuilt from 2019. **The design never changed; one appointment did.**

An allegation that SARS had run an **unlawful covert intelligence unit**, used from 2014 to justify suspensions, dismissals and the removal of the officials who had built SARS's enforcement capacity. It rested on **the Sikhakhane panel (2014)** and **a KPMG report (2015) that KPMG later withdrew and apologised for**, and was repeated in aligned media. **Nugent found it had no proper basis as used.** A stage 1 lesson: an allegation repeated in aligned media is not corroboration.

Judge **Robert Nugent** on SARS. Found **"a massive failure of integrity and governance"**; that **the restructuring was destructive with no coherent rationale**; recommended **Moyane's removal**, which followed; criticised the consultancy's role (**the firm repaid its fees**); and recommended **restoring the capability and insulating the Commissioner's appointment.** **Short, readable and free — the best single document on how a competent SA institution was dismantled.**

**To build SARS: about twelve years. To break it: about four. To rebuild it: about five — and the compliance culture recovers more slowly than the systems.** Under **Edward Kieswetter** from 2019 the Large Business Centre, enforcement and specialist audit were restored and revenue has exceeded estimates in several years. **The most hopeful fact in the stage: an institution can be rebuilt, with a competent appointment and nothing legislative.**

The Reserve Bank.back: **224(1): "The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth in the Republic."** **224(2):** it must perform its functions **independently and without fear, favour or prejudice**, with regular consultation with the finance minister. **A negotiated requirement of the stage 6 settlement**, and one of only a handful of constitutions entrenching central bank independence. Note the mandate is price stability **with a stated purpose** — the textual hook for the growth argument.

About **two million shares held by roughly 600–800 shareholders**, who receive **a capped dividend** and **elect seven of the fifteen board directors** — and have **no influence over monetary policy or regulation.** Very few central banks are like this (Belgium, Switzerland, Japan, Turkey have variants). **Nationalising the shareholding is an ANC conference resolution from Nasrec 2017, never implemented** — the reasons given being cost, no policy benefit, and signalling risk.

**For change:** 224(1) already names *balanced and sustainable economic growth*; unemployment above 30% is the defining problem; other central banks have dual mandates; QE could fund development. **Against:** the primary object is price stability and the growth clause states its purpose; **a central bank cannot create jobs but can create inflation, which falls hardest on the poor**; monetary financing in an open emerging economy risks a currency and debt spiral; **the Bank's independence is one of the few institutions that held.** Not settled by economics alone.

The Reserve Bank.front: The Bankorp report, and the personal costs order
The Reserve Bank.back: In **2017 the Public Protector** issued a report on an apartheid-era Bankorp lifeboat whose remedial action **directed Parliament to amend section 224 of the Constitution** to change the Reserve Bank's mandate. **The courts set it aside**, finding she had acted beyond her powers, without an open mind, and had met the Presidency and the SSA without disclosing it — **with a personal costs order against her.** **A Chapter 9 institution tried to direct a constitutional amendment, and the courts stopped it.**

Treasury, and the budget.back: **216: the national treasury must prescribe uniform treasury norms and standards — and may stop the transfer of funds to an organ of state that commits a serious or persistent material breach.** **The strongest administrative weapon in South African government**, and it has been used against provinces and municipalities. **217: procurement must be fair, equitable, transparent, competitive and cost-effective — and may provide for preferential procurement to protect or advance disadvantaged persons.** The constitutional basis of both the procurement rules and BEE procurement.

**October/November: the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement** — fiscal framework, division of revenue, macro forecasts. **February: the Budget** — the speech, the **Budget Review**, the Division of Revenue Bill and the Appropriation Bill. **February–July: committees consider the fiscal framework, then the two Bills**, with public hearings. Then adjustments appropriations, then annual reports, the Auditor-General and SCOPA. **The Budget Review each February is the clearest single free document on what the SA state actually does.**

**9 December 2015: Finance Minister Nhlanhla Nene dismissed and David van Rooyen, a little-known backbencher, appointed.** The rand fell sharply, bond yields spiked, bank shares collapsed. **13 December: Gordhan reappointed. Four days.** The most instructive episode in modern SA political economy — **and the reversal was secured by business, ANC figures and the markets, not by any constitutional mechanism.** In **March 2017** Gordhan and Jonas were dismissed; **S&P and Fitch downgraded to sub-investment grade that April.**

Treasury, and the budget.front: Why Treasury was the institution capture most needed
Treasury, and the budget.back: **Every large irregular payment must pass a procurement process and a budget.** Capturing SOEs delivers contracts; **capturing Treasury would have delivered the fiscus.** It was attacked twice (2015, 2017), and **its officials resisted** — declining and delaying the nuclear programme, SAA guarantees and specific transactions, in some cases litigating, several losing their jobs. **Mcebisi Jonas gave evidence that he was offered a very large sum and the finance ministership by the Gupta family. He refused.**

**As of the 2025–26 Budget: gross national debt is around 75–77% of GDP, up from about 26% in 2008**, and **debt-service costs are among the largest single items of spending**, exceeding several major functions. The primary balance has recently moved into surplus with debt projected to stabilise. **Check the current Budget Review.** From stage 6: the apartheid debt was honoured and crowded out the RDP; **this debt crowds out the same things, and was accumulated after 2008.**

The Auditor-General.back: **Unqualified with no findings** — a "clean audit": reliable statements **and** no material findings on performance or compliance. **Unqualified with findings** — reliable numbers, findings elsewhere. **Qualified** — parts materially misstated. **Adverse** — the whole materially misstated. **Disclaimer** — not enough evidence to form an opinion at all. **Outstanding** — not submitted. **A clean audit means the records are in order and the rules were followed. It does not mean the money achieved anything.**

**Irregular expenditure** is expenditure **incurred in contravention of legislation** — a compliance finding. **Fruitless and wasteful** was made in vain and would have been avoided with reasonable care. **Unauthorised** is outside the vote or purpose appropriated. **Some irregular expenditure is theft and some is paperwork** — procurement without three quotes, a contract extended without approval. **The AG says so in every general report, and it is routinely reported as if the whole figure were stolen.**

The Auditor-General.front: Material irregularity, and the certificate of debt
The Auditor-General.back: The **Public Audit Amendment Act of 2018**, effective April 2019, lets the AG identify a **material irregularity** — non-compliance, fraud, theft or a breach of fiduciary duty causing or likely to cause material financial loss — **refer it** to the Hawks, NPA or Public Protector, **take binding remedial action**, and **issue a certificate of debt against an accounting officer personally.** **Personal liability is the point**, because the consistent failure is consequence management. **Used sparingly; deterrent effect not yet established.**

Repeated across general reports for a decade: **instability in accounting-officer and CFO posts; absent basic financial controls — not sophisticated fraud, record-keeping; non-compliance with supply chain rules; no consequence management (the central finding); and reliance on consultants**, including to prepare the statements officials should prepare. **The capacity thesis stated by the institution with the best evidence.**

**Nominated by a National Assembly committee and appointed by the President on a resolution of the Assembly**, for a **non-renewable** five-to-ten-year term; **largely self-funding through audit fees**, so less dependent on a departmental vote; **a technical, rule-bound mandate** with professional standards behind it; and staffed by chartered accountants with an external professional identity. **Compare the Public Protector: same chapter, same independence clause, different appointment and a discretionary mandate.**

The Public Protector in practice.back: The Public Protector may **investigate any conduct in state affairs, or in the public administration in any sphere of government, that is alleged or suspected to be improper or to result in any impropriety or prejudice**; must **report** on it; and may **take appropriate remedial action**. May not investigate court decisions (182(3)), and must be **accessible to all persons and communities** (182(4)). **An extraordinarily broad jurisdiction — and the Constitution does not say whether "appropriate remedial action" binds.**

The Public Protector in practice.front: EFF v Speaker (2016) — the Nkandla judgment
The Public Protector in practice.back: Held **the Public Protector's remedial action is binding unless set aside by a court** — because a watchdog whose findings may be ignored is **"a toothless bulldog"**, and the Constitution does not create meaningless offices. Also held the **National Assembly's resolution absolving the President was unlawful** and that **the President had failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution.** Treasury set the amount; he repaid it. **And the holding binds whoever holds the office, whatever the quality of the report.**

**Thuli Madonsela's** last report, on the Gupta family's influence over appointments and contracts, **whose remedial action directed the President to appoint a commission of inquiry headed by a judge selected by the Chief Justice.** **That is where the Zondo Commission came from** — a Chapter 9 institution with a small budget and no police powers produced the commission that produced 5,000 pages on the executive.

A Chapter 9 office-holder is removed for **misconduct, incapacity or incompetence**, on a **National Assembly committee finding** and **a resolution supported by two-thirds of members**. **The first section 194 inquiry ever held ran from 2022** — with rules the Constitutional Court had to clarify in litigation first — found **Busisiwe Mkhwebane guilty of incompetence and misconduct**, and **the Assembly removed her on 11 September 2023.** **Seven years, about a dozen reports set aside, and an inquiry litigated into existence.**

The Public Protector in practice.front: What the Public Protector's history proves
The Public Protector in practice.back: **The design was mostly adequate** — broad mandate, binding remedial action, a 60% appointment threshold, a two-thirds removal threshold — and **the same design produced opposite results under two successive holders.** **The appointment failed.** The courts worked throughout; the Assembly worked eventually. **The structural weakness: the office's power now rests almost entirely on the holder's judgment, and correcting it runs through litigation at the complainant's cost.**

The other Chapter 9s.front: Section 181(5), and the committee that does not exist
The other Chapter 9s.back: Chapter 9 institutions are **accountable to the National Assembly and must report on their activities and performance at least once a year** — **and the Assembly has no dedicated committee for them**, so an annual report is received by whichever portfolio committee is nearest. **The Asmal review recommended one in 2007.** A power that exists and is not exercised — the same finding as Parliament's oversight.

**Organs of state must report annually to the SAHRC on the measures they have taken towards realising the rights in the Bill of Rights concerning housing, health care, food, water, social security, education and the environment.** **This is the only systematic monitoring of the stage 7 socio-economic rights that exists.** The Commission may also **investigate, report, subpoena and litigate in its own name**, and supports cases in the Equality Courts under PEPUDA.

An ad hoc National Assembly committee chaired by **Kader Asmal** reviewed all the Chapter 9 institutions and recommended: **merging the SAHRC, CGE and CRL Commission into one human rights commission** with specialised units; **funding as a direct charge on the National Revenue Fund** rather than through a department; a single transparent appointment process; and **a dedicated parliamentary committee** to receive their reports. **Almost none of it implemented, nineteen years later.**

**A body that must oversee the executive receives its budget through the executive's budget process** — with the partial exception of the self-funding Auditor-General. The result is chronic under-funding, vacancies, and an incentive not to be troublesome. **Section 181(3) says organs of state must assist and protect these institutions to ensure their effectiveness.** **Whether under-funding breaches it is arguable and has never been litigated** — a live constitutional question nobody has taken to court.

The Constitutional Court held the Electoral Act unconstitutional for **requiring candidates to stand only through political parties**, producing the **2023 amendment permitting independent candidates**, first used in 2024. The IEC's wider record: **seven national and six local elections since 1994, none of whose results has been successfully overturned** — a technical mandate, an auditable process, party agents at every station, and a dedicated Electoral Court. **Its weak point is the voters' roll and address data**, addressed in the *Tlokwe* litigation.

The judiciary, and the JSC.front: Why judges held and prosecutors did not
The judiciary, and the JSC.back: **The NDPP and the National Commissioner of Police are appointed by the President alone.** **Judges are appointed through a commission, from a published list, after public interviews** — section 174(6) for most judges, and 174(4) for the Constitutional Court, where the JSC supplies a list with **three names more than the vacancies** and the President may reject nominees only with reasons. **The decisive institutional difference in the whole stage, and the outcomes track it.**

**23 members**: the Chief Justice (presiding), the SCA President and one Judge President; **the justice minister**; two advocates; two attorneys; one teacher of law; **six National Assembly members, at least three from opposition parties**; **four NCOP delegates supported by at least six provinces**; and **four presidential designees**. **Fourteen of twenty-three are politically designated — a majority, deliberately.** Plus the division's Judge President and the province's Premier when its matters are considered (25).

**For:** appointment should have a democratic element; a self-selecting judiciary is also a political choice; **the 1994 bench was 97% white and 99% male and would not transform itself**; and this JSC appointed the judges who decided *Glenister*, *Nkandla* and *Corruption Watch*. **Against:** the overseen branch's politicians hold a majority on the body appointing its overseers; **interview quality has been poor** — the 2021 Chief Justice interviews were very widely criticised; unsuccessful candidates have litigated successfully; party-political questioning of candidates about rulings.

**176(1): a Constitutional Court judge serves a non-renewable twelve-year term or until 70**, whichever comes first. **176(3): salaries and benefits may not be reduced.** **177: removal requires a JSC finding of incapacity, gross incompetence or gross misconduct AND a National Assembly resolution supported by two-thirds of members**, after which the President must remove the judge. **A judge who cannot be reappointed cannot be courted — the non-renewable term is one of the strongest independence provisions in the document.**

**Section 177 was used for the first time in February 2024**, when the National Assembly removed **Judge Nkola Motata** and **Judge President John Hlophe** by the required two-thirds. Hlophe had been found guilty of gross misconduct for **attempting to influence two Constitutional Court justices in 2008** — a matter that took **fifteen years** through the JSC and the courts. He was elected to the Assembly in 2024 and **his party's designation of him to the JSC was litigated and found unlawful.**

The judiciary, and the JSC.front: The judicialisation of politics, both sides
The judiciary, and the JSC.back: **The criticism:** the courts decide too much — political disputes that belong in Parliament or at the ballot box arrive as litigation (*EFF v Speaker*, *UDM v Speaker*, the impeachment rules, the secret ballot, cadre deployment, the NDPP appointments). **The answer:** the Court decides what is brought to it, has ordered processes rather than outcomes where it could, and **cannot refuse a case because the subject is political.** **The deeper point: the litigation went up because the alternatives went down.**

The provinces in practice.back: **Basic education, public health services, housing and social welfare services** — Schedule 4 concurrent functions — plus Schedule 5 exclusives like provincial roads, liquor licences, abattoirs and ambulance services. **About a third of all government spending passes through provincial budgets, almost all of it on those four.** A Premier plus **a maximum of ten MECs** (s125); a legislature of **30 to 80 members** (s105).

The provinces in practice.front: Why provinces are not taxing governments
The provinces in practice.back: **Section 227** entitles them to an equitable share of nationally raised revenue; **section 228** lets them impose only surcharges on tax bases and limited taxes — **not income tax, VAT or company tax.** **So roughly 95% or more of provincial revenue comes from national transfers.** A province spends enormous sums it did not raise and cannot increase — **the opposite of a municipality, which has rates and service surcharges under section 229.**

From the AG's PFMA general reports over a decade: **the Western Cape and Gauteng consistently do better; the Eastern Cape, Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North West and Free State consistently worse.** **Same Constitution, same transfers formula, same legislation — very different results.** **The single best argument for the capacity thesis:** the design is identical across all nine and the outcomes are not. **Section 100 national interventions** were used in Limpopo (2011, five departments) and North West (2018, health).

**In 2015–16 the Gauteng health department moved about 1,700 psychiatric patients from Life Esidimeni facilities to NGOs, many unlicensed and unequipped. At least 144 died.** The **Health Ombud's 2017 report** found the decision unlawful and the deaths avoidable; **the 2018 arbitration before former Deputy Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke awarded constitutional damages**; a years-long inquest found grounds for liability against the former MEC and a senior official and referred it for prosecution. **Nobody has been convicted.**

Local government: the system.back: **151(3): "A municipality has the right to govern, on its own initiative, the local government affairs of its community, subject to national and provincial legislation, as provided for in the Constitution."** **151(4): "The national or a provincial government may not compromise or impede a municipality's ability or right to exercise its powers or perform its functions."** **This makes a municipality a government, not a branch office** — which is why a province must use section 139 rather than simply taking over.

Local government: the system.front: The three categories, and the count
Local government: the system.back: **Category A — metropolitan: eight metros** (Johannesburg, Tshwane, Ekurhuleni, Cape Town, eThekwini, Nelson Mandela Bay, Buffalo City, Mangaung), with exclusive executive and legislative authority. **Category B — local: about 205**, sharing authority with a district. **Category C — district: about 44.** **257 in total.** Councillors: **half elected in wards first-past-the-post, half from party lists to make the council proportional.**

A municipality **buys bulk electricity from Eskom and resells it at a regulated markup, and that surplus cross-subsidises everything else it does** — parks, libraries, roads. So **Eskom tariff increases squeeze it from below; rooftop solar and large-user defection remove its highest-paying customers, which is structural rather than cyclical; and distribution losses come straight off the surplus.** **The municipal fiscal crisis of the 2020s is substantially an electricity story.**

**Provincial intervention in a municipality.** **139(1): a province MAY intervene** where a municipality fails to fulfil an executive obligation — by directive, by assuming responsibility, or by **dissolving the council**. **139(4): it MUST intervene** where a municipality cannot approve a budget or revenue-raising measures. **139(5): it MUST impose a recovery plan** where there is a serious or persistent material breach of financial commitments. **Dozens of municipalities are under some form of intervention at any time, and most end without recovery.**

Local government: why it fails.front: The revenue model does not fit most municipalities
Local government: why it fails.back: **Section 229 assumes a municipality funds itself substantially from property rates and service surcharges.** That works for **the eight metros and roughly twenty secondary cities.** It cannot work for most of the remaining 230 — especially those drawn over former homeland territory, with **little rateable property, high unemployment and no commercial base.** **The result is a structural deficit no amount of competence closes** — which is why serious reform proposals are for a **differentiated model**, not better management of a uniform one.

Local government: why it fails.front: Why instability hurts a municipality more than a national department
Local government: why it fails.back: **A municipality's work is operational.** A water network needs a five-year capital plan, and **no plan survives a management change every nine months.** Since 2016 and far more after 2021 **many councils are hung**, mayors and councils change frequently — sometimes several times in a year — and **each change replaces the senior management.** Johannesburg is the standing example: a succession of mayors since 2016.

**A cholera outbreak in May 2023 killed about 30 people**, following the long-known failure of the **Rooiwal waste-water treatment works.** **The lesson in one event: a documented, funded-and-unspent treatment works failure killed people.** Not a policy dispute — an unmaintained plant. Nationally, **non-revenue water runs around 40–50%** against a well-run utility's 15%, and **repairs and maintenance budgets sit below the 8%-of-asset-value benchmark**, converting an operating saving into a capital loss.

Local government: why it fails.front: The two hundred and the thirty
Local government: why it fails.back: The stage's thesis in its hardest form: **about thirty municipalities are viable institutions with fixable problems; about two hundred are administering a mandate they were never funded to carry, with staff they cannot recruit, over infrastructure they cannot maintain.** **Those are different problems and they have been treated as one** — which is why the Turnaround Strategy (2009), Back to Basics (2014) and the District Development Model (2019) all had the right lists and no effect.

Imposes **minimum competency requirements** for municipal managers and section 56 managers, **bars a municipal manager from holding political office in a party**, and regulates appointment procedures. **An earlier 2011 version was struck down in 2017 on the tagging ground**, like *Tongoane*, and had to be re-enacted. **The legislation is in place; evidence that it has changed appointments is thin.** The underlying problem is technical: **a water and sanitation function needs registered professional engineers, and many municipalities employ none.**

Traditional authority.back: **211(1): "The institution, status and role of traditional leadership, according to customary law, are recognised, subject to the Constitution."** **211(2):** a traditional authority may function subject to applicable legislation and customs, **"which includes amendments to, or repeal of, that legislation or those customs"**. **211(3): "The courts must apply customary law when that law is applicable, subject to the Constitution"** — making customary law **a source of law**, so South African law has three: legislation, common law and customary law. **212** allows a role at local level and houses of traditional leaders.

Traditional authority.front: Why traditional authority is a politics question
Traditional authority.back: **About 13% of South Africa** — the former reserves and homelands — is held under **communal tenure, formally in trust by the state and administered through traditional councils**, and **on the order of 17 to 18 million people live there.** The **Ingonyama Trust** holds about **2.8 million hectares** in KwaZulu-Natal with the Zulu king as sole trustee. Traditional councils **allocate land and consent to or refuse development and mining.** **"Who may sign away land rights in the former homelands" is one of the largest unresolved property questions in the country.**

**The Constitutional Court declared the whole Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019 unconstitutional for failure to facilitate public involvement**, following *Doctors for Life*, with the declaration suspended for re-enactment. The Act had **recognised Khoi-San leadership for the first time** — a genuine advance — but its **section 24 allowed traditional councils to enter agreements and partnerships over communal land**, which critics said permitted deals without the community's consent. **Three major statutes on this subject have been struck down, twice on process grounds.**

***Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha* (2004)** struck down **male primogeniture in customary intestate succession** under section 9. ***Shilubana v Nwamitwa* (2008)** upheld **a community's own development of its custom** to appoint a woman as hosi, holding that a traditional community may change its own law. **The rule: customary law is living and the community may develop it; where it discriminates and has not been developed, section 9 applies.**

State-owned enterprises.front: Why state capture used the SOEs
State-owned enterprises.back: **Very large procurement budgets** — capital programmes in the tens of billions with specifications few can evaluate. **Board appointment by a single minister** — no commission, no public interviews, no parliamentary confirmation. **Weaker oversight than a department** — one step removed from the vote, with a portfolio committee receiving an annual report rather than a budget line. **Guaranteed borrowing** against the state's credit, so capture needs no appropriation. **Capturing a department gets you a scrutinised vote; capturing an SOE gets you a procurement programme.**

Roughly **48 GW nominal capacity**, mostly coal. **A 1998 White Paper said new capacity would be needed by about 2007**, and the decision was deferred; **load-shedding began in 2007.** The **energy availability factor fell from about 85% in the mid-2000s to the mid-50s by 2022–23**, with 2023 the worst year. **Medupi and Kusile were budgeted at roughly R80bn each and cost on the order of R145bn and more**, about a decade late, with persisting design defects. **Debt peaked above R400bn, with about R254bn of relief in the 2023 Budget.**

**As of 14 October 2026** load-shedding has been largely suspended since 2024 with intermittent returns, and the EAF has improved. **Three causes, and they are not the same thing:** better maintenance and management; **a large volume of private renewable and rooftop generation** after the licensing threshold was lifted; and **demand that fell because the economy and the industrial base shrank.** The reform is **unbundling** — the National Transmission Company South Africa became operational in 2024, and the **Electricity Regulation Amendment Act of 2024** created a market operator and third-party access.

**Freight rail volumes fell from about 226 million tonnes in 2017–18 to roughly 150 million**, with port performance among the worst ranked globally and **the export of coal, iron ore and manganese constrained by rail rather than by demand.** The **1,064-locomotive contract** was examined at length by Zondo. **A mining economy that cannot move its product to a port is losing export revenue it has already paid to extract** — the largest single economic consequence of SOE failure.

State-owned enterprises.front: The SOE argument, and the actual direction
State-owned enterprises.back: **Privatise:** the state has failed as an owner for two decades; the entities need capital the fiscus cannot provide; a private board cannot be captured by a minister; the guarantees are a contingent liability of hundreds of billions. **Keep public:** the failures are of appointment and oversight, not ownership; **a monopoly network sold is still a monopoly**; universal service obligations; the assets are strategic and sale is irreversible. **The direction since 2019 is neither: structural separation, with private participation in the competitive parts and the network kept in state hands.**

What would have to change.back: **Commission- or legislature-mediated appointments mostly held**: the judiciary (a commission, a published list, public interviews), the Auditor-General (an Assembly committee and resolution, non-renewable term), the IEC (a panel including the Chief Justice), the Reserve Bank (an entrenched mandate). **Single-appointer institutions mostly did not**: the NDPP and the National Commissioner of Police (**the President alone**) and SOE boards (**one minister**). **The correlation is not subtle, and it is this stage's conclusion.**
