**Panel-based, transparent appointment with security of tenure for the NDPP and the National Commissioner**; **an independent appointment process with published criteria for SOE boards**, and a standing committee on public entity appointments; **a single permanent anti-corruption agency with its own investigators and prosecutors, outside the police** — the *Glenister* obligation; **ending cadre deployment**, found unlawful and unconstitutional; **lifestyle audits**; **a single procurement regulator and a professional supply chain function**; and **enlarging Parliament's oversight capacity, with the closed-list electoral system reconsidered.**

What would have to change.front: Why none of it is self-executing
What would have to change.back: **Every reform the evidence points to is a reform of patronage** — appointment power, procurement and discipline **are the currency of political organisation.** So the question is not what should change but **what makes a governing party give up appointment power.** The two candidate answers are **electoral competition** (stage 10) and **coalition arithmetic forcing negotiated appointments** (stage 11). **For:** the better-performing province and metros are those where power is contestable. **Against:** coalition instability has made local government worse, and competition has not yet produced appointment reform nationally.

**Clean audits, national/provincial and local** (AG's PFMA and MFMA general reports); **certificates of debt issued and material irregularities resolved** (AG); **DG vacancy and acting rates, and average DG tenure** (Public Service Commission); **murder detection and conviction rates** (SAPS, NPA); **corruption convictions and amounts recovered by the Asset Forfeiture Unit** (NPA annual report); **Eskom's EAF and Transnet's rail volumes**; **non-revenue water and municipal debt to Eskom.** **If you track only one, track consequence management** — everything in this stage follows from whether a finding has a consequence.

Why the economy is a politics stage.front: The stage 9 thesis, and its counter
Why the economy is a politics stage.back: **The thesis:** South Africa's economy was built to extract minerals using cheap controlled labour and cheap electricity, and the unemployment rate, the labour market's shape, the tiny informal sector, the cities' layout and the concentration of ownership are **legacies of that system rather than failures of post-1994 policy.** **The counter:** thirty-two years is long enough, and the binding constraints now — **electricity, logistics, state capacity, policy uncertainty** — are current choices. **Both are held by serious people with evidence.**

Why the economy is a politics stage.front: The ten recurring numbers, as orders of magnitude
Why the economy is a politics stage.back: **Official unemployment: low 30s per cent. Expanded: low 40s. Absorption: about 40%. Gini: 0.63 on consumption, higher on income. Top decile income share: about two-thirds. Gross debt: mid-to-high 70s per cent of GDP. Debt service: among the largest spending items. Grants: about 19 million regular, plus an income grant. Mining: ~6% of GDP, about half of merchandise exports. Manufacturing: ~13% of GDP, from over 20% in the early 1980s.** **Know which are a third, which two-thirds, and which single digits.**

The minerals-energy complex.back: From **Fine and Rustomjee (1996)**. The claim: **South Africa developed not a diversified economy that included mining, but a system of accumulation centred on mining and the energy and heavy industry it required** — with the state, the banks, the labour system, the railways and the electricity utility all built to serve that core. Components: **deep-level gold and coal, cheap controlled migrant labour, cheap electricity (Eskom, 1923), state heavy industry (Iscor 1928, Sasol 1950), state rail, conglomerate finance, protective tariffs.**

The minerals-energy complex.front: What the MEC predicts about the economy's shape
The minerals-energy complex.back: **Energy-intensive output** — cheap power was the comparative advantage, so smelting, refining and chemicals got built, not light manufacturing. **Capital-intensive production**, creating few jobs per rand. **A skills structure with a hole in the middle** — a few highly skilled and very many unskilled, which the education system was built to produce. **Spatial dislocation** — labour housed where it was not needed. **Concentrated ownership.** **An export basket of unprocessed minerals**, so the economy rides the commodity cycle.

The minerals-energy complex.front: The strongest objection to the MEC framework
The minerals-energy complex.back: **Australia, Canada and Chile are also mineral economies without South Africa's labour market** — which suggests the operative variable was **the labour system, not the minerals.** Three further objections: **services (finance, retail, telecoms, tourism) are now far larger than mining and manufacturing combined**, and the framework predates that; **1994–2008 growth averaged over 3% while mining declined**, which a mining-centred account predicts poorly; and it is **too deterministic**, leaving little room for policy.

Mining now.back: **About 6% of GDP directly, and roughly half of merchandise exports** — employing on the order of 450,000 to 480,000 people. **Mining is no longer how most value is added, and it is still how the country earns foreign exchange**, so the current account, the exchange rate and the cost of imported fuel and machinery all move with commodity prices. **PGMs are the largest earner; coal the largest by volume; iron ore and manganese are entirely rail-constrained; gold is a fraction of what it was.**

Mining now.front: What happened to gold mining employment
Mining now.back: **Over 500,000 people in gold mining in 1986–87; on the order of 90,000 to 100,000 now.** Total mining employment fell from **around 760,000 at the late-1980s peak** to **450,000–480,000.** The cause is **depth and declining grade** — output has fallen for decades as mines go deeper for less metal at higher cost. **The roughly 300,000 jobs shed were the migrant labour jobs, and the places the workers came from had no replacement** — which is why part of structural unemployment is geographic.

The **Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act 28 of 2002**, in force 2004: **all mineral and petroleum resources are the common heritage of all South Africans, with the state as custodian.** Nobody owns minerals; **the state grants prospecting and mining rights** on conditions including a work programme, environmental authorisation, a social and labour plan and Mining Charter compliance. ***Agri South Africa v Minister for Minerals and Energy* (2013)** held the conversion regime **was not an expropriation requiring compensation**, because the right to apply was preserved.

Deindustrialisation.back: **Manufacturing fell from over 20% of GDP in the early 1980s — at times near a quarter — to about 13%**, with employment around 1.5–1.7 million. Some decline is normal as countries get richer. **The South African case is argued to be different on two grounds: it happened at a far lower income level, and it happened while unemployment was already a third** — losing the sector that absorbs semi-skilled labour before the labour was absorbed.

**1 Trade liberalisation** — fast tariff reduction after 1994 exposed clothing, textiles and appliances; implies selective protection. **2 Electricity and logistics** — the cheap-power advantage ended after 2008; implies fix the infrastructure. **3 Wages and labour regulation** — extended bargaining council minima and dismissal costs; implies exemptions. **4 The structure itself** — manufacturing was always upstream and capital-intensive, so there was no broad labour-absorbing base to lose; implies target services and agriculture instead. **Each implies a different policy, which is why the argument matters.**

**The Motor Industry Development Programme (1995), then the Automotive Production and Development Programme (2013, extended to 2035)** — import duty credits earned by exporting plus production incentives. **Result: seven global manufacturers assembling in South Africa**, vehicles and components among the largest manufactured export categories, and a components supply chain. **Cost: large and continuing fiscal support**, questioned by Treasury reviews on a cost-per-job basis. **Proof that long-horizon conditional industrial policy works, or an expensive enclave that did not generalise** — the disagreement is really about cost per job.

The two agricultures.back: **Commercial: on the order of 40,000 farming units**, producing the overwhelming majority of marketed output, **about 2.5–3% of GDP and roughly 10% of merchandise exports** (citrus, table grapes, wine, apples, macadamias, maize, sugar, wool), employing 750,000–900,000. **Smallholder and subsistence: on the order of 2 to 2.5 million households**, mostly in the former homelands under communal tenure, producing mainly household food. **Export success and rural poverty are both true at once — they describe different sectors.**

**From on the order of 120,000 units in the 1950s to about 58,000 in 1993 and about 40,000 since 2007** — with a far larger export business. Causes: **the marketing boards were abolished by the Marketing of Agricultural Products Act of 1996** (single-channel schemes, controlled prices and guaranteed offtake all ended); **South African agriculture is among the least subsidised in the world**; scale economics in mechanisation, irrigation and cold chains; the 1980s drought and debt crisis; and the shift from resident to seasonal labour.

The two agricultures.front: Why land transfer alone does not produce farmers
The two agricultures.back: **Tenure** — communal land cannot be used as collateral. **Water** — entitlements are historically allocated and reallocation is slow, and irrigation is where the value is. **Extension services** — collapsed, in provinces with the weakest audit outcomes. **Market access** — retail supply chains need volume, consistency and food-safety certification a one-hectare producer cannot meet. **Infrastructure** — rural roads, cold chains, storage. **Transferring land without bankable tenure, water, extension and market access transfers an asset that cannot be used.**

Why unemployment is a third and not a te.front: The absorption rate, and why to use it
Why unemployment is a third and not a te.back: **The share of the working-age population that is employed — roughly 40% in South Africa, against about 60% in middle-income peers.** **Use it because it does not depend on the definition of "actively searching"**, which is what separates the official rate (low 30s) from the expanded rate (low 40s). **Roughly four in ten working-age South Africans have a job, and the twenty-percentage-point gap to the peer figure is the thing to be explained.**

Why unemployment is a third and not a te.front: The eight explanations for unemployment, ranked
Why unemployment is a third and not a te.back: **1 Schooling** — in PIRLS 2021 about **81% of Grade 4 learners could not read for meaning in any language.** **2 Spatial geography** — commuting and job search cost a quarter to a third of a low wage. **3 Demand** — growth averaged above 3% to 2008 and about 1% after, and the rate followed. **4 Capital-intensive production.** **5 The unusually small informal sector.** **6 Wages and labour regulation** — real, contested, smaller than 1–3. **7 Concentration and a missing middle of firms.** **8 Grants and reservation wages — the weakest on evidence, and the most asserted.**

Why unemployment is a third and not a te.front: Why the grants-discourage-work claim is weak
Why unemployment is a third and not a te.back: **The evidence mostly runs the other way.** Grant receipt — particularly an old age pension or child support grant in a household — is associated with **more** job search by working-age members, **because a grant pays the transport fare.** The mechanism cuts against the claim. **This is the most frequently asserted of the eight explanations and the weakest on current evidence**, which is a stage 1 point: check which assertions have studies behind them.

The informal sector, and why it is small.back: **Informal employment is roughly 18–20% of total employment in South Africa, against 70–90% in most of sub-Saharan Africa, around 80% in India, around 40% in Brazil and 50–60% in Indonesia, Peru and Mexico.** In most countries with a third of the workforce out of formal work, those people are trading, repairing and transporting. **Here they are unemployed — which is why the rate is measurable and so high. In an economy with an 80% informal sector, a 33% unemployment rate is arithmetically impossible.**

The informal sector, and why it is small.front: Why black business could not accumulate
The informal sector, and why it is small.back: **Trading licences in urban areas were restricted and refusable.** **The "one man, one business" rule** limited a township trader to a single enterprise, barred companies and partnerships, and barred certain trades. Permitted trades were at times a short list of "daily essential necessities". **The Group Areas Act removed established Indian and coloured traders from city business districts.** **Influx control** barred a visible business without urban rights. **Townships were built as dormitories** — few commercial sites, no light industrial zones. **Informal economies elsewhere rest on generations of accumulated trading capital; South Africa's was prevented from accumulating.**

The informal sector, and why it is small.front: SA Informal Traders Forum v Johannesburg (2014)
The informal sector, and why it is small.back: The Constitutional Court held that **"Operation Clean Sweep", which removed thousands of traders from the Johannesburg inner city, was unlawful**, and ordered them allowed back. The pattern it illustrates: **the Businesses Act of 1991 liberalised street trading, and municipal by-laws then set where, when and whether** — permits with waiting lists, restricted zones, confiscation and periodic removals. **The sphere closest to informal traders is the one with the least capacity and the most discretion.**

Wages, bargaining and strikes.back: **The Minister may extend a bargaining council agreement to non-parties**, binding firms that never negotiated it. **For:** it prevents undercutting, makes bargaining meaningful, and is standard in European systems. **Against:** the parties are the established firms and unions, whose interest is in raising rivals' costs; it binds small and new firms that were not represented; **in a 33% unemployment economy a floor set by insiders excludes outsiders**; and exemptions are administered by the interested council. **The Newcastle clothing cases are the whole argument in one place.**

In force **1 January 2019 at R20 an hour**, set after Nedlac negotiation on research into employment effects, and **reviewed annually by the Minister and published in the Gazette** — passing R28 an hour by the mid-2020s. **Farm workers were brought up to the general level in 2021 and domestic workers in 2022**, having had lower sectoral rates. **Large job losses were predicted; the published studies find wage gains with employment effects much smaller than predicted.** A rare policy with a researched before and after.

Wages, bargaining and strikes.front: Why COSATU's composition is a fiscal fact
Wages, bargaining and strikes.back: **COSATU's centre of gravity moved from mining and manufacturing to the public service** — its largest affiliates are now **SADTU (teachers), NEHAWU (health and public service) and POPCRU (police and prisons).** A mineworkers' federation wants wages, safety and industrial employment. **A public service federation wants the wage bill, state employment levels, and resistance to retrenchment and performance management.** **So the labour movement's position on the central fiscal question of the 2020s is determined by its membership composition.**

The labour law architecture.back: **LRA 66 of 1995** — organisational rights, bargaining councils, the right to strike and its procedure, unfair dismissal, retrenchment (ss189 and 189A), the CCMA and the Labour Court. **BCEA 75 of 1997** — hours, overtime, leave, notice, deductions. **EEA 55 of 1998** — designated employers must plan and report; the **2022 Amendment** adds ministerial sectoral targets. **Skills Development Act 97 of 1998** — a 1% payroll levy funding SETAs. **National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018.** Plus the UIF and COIDA.

The labour law architecture.front: Nedlac, and who is not at the table
The labour law architecture.back: Under the **National Economic Development and Labour Council Act of 1994**: government, organised business, organised labour and a community constituency, **with all labour and most economic legislation passing through it before Parliament.** **For:** the parties who must implement a law negotiate it, producing durable legislation. **Against: the represented parties are the insiders, and the unemployed have no seat**, so the output reflects insiders' interests. **And Nedlac is not Parliament** — a Bill agreed there still needs the s75/76 process and the *Doctors for Life* obligation.

**Free, no lawyer required at conciliation, handling on the order of 200,000 referrals a year**, with most matters resolved at conciliation within weeks. **Reinstatement is the primary remedy for unfair dismissal**, with compensation capped at 12 months' pay (24 for automatically unfair dismissals). **One of the better-functioning institutions in the country** — it gives a worker with no money a forum, which answers stage 7's access-to-justice point in one sector. **The criticism is that procedural complexity deters hiring; the empirical studies are mixed.**

How inequality is measured.back: **Gini on consumption: about 0.63.** **Gini on income: about 0.65–0.68.** **Top decile income share: around two-thirds.** **Wealth: a Gini around 0.93, with the top 10% holding roughly 85% of wealth.** **0.63 and 0.68 are not the same claim — the base matters**, and cross-country comparisons often compare different bases. **And surveys under-capture the top**, so survey Ginis understate inequality; the tax-data corrections push concentration higher. **Ask which base, which year, which source.**

**In 1993–95 the majority of South African income inequality was between racial groups — on the order of 60% or more. By the 2010s that share had fallen to roughly 40–50% while total inequality did not fall**, because **inequality within the African population rose sharply** as a professional and managerial class grew while unemployment at the bottom stayed. **Both halves are used politically and both are correct** — and this is the central evidential fact in the argument about whether BEE addresses inequality or relocates it.

**Fiscal incidence studies put market-income Gini around 0.77 and final income — after taxes, cash grants and the valued in-kind benefits of public health and schooling — around 0.59–0.60: among the largest reductions measured anywhere.** So **South Africa has both the highest measured market inequality and one of the most redistributive fiscal systems measured.** **The strongest technical objection:** valuing a school place at its cost assumes the schooling is worth what it costs, and the PIRLS result says it is not. **Value services by outcome and the measured redistribution falls.**

**The large majority — roughly 70% or more in standard decompositions — is attributable to the labour market**, through two channels: **who has a job at all** (a household with no earner is poor regardless of wage structure) and **the dispersion of wages among those who do**, which is unusually wide and tracks the minerals-energy complex's skills structure. **So inequality cannot be fixed by transfers alone, because the thing generating it is the absence of earnings.**

Poverty, and the social wage.back: **The food poverty line (FPL)** — the cost of the minimum daily energy intake; also called extreme poverty. **The lower-bound line (LBPL)** — the food line plus the average non-food spending of households whose *total* spending equals the food line, so **a person at it sacrifices food to pay for transport and housing.** **The upper-bound line (UBPL)** — the food line plus the non-food spending of households whose *food* spending equals the food line; **the line usually meant by "the poverty rate".** **More than half the population is below the UBPL; roughly a fifth to a quarter below the FPL.**

Poverty, and the social wage.front: The SRD grant, and the hole it filled
Poverty, and the social wage.back: **Before 2020 South Africa paid grants to children, the elderly and the disabled — and nothing at all to an unemployed working-age adult without a disability.** In a country with 33% unemployment that was the system's largest gap. **The Social Relief of Distress grant, created as a Covid emergency measure in 2020 at R350, now reaches 8 to 9 million people and remains below the food poverty line** — and has proved impossible to withdraw. **Its future is one of stage 12's live arguments.**

**Social grants (about 19 million regular grants, plus the SRD); no-fee schools (roughly 75–80% of public schools); the National School Nutrition Programme (9–10 million learners a meal a day); free primary health care; the world's largest HIV treatment programme (on the order of 5.5 million people); free basic water and electricity for registered indigent households; 4–5 million housing opportunities since 1994; and NSFAS.** **Learning and culture, health, social development and community development together are roughly 60% of consolidated non-interest spending — that is what the South African state is, measured by where the money goes.**

Poverty, and the social wage.front: The point both sides of the social wage argument concede
Poverty, and the social wage.back: **The cash transfer system works administratively and the in-kind services do not.** SASSA pays 19 million grants monthly with low leakage, and the grants demonstrably reduce child stunting, raise school attendance and fund job search. **The quality of schooling and provincial health care is poor, so the in-kind spending buys less than it costs.** **That is a stage 8 capacity finding, not an economic one — and the strongest argument for expanding cash while reforming delivery rather than the reverse.**

Tax: who pays.back: **Personal income tax: roughly 35–38% of total — the largest source. VAT: roughly 25%, at 15% with a zero-rated basket. Corporate income tax: roughly 16–18%, at 27% since 2022. Customs, excise and the fuel levy: roughly 12–15%.** Total gross tax revenue is on the order of **R1.7 to R2.0 trillion**, and **tax-to-GDP is around 25%** — high for a middle-income country, low for the spending it funds. **SARS's annual Tax Statistics is the best free document on this.**

Tax: who pays.front: How narrow the tax base is
Tax: who pays.back: **About 63 million people; 16–17 million employed; on the order of 7 million registered individual taxpayers expected to submit; the top decile of taxpayers pays the clear majority of PIT, and those earning over about a million rand — a few hundred thousand people — pay on the order of 40% of all PIT.** **Both conclusions are coherent:** the base cannot bear more and is fragile; **or** the narrowness is a symptom of unemployment, and the top decile's two-thirds income share means its tax share is not disproportionate.

**VAT is mildly regressive in itself** — the poor spend a larger share of income — **but South Africa zero-rates a basket of about 19 basic foodstuffs**, extended in 2019 to bread flour, cake flour and sanitary products. **Zero-rating is poorly targeted** (a wealthy household buying brown bread benefits more in rand terms) **and administratively simple and immediate.** **South Africa has a working transfer system, which is why economists prefer taxing VAT broadly and compensating through grants, and politics prefers zero-rating.**

**19 February 2025: the Budget was postponed on the day it was due — the first time in South African history** — the Cabinet having not agreed a framework reportedly including a two-point VAT increase. **12 March: a Budget proposing 0.5 points in 2025 and another in 2026.** **April: the fiscal framework adopted on a contested vote that split the coalition, with two parties going to court; the increase was then withdrawn.** **21 May: a third Budget, without it.** **A budget is now negotiated, and Parliament's Money Bills Act powers were finally used.**

Debt, and the fiscal question.front: The debt path, and the number that matters
Debt, and the fiscal question.back: **Gross national debt: about 26% of GDP in 2008–09, about 40% by 2012–13, about 50% by 2016–17, and mid-to-high 70s by the mid-2020s.** **Debt-service cost — on the order of R400bn a year, more than 20% of main budget revenue — is the number that matters, not the ratio.** A ratio is a claim about sustainability; **the interest bill is money that cannot be spent**, and it exceeds what is spent on health, or on police.

**The 2008–09 revenue collapse and a counter-cyclical response that became structural** (large). **The public wage bill** (large). **SOE bailouts and guarantees** — Eskom alone in the hundreds of billions, including about R254bn in 2023 (large and visible). **Slow growth** — the denominator. **The cost of borrowing** after the 2017 and 2020 downgrades to sub-investment grade. **Not on the list: social grants.** Grant spending grew and is not a principal driver — **the Budget Review's own figures do not support the most frequently blamed item.**

**For:** the interest bill's crowding-out is arithmetic, not opinion; a debt spiral is real if the interest rate exceeds the growth rate; the primary surplus is the stabilising condition. **Against:** the consolidation is real austerity, with real per-person spending falling; **its composition is wrong — it protected the wage bill and cut maintenance and capital**, converting an operating saving into a capital loss; and the debt is overwhelmingly rand-denominated and domestically held. **Both strongest points can hold at once, which means the real argument is about the wage bill.**

**Nominal GDP growth above the average effective interest rate on debt, with a primary surplus.** So the three numbers to watch are **nominal growth, the effective interest rate and the primary balance** — all in chapter 3 of every Budget Review. **And separately, the contingent liabilities: government guarantees to SOEs, which are not in the debt figure until they are called.** **GFECRA**, the Reserve Bank's foreign reserve valuation account, was drawn down from 2024 (on the order of R150bn over three years) — a real asset, not a repeatable source.

The public wage bill.front: The wage bill grew through pay, not headcount
The public wage bill.back: **Headcount has been roughly flat since about 2012 and falling in some functions; average real remuneration rose substantially over 2007–2020.** So **by headcount per capita South Africa's public service is not unusually large; it is unusually well-paid relative to the private sector at comparable skill levels**, particularly in the middle and lower grades. **Occupation-specific dispensations** for teachers, nurses, doctors and police drove much of it. **Compensation is on the order of R700–800bn, roughly a third of consolidated non-interest spending and 10–11% of GDP.**

The public wage bill.front: Why "cut the wage bill" does not meet the arithmetic
The public wage bill.back: **The composition is roughly 400,000 teachers, the health personnel, and 180,000–190,000 police.** So cutting it means **employing fewer teachers, nurses or police, or paying them less** — while stage 8's capacity problem is a shortage of skilled people in the state. **And the post-2020 consolidation held compensation roughly flat in nominal terms by not filling vacancies**, which protected the salaries of those in post and starved the functions that needed staff. **The worst available outcome for capacity.**

A three-year public service wage agreement was concluded in 2018; **the state did not implement the third year's increases in 2020**, citing unaffordability. **The Labour Appeal Court held clause 3.3 unlawful and invalid — concluded without compliance with the Treasury regulations requiring certification that an agreement with budget implications is affordable** — and the Constitutional Court declined to disturb it. **The principle: section 216 and the PFMA framework bind the bargaining process, so the state cannot validly sign what the fiscus cannot carry.**

Electricity as an economic constraint.back: **Began 2007.** Roughly **2,500 GWh shed in 2021; on the order of 11,500 GWh across about 3,800 hours in 2022; over 15,000 GWh across about 6,900 hours in 2023** — more than 70% of that year's hours at some stage of shedding — **and largely suspended from 2024.** The Reserve Bank and Treasury put the drag at **one to two percentage points of GDP growth** in the worst years. **The CSIR's annual Statistics of Utility-Scale Power is the free authoritative source.**

Electricity as an economic constraint.front: Why the electricity price matters more than the outages
Electricity as an economic constraint.back: **Before 2007 South Africa had among the cheapest electricity in the world — that was the minerals-energy complex's industrial strategy.** Since 2008 **Eskom's standard tariff has risen several hundred per cent nominally, far faster than inflation**, driven by Medupi and Kusile's capital cost, falling sales volumes, coal and diesel costs and the debt. **The energy-intensive industries built on cheap power — smelters, ferrochrome, aluminium — lost their reason to be here.** And **municipalities add their own markup on top.**

Electricity as an economic constraint.front: REIPPPP, and what the bid windows proved
Electricity as an economic constraint.back: The **Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme**, from 2011: **early solar PV bids around R3.50 per kWh, by the fourth window around R0.62** — one of the clearest demonstrations anywhere that **competitive procurement collapses renewable costs.** **The programme was obstructed between roughly 2015 and 2018 when Eskom declined to sign power purchase agreements.** Then **the embedded generation threshold went from 1 MW to 100 MW in August 2021 and licensing was dropped entirely**, producing a very large private build-out. **Transmission is now the binding constraint.**

**Move faster:** renewables are the cheapest new capacity, demonstrated by the bid windows; the export economy faces carbon pricing at the border regardless (**the EU's CBAM**); and **the *Deadly Air* judgment of 2022 held that Highveld air quality breached section 24.** **Move carefully:** the coal fleet is paid for; **Mpumalanga has 80,000–90,000 direct coal jobs** plus Eskom's, concentrated in a few towns; **Komati's decommissioning in 2022 ran far ahead of its repurposing**; and the JETP finance — $8.5bn pledged at COP26, later raised — **is mostly loans.**

Logistics: rail, ports and roads.back: **Transnet National Ports Authority is the landlord of the eight commercial ports and Transnet Port Terminals operates most of them** — so **the regulator of port access competes with the people who want access.** The same structural problem the electricity reform addressed by separating the grid, and what the **Economic Regulation of Transport Act (2024)** — creating an independent **Transport Economic Regulator** for ports, rail and pipelines — is meant to fix, as the precondition for fair third-party access.

Logistics: rail, ports and roads.front: The rail volume collapse, and its causes
Logistics: rail, ports and roads.back: **From about 226 million tonnes in 2017–18 to about 149 million in 2022–23** — a third of the volume in five years — with the coal export line railing around 47–50Mt against 81Mt of capacity. Causes in order: **locomotive availability** (the 1,064-locomotive programme left hundreds standing without spares after the supplier relationship broke down); **cable theft and vandalism** stripping whole corridors; **maintenance backlog**; **skills loss**; and **derailments and operating discipline.**

Logistics: rail, ports and roads.front: Ports, and the shift to road
Logistics: rail, ports and roads.back: **South Africa's container ports — Durban, Cape Town, Ngqura — have ranked near the very bottom of the World Bank and S&P Container Port Performance Index**, Durban at times in the last handful of several hundred. Causes: **equipment out of service, wind delays at Cape Town, landside congestion, systems failures** — with ships waiting days, which carriers price into freight rates. **Freight shifted to road, at several times the cost per tonne-kilometre for bulk** — money off the exporter's margin, or ore left in the ground, plus the road damage.

Land: the figures everybody cites.front: What the 2017 Land Audit's 72% is a share of
Land: the figures everybody cites.back: **Of the 37 million hectares of farms and agricultural holdings held by individuals — natural persons — white South Africans hold about 26.7m ha, roughly 72%.** **That is 72% of individually owned farmland, not of South Africa (122m ha) and not of all farmland.** The other 85m ha is state and trust land, and land held by **companies, trusts, close corporations, CPAs and churches — whose ownership the audit did not pierce.** **The skew is not in doubt; the exact degree is not measured.** State land is on the order of 14% of the surface.

**The Restitution of Land Rights Act 22 of 1994** gives a right to restitution to those dispossessed **after 19 June 1913** by racially discriminatory law or practice. **About 80,000 claims were lodged by the 31 December 1998 deadline**; most were settled, **most urban claimants took financial compensation**, and **3.5–4 million hectares were restored.** **The 2014 Act reopened the window (about 160,000 new claims) and was declared invalid in *LAMOSA v Chairperson, NCOP* (2016) for inadequate public involvement.** The 1913 cut-off is itself contested, and reasonably.

**A policy choice made after 1994, not a constitutional requirement.** **Section 25(3) requires "just and equitable" compensation reflecting an equitable balance between the public interest and the interests of those affected, having regard to five factors: current use; the history of acquisition and use; market value; the extent of direct state investment and subsidy; and the purpose of the expropriation.** **Market value is one of five factors, not the measure — so the compensation standard was never the constraint, because it was never tested.**

**The target of transferring 30% of commercial agricultural land was set in 1994 for five years, then moved to 2014, then to 2025. On the order of 10% has been transferred.** **Land reform has consistently received well under 1% of the national budget — on the order of 0.4%, declining in real terms through the 2010s.** **The target was never funded**, which the Motlanthe panel demonstrated by costing 30% at market value against the allocation.

Land reform: why it has not worked.back: **25(5) redistribution** — the state must take reasonable measures, within available resources, to foster conditions enabling citizens to gain access to land on an equitable basis. **25(6) tenure security** — for those whose tenure is insecure as a result of past racially discriminatory laws. **25(7) restitution** — for those dispossessed after 19 June 1913. **25(8)** — nothing in section 25 may impede land, water and related reform, subject to section 36. **The public argument is almost entirely about redistribution; tenure reform affects the most people and is barely discussed.**

Chaired by **former President Kgalema Motlanthe**, after extensive public hearings. On land it found **no evidence that section 25 was the binding constraint**, and identified instead **"increasing evidence of corruption by officials, the diversion of the land reform budget to elites, lack of political will, and lack of training and capacity"**, plus a budget far too small for the targets. **It recommended against amending section 25.** The **2019 Presidential Advisory Panel** reached broadly the same conclusion, with a majority against amendment and a dissenting minority for it.

**Post-settlement support** — land transferred without finance, equipment, extension advice, water or market access, with a substantial proportion of redistributed farms ceasing commercial production. **The leasehold turn: the State Land Lease and Disposal Policy of 2013 stopped transferring title**, so the state retains ownership and grants leases — **the beneficiary has no collateral and no asset, and the state becomes the landlord of farmers.** Plus **elite capture**, dysfunctional **Communal Property Associations**, and poor records of who received what.

**The Constitutional Court appointed a special master to oversee the processing of labour tenant claims** under the Land Reform (Labour Tenants) Act of 1996 — roughly 20,000 claims lodged by the 2001 deadline, which the department had failed for two decades to process. **A court taking over the administration of a statutory programme is an extraordinary remedy, and the Court said so.** **It is the clearest judicial statement that the land reform failure is administrative.**

BEE: what the law requires.back: **The Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment Act 53 of 2003 creates a measurement system; it does not require any private company to do anything.** It bites through three channels: **the state buys** (procurement on the order of a trillion rand a year, where a scorecard affects a bid); **licences and rights are conditional** (mining rights under the MPRDA and the Mining Charter, telecoms, financial services, liquor, gambling); and **large firms' own enterprise and supplier development points make them require compliant suppliers** — the mechanism that reaches the whole private economy.

BEE: what the law requires.front: The five elements and their weights
BEE: what the law requires.back: **Ownership 25 points** (priority). **Management control 19.** **Skills development 20** (priority). **Enterprise and supplier development 40** — the largest element (priority). **Socio-economic development 5.** Total 105–109 with bonus points. **So on the law's own arithmetic, 60 of 109 points are about procurement, supplier support and training, and 25 are about ownership** — which matters because the critique of BEE is overwhelmingly about ownership deals. **Miss a priority element's sub-minimum and your level drops one — the discounting principle.**

**The Constitutional Court held the 2017 Preferential Procurement Regulations invalid** — which had allowed an organ of state to require a minimum B-BBEE level or black ownership percentage **to bid at all** — **on the ground that the Minister exceeded the powers the PPPFA gave him**, with the declaration suspended twelve months. **Not that preference is unconstitutional: that these regulations were not authorised by the empowering statute.** The replacement is **the Public Procurement Act 28 of 2024**, with an explicit statutory basis for preference and set-asides and a single regulator.

BEE: what the law requires.front: Minister of Finance v Van Heerden (2004)
BEE: what the law requires.back: The test for a measure under **section 9(2)**, which permits measures designed to protect or advance persons disadvantaged by unfair discrimination: **does the measure target the disadvantaged; is it designed to protect or advance them; and does it promote the achievement of equality?** **So preferential measures are constitutionally authorised and are not exempt from scrutiny — a measure that fails the test is unconstitutional.** **Section 217(2)** separately permits categories of preference in procurement.

BEE: the evidence, both sides.front: Why measured black ownership ranges five-fold
BEE: the evidence, both sides.back: **The JSE's 2017 study found black South Africans held on the order of 23% of the available shares in the top 100 companies, counting direct holdings plus mandated investments — principally pension funds. An earlier NEF-commissioned study put it near 27%. Direct black ownership is much lower — single digits to low double digits.** **"Available shares" excludes the large foreign free float, and counting a pension fund's holding is contested: economically real for the member, conferring no control.** **A figure whose range is five-fold is a definitional dispute, not a factual one.**

**From the Commission for Employment Equity's annual report — every designated employer files into it — African South Africans remain a small minority of top management, on the order of a sixth to a fifth of posts, against roughly 80% of the economically active population, while white South Africans hold a clear majority.** **Lower and middle management and the professional grades have changed substantially.** **Transformation moved up the hierarchy slowly and stalled near the top — the strongest single piece of evidence in the argument, published annually.**

BEE: the evidence, both sides.front: What cannot be measured about BEE
BEE: the evidence, both sides.back: **There is no credible aggregate estimate of the BEE system's cost** — claims circulate; none rests on a defensible method. **The counterfactual is unknowable**, so both sides' assertions about it are assertions. **Growth-effect studies exist in both directions and none is decisive.** **Saying so is not evasion; it is the state of the evidence.** And the most interesting fact: **the obvious alternative — a class-based rather than race-based criterion — is widely proposed across the spectrum and has never been piloted at scale.**

BEE: the evidence, both sides.front: Where the black middle class came from
BEE: the evidence, both sides.back: **Its growth is substantial and not seriously disputed** — several-fold since the early 2000s, into the millions. **It came principally from the public service, state-owned enterprises, the professions, financial services and management posts in large firms — so substantially from employment and employment equity rather than from ownership deals.** **The most consequential redistribution of the post-1994 period happened through jobs and salaries, not through equity.**

RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela.back: **Growth, Employment and Redistribution**, announced February 1996, **not negotiated with the alliance partners and presented as "non-negotiable".** Targets: **6% growth and 400,000 jobs a year by 2000**, the deficit cut to 3% of GDP, tariffs down, exchange controls relaxed. **The macro stabilisation worked** — the deficit fell, inflation came down, debt fell toward the 26% of GDP the debt story starts from. **The growth and employment targets were missed substantially and formal employment fell.** **It bought the fiscal space that funded the grant system — and ruptured the alliance for a decade.**

**Vision 2030**, from the National Planning Commission chaired by Trevor Manuel — **the most intellectually serious of the six plans.** Targets: **11 million new jobs by 2030, unemployment down to 6%, growth averaging 5.4%, investment at 30% of GDP.** Its diagnosis names **"too few people work"** and **"the standard of education for most black learners is of poor quality"** first. **Adopted by Cabinet and endorsed by the ANC in 2012 — and never translated into departmental mandates, budgets or accountability.** No minister was measured against it.

RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela.front: Why Vulindlela worked and the plans did not
RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela.back: **RDP, GEAR, ASGISA, the New Growth Path and the NDP all specified outcomes — growth rates, job numbers — none specified who would be accountable for which action by when, and none met its headline target.** **Operation Vulindlela (2020), a small Presidency–Treasury unit, specified actions, owners and dates and published progress quarterly** — electricity, logistics, water, the 2022 spectrum auction, skilled immigration visas; then local government and housing from 2024. **A plan that names an outcome is a wish; one that names a regulatory change, an owner and a date is an instrument.**

RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela.front: The central dilemma of SA economic policymaking
RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela.back: **GEAR was imposed, achieved its macro targets, and cost alliance unity. The NDP was consensual and was never implemented.** Those two facts together are the dilemma, and nobody has a general solution to it. **And Vulindlela's limit: it works on things a regulation can fix.** It has no answer to the schooling system, the labour market or inequality — **the things that need money and decades rather than a regulatory change.**

Growth, and how to argue about the econo.back: **1994–2008: real GDP growth averaged on the order of 3.3–3.6%. 2009–2024: on the order of 1%.** And **from about 2012 GDP per capita has been falling** — population growth above 1% against output growth below it. **Say it plainly: the average South African has been getting poorer since roughly 2014. Not stagnant — poorer.** That is the economic condition in which the 2024 election happened.

**Gross fixed capital formation is around 14–15% of GDP, against the NDP's 30% target and fast-growing middle-income comparators at 25–35%.** **The cleanest single diagnostic: the economy is not replacing and expanding its capital stock fast enough to grow**, and both public and private investment are weak.

Growth, and how to argue about the econo.front: The five explanations for the post-2009 slowdown
Growth, and how to argue about the econo.back: **1 State capacity and capture** — electricity, rail, ports, water and municipal degradation as a direct supply constraint; the timing matches closely. **2 The commodity cycle** — the 1994–2008 boom was Chinese industrialisation, and its end explains the slowdown. **3 Electricity and logistics** — one to two points of growth in the worst years. **4 Policy uncertainty and the cost of doing business.** **5 Structure and demand** — an economy where 40% of working-age people have income has a small domestic market. **Not mutually exclusive; the weighting is the whole argument.**

Growth, and how to argue about the econo.front: The live test of the electricity explanation
Growth, and how to argue about the econo.back: **Load-shedding has largely stopped since 2024. If electricity carries most of the weight in explaining the post-2009 slowdown, growth should recover materially.** **That is a falsifiable prediction with a date, and it is being tested now** — which is what stage 1's "what would change your mind" looks like in practice. The counter to the commodity-cycle explanation runs the same way: **other commodity exporters did not stagnate for fifteen years, and South Africa failed to supply during the 2021 price spike because of rail and electricity.**

Growth, and how to argue about the econo.front: Four rules for arguing about the economy
Growth, and how to argue about the econo.back: **1 Name the base of every number** — an unemployment rate without its definition, a Gini without its base, a land percentage without its denominator, a BEE ownership figure without its method. Most economic disagreement here is definitional. **2 Separate the inherited from the current** — structure, geography and schooling are slow; electricity, logistics, appointment and procurement are fast. **3 State the counterfactual** and ask whether it is observable. **4 Name the test.** **A position that specifies no test is not an analysis.**

Why the parties are the unit.back: **South Africa's electoral system makes parties, not individuals, the units of political competition.** A national or provincial legislator sits on a list the party controls, owes their seat to the party rather than to any voter, and can be removed from the list. **Almost every accountability failure in stage 8 runs through that fact, and almost every reform proposal addresses it.** **The counter: closed-list PR delivered an accurately proportional Parliament, high women's representation, real seats for small parties, and no disputed national result.**

Why the parties are the unit.front: Parties as private organisations with public power
Why the parties are the unit.back: **Section 1 names a multi-party system; section 19 gives every citizen the right to form a party, participate in its activities and recruit members.** But parties are **voluntary associations whose internal rules are their own constitutions** — and **the courts enforce those rules, repeatedly, including by setting aside provincial conferences of the governing party.** **When a party holds a parliamentary majority, its internal rules are effectively part of the constitutional order.**

How a ballot becomes a seat.front: The 400 seats, and the two halves
How a ballot becomes a seat.back: **200 regional seats, allocated province by province from each party's regional list**, with provinces' totals fixed by their share of registered voters. **200 compensatory seats from a national list, bringing each party's total up to its national proportion.** The regional half gives provincial representation; **the compensatory half corrects any disproportionality, so the combined result is almost exactly proportional.** **Section 46 requires proportionality; it does not require closed lists — those are in the Electoral Act, which Parliament can change by ordinary legislation.**

How a ballot becomes a seat.front: The quota, and the absence of a threshold
How a ballot becomes a seat.back: **The Droop quota: total valid votes divided by 401, plus one.** Each party gets a seat per full quota, then **the remaining seats go to the largest remainders.** With roughly 16 million valid votes **a seat costs on the order of 40,000 votes.** **There is no threshold** — a party with roughly a quarter of one per cent gets a seat, which is why the Assembly holds more than a dozen parties. **A voter marks three ballots: national compensatory, regional, and provincial.**

The response to ***New Nation Movement v President* (2020)**, which held the Electoral Act unconstitutional for requiring candidates to stand only through parties, contrary to **section 19(3)(b)**. It allows an independent to contest **the regional ballot only**, on a signature requirement set as a percentage of the previous quota, **with no access to the 200 compensatory seats and no transferability of votes above one quota.** **Criticised as making the route formally available and practically unusable. No independent won a seat in 2024, and whether the Act satisfies the judgment is a live question.**

The local ballots, and the district oddi.front: Why winning wards does not win a council
The local ballots, and the district oddi.back: **Half a metro council is ward councillors elected first-past-the-post, half is list councillors — and the list seats are allocated so the council as a whole is proportional to the PR vote.** **So if a party wins more wards than its PR share justifies, it gets correspondingly fewer list seats.** The PR vote determines the council's composition; the ward vote determines who occupies your party's share of it. **Same principle as the national compensatory list.**

**A district council is 40% directly elected (the district PR ballot) and 60% made up of councillors appointed by the local councils in proportion to their populations.** **So you cannot vote a district council out**, and its accountability runs through the local councils. **Districts hold bulk water and sanitation in many areas, district health, regional planning, firefighting and disaster management** — so **the water function in much of rural South Africa sits with a council most residents did not elect and cannot name.**

The local ballots, and the district oddi.front: Why councils are so much less stable than Parliament
The local ballots, and the district oddi.back: **Proportional composition with no threshold plus many contesting parties means a council frequently has no majority** — after 2021, **on the order of 60 to 70 of 257.** **The council elects the mayor by majority and can remove them by simple majority at any time**, so a shift of two or three councillors changes the government of a city, **and a party with one or two seats can hold the balance.** **Parliament's five-year terms and the section 102 route make national government far more stable.**

The ANC as a movement.back: The ANC describes itself as **"a national liberation movement"** pursuing **"the National Democratic Revolution"**, of which winning elections is one instrument. **Four facts explain it: it was founded in 1912 against the 1913 Land Act, so it predates the apartheid state; it is a broad front by design — nationalists, communists, unionists, Christians and Africanists in one organisation; it was an army and a government-in-exile, which produces discipline and intolerance of public dissent; and it is the Freedom Charter's custodian.**

Adopted at the Congress of the People at Kliptown. Ten clauses, headed **"The People Shall Govern!"** The contested one: **"The mineral wealth beneath the soil, the banks and monopoly industry shall be transferred to the ownership of the people as a whole"**, and **"all the land re-divided amongst those who work it".** **Whether stage 6's settlement honoured or abandoned that clause is the argument that produced GEAR's reception, the nationalisation debates and the EFF.** **Those who read it as mandating nationalisation and those who read it as an anti-discrimination charter are both reading real text.**

**Internal decisions carry public authority** — a conference resolution is treated as a mandate, and the Scorpions' disbandment is the clearest case. **Collective discipline over individual mandate**, which interacts badly with the closed list and with oversight. **The movement outranks the state** — two presidents removed by a body with no constitutional standing. **"Deployment" rather than appointment** — coherent if the party is the revolution's custodian, unlawful according to Zondo. **And the defence: the broad-front character is also why the transition held.**

The ANC as an organisation.front: Why ANC branch procedure is a national matter
The ANC as an organisation.back: **Branch members elect conference delegates → conference elects the NEC and the party President → the party President becomes the country's President if the party holds a majority.** So for most of the period since 1994 **the decisive electorate was a few thousand conference delegates selected through branch meetings** — which creates an incentive to control branch membership. Hence **"gatekeeping", membership fraud and branch audit disputes**, and **courts repeatedly setting aside provincial conferences for breach of the party's own constitution.**

**Candidates run as a package** — a presidential candidate with a named Deputy, Secretary-General and so on — which concentrates support and **converts a leadership election into a factional contest.** The party's own conference resolutions and organisational reports have criticised the practice. **The consequence: the losing slate holds NEC seats, so the leadership is divided from the day it takes office** — which is the key to understanding the ANC-in-government's behaviour in stage 11.

Resolved at **Nasrec in 2017**, implemented by **NEC guidelines in 2021** requiring a member **criminally charged with corruption or another serious offence to step aside within 30 days**, failing which they are suspended; **the Secretary-General was suspended under it in 2021** and litigated; **the 2022 conference kept it.** **The only mechanism in South African politics that removes a person from office on being charged rather than convicted — and it is a party rule, not a law.** **Objection: it bypasses the presumption of innocence. Defence: a party may set standards for holding office in its name.**

**It controls membership records, branch audits and the organisational machinery — therefore who is in good standing and therefore who may vote at a conference.** **That is why the position is contested as hard as the party presidency.** And ANC membership **peaked above a million around 2012 and has fallen to the hundreds of thousands** at recent conference audits — read either as declining commitment or as the removal of fraudulent memberships by better auditing. **Both are claimed and both are partly true.**

Recalls, and the party above the state.back: **1** The party holds a majority of Assembly seats. **2** Those members sit on closed party lists. **3** **Section 47(3)(c): a member who ceases to be a member of the party loses the seat.** **4** So an MP who defies the party loses seat and salary. **5** The party's instruction to vote for a motion of no confidence is therefore credible. **6** A President who refuses to resign faces a section 102 motion they will lose. **7** Resignation is rational, and no vote is needed. **The closed list is what converts an internal party decision into a constitutional outcome.**

**September 2008: the ANC's NEC resolved to recall President Thabo Mbeki**, who resigned the next day nine months before his term's end; **Kgalema Motlanthe served as caretaker.** **February 2018: after the December 2017 conference elected a new party President, the NEC resolved to recall President Jacob Zuma**, who resisted for days and then resigned. **The constitutional basis of either recall: none. The NEC is a party body.** Premiers and mayors are recalled the same way, routinely.

Recalls, and the party above the state.front: Phala Phala, and the route that was used
Recalls, and the party above the state.back: In **2022 an independent panel under section 89**, appointed by the Speaker and chaired by a former Chief Justice, found **prima facie evidence of a serious violation warranting a full inquiry** into the Phala Phala matter. **The National Assembly voted not to proceed**, with the governing party's members voting as a bloc. **So the section 89 route exists, was exercised to the point of a panel report, and was stopped by the same majority-plus-closed-list mechanism that removed two previous Presidents.** **Both outcomes were produced by party discipline, not constitutional design.**

The Alliance.back: **The ANC, the SACP and COSATU**, with **SANCO** often counted as a fourth — **and only one of them contests elections.** The ANC gets electoral machinery and legitimacy with labour and the left; **the SACP gets positions and policy influence without ever testing its support at the ballot box**; COSATU gets direct access to government and the Nedlac seat. **The forum is the Alliance Political Council and periodic summits — which have no minutes, no statutory basis and no public reporting, and have shaped national policy.**

**1996 — GEAR**, announced without consultation and declared non-negotiable, which structured alliance politics for a decade. **2005–07 — the Zuma turn**: COSATU and the SACP backed Zuma against Mbeki, and **Polokwane in 2007 was substantially an alliance revolt.** **2012–15 — NUMSA**, COSATU's largest affiliate, called for a workers' party and was expelled; **SAFTU formed outside the alliance in 2017.** **2024 — both COSATU and the SACP opposed including the DA in the GNU, and the ANC did it anyway.**

The DA and its lineage.back: **United Party (1934–77) → Progressive Party (1959, eleven UP MPs broke away) → Progressive Reform Party (1975) → Progressive Federal Party (1977, official opposition) → Democratic Party (1989) → Democratic Alliance (2000, DP + New National Party + Federal Alliance).** **The NNP left in 2001 and merged into the ANC; the DA kept the name.** **Helen Suzman was the Progressive Party's only MP from 1961 to 1974** — thirteen years as a one-person opposition, which is the party's founding story, **and the 2000 absorption of the National Party's successor is the other half of the record.**

The DA and its lineage.front: The DA's vote share, and the plateau
The DA and its lineage.back: **1.7% (1994, DP) · 9.6% (1999) · 12.4% (2004) · 16.7% (2009) · 22.2% (2014) · 20.8% (2019) · 21.8% (2024).** **From 1.7% to 22% in twenty years, then a plateau at just over a fifth for three successive elections** — which is what the party's internal argument is about. **It has governed Cape Town since 2006 and the Western Cape since 2009**, with the best audit outcomes in the country and a real base-effect objection against that record.

**Should the party accept race-based redress?** **No:** non-racialism means the state must not classify by race; means-testing reaches the disadvantaged without the category; BEE's record shows race-based redress producing an elite. **Yes:** disadvantage was imposed by race and is still distributed by race; section 9(2) permits such measures; a party rejecting redress cannot win a majority here. **Under Maimane (2015–19) the party moved toward accepting it; after 2019 he left and a 2020 policy conference resolved against race as a proxy. Both sides cite the 21.8% of 2024.**

The EFF.back: **1** Expropriation of land without compensation for equal redistribution in use. **2** Nationalisation of mines, banks and other strategic sectors without compensation. **3** **Building state and government capacity, leading to the abolishment of tenders.** **4** Free quality education, healthcare, houses and sanitation. **5** Massive protected industrial development, including minimum wages. **6** Massive development of the African economy; from reconciliation to justice. **7** **Open, accountable, corruption-free government without fear of victimisation by state agencies.** **Pillars 3 and 7 are substantive institutional positions and are rarely engaged with.**

**The conduct:** "Pay back the money" in August 2014, repeated SONA disruptions including the 2015 signal jamming, removals by security. **The litigation:** ***EFF v Speaker* (2016)** — the Public Protector's remedial action binds unless set aside; ***UDM v Speaker* (2017)** — the Speaker may allow a secret ballot; ***EFF v Speaker* (2017)** — the Assembly was ordered to make section 89 impeachment rules, **which is why the 2022 Phala Phala panel existed.** **The party most criticised for disrupting Parliament created Parliament's impeachment procedure.**

The EFF.front: The EFF's results, and the 2024 reverse
The EFF.back: **6.35% (2014), from a standing start fourteen months after founding · 8.2% (2016 local) · 10.8% (2019) · 10.3% (2021 local) · 9.5% (2024), fourth place.** **The 2024 reverse has a specific cause: MK took a substantial share of the same constituency**, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal, and the EFF's own former deputy president left to lead MK's caucus. **The defence even opponents concede: expropriation without compensation, free higher education and the nationalisation question were marginal in 2013 and central by 2017.**

The IFP, and the regional parties.front: The IFP's record, which runs three ways
The IFP, and the regional parties.back: **Inkatha was founded in 1975 by Mangosuthu Buthelezi** and functioned as **the ruling party of the KwaZulu homeland.** Three established facts: **Buthelezi refused "independence" for KwaZulu — the only major homeland leader to do so, denying apartheid its central objective**; **the state security services covertly supported Inkatha in the 1990–94 violence** (about 14,000 deaths; roughly 200 Caprivi trainees trained by the SADF in 1986); and **the IFP's entry into the 1994 election a week before it prevented a catastrophe.** **All three are true.**

The IFP, and the regional parties.front: Why the long tail exists, and what it does
The IFP, and the regional parties.back: **No threshold, and a seat costs roughly a quarter of one per cent** — so in 2024 more than fifty parties contested and about eighteen won seats. **For no threshold:** every vote elects somebody; minority and regional views get real representation; new entry is possible, which is how the EFF and MK grew; it is what section 46 most naturally produces. **Against:** fragmentation makes coalitions unstable; **a party with one seat held the Johannesburg mayoralty from 2023**; and COPE's collapse shows low barriers also produce parties that cannot sustain themselves.

**The Congress of the People, formed in 2008 by the Mbeki-aligned faction after his recall**, led by Mosiuoa Lekota. **It won 7.4% in 2009 — then collapsed through internal leadership litigation to a fraction of a per cent.** **The cautionary tale of South African splits, and the base rate against which MK's durability should be judged.** Others in the tail: **FF+ (1994, Constand Viljoen, section 235 self-determination), ACDP, UDM (1997, Bantu Holomisa), GOOD (2018), ActionSA (2020), the Patriotic Alliance (2013), Al Jama-ah, Rise Mzansi, BOSA, the NFP.**

MK, and the 2024 realignment.back: **September 2023: the uMkhonto weSizwe Party was registered with the IEC by a private individual.** **16 December 2023: Jacob Zuma announced he would campaign for it.** **January 2024: the ANC suspended and later expelled him; its litigation to deregister the party failed.** **20 May 2024: the Constitutional Court held Zuma ineligible to stand under section 47(1)(e)** — convicted and sentenced to more than twelve months without the option of a fine. **29 May 2024: MK won 14.58% and 58 seats — third place — and about 45% in KwaZulu-Natal.**

**The party's platform proposes replacing constitutional supremacy with the sovereignty of Parliament**, so that Parliament rather than the Constitutional Court has the final word, plus **an unelected chamber of traditional leaders with legislative power.** **For:** the judicialisation critique taken to its conclusion — an elected majority should act without judicial veto. **Against:** every institutional gain in stages 7 and 8 came from justiciable rights and binding judgments, **and parliamentary sovereignty was the apartheid order's doctrine.** **And section 1 needs 75% plus six provinces, so it is unachievable.**

Why the ANC lost its majority.front: The ANC's vote share and vote count
Why the ANC lost its majority.back: **62.65% / 12.2m (1994) · 66.35% (1999) · 69.69% (2004) · 65.90% (2009) · 62.15% (2014) · 57.50% / 10.0m (2019) · 40.18% / about 6.5m (2024).** **A gradual decline from 2004, then seventeen points in one election — and about 3.5 million voters lost between 2019 and 2024, about 5.7 million against the 2009 peak.** Turnout, as a share of registered voters, fell every election: **about 89% (1999), 77% (2004 and 2009), 73% (2014), 66% (2019), 59% (2024), and 46% at the 2021 local elections.**

**Voting-age population about 42 million. Registered about 27.8 million — so roughly 14 million eligible adults were not on the roll. About 16.2 million voted — roughly 39% of eligible adults. The ANC's 40.18% of that is about 6.5 million: roughly one in six adults.** **The largest category by far is the roughly 26 million eligible adults who did not vote**, and **registration among 18-to-29-year-olds is far below the older cohorts.** **The born-free generation is substantially outside the system rather than voting against the ANC within it.**

**The MK split is the largest single factor** — 14.58%, concentrated in KwaZulu-Natal, most of it from the ANC's 2019 vote; without it the ANC would plausibly have been in the low 50s. Then **load-shedding in 2022–23 and municipal service failure; a decade of falling GDP per head; the Zondo findings with almost no prosecutions; July 2021; and generational replacement.** **Most of these are stage 8 and stage 9 material — the electoral result is the dependent variable.**

Coalitions, 2016 to now.front: Why the ANC chose the DA in 2024
Coalitions, 2016 to now.back: **The arithmetic forced a choice: 40.18% needed partners worth at least 10 points.** **ANC + MK** — MK's reported price was the President's removal, and they had just fought each other. **ANC + EFF** — the policy distance on property and the Reserve Bank, and the market reaction that Nenegate makes concrete. **ANC + DA + others** — taken. **A Statement of Intent signed 14 June 2024 by ten parties; Cabinet announced 30 June with roughly a dozen posts outside the ANC, the DA taking six.**

Coalitions, 2016 to now.front: The GNU's decision rule, and its weakness
Coalitions, 2016 to now.back: **"Sufficient consensus", with a clearing house mechanism for resolving disputes before they become public — both terms borrowed from CODESA.** **The structural problem: the agreement has no enforcement mechanism.** Sufficient consensus means a party can block and nothing happens if it does. **The 1994 precedent is the warning: the National Party walked out of the constitutionally mandated GNU in 1996 with two years to run, and nothing followed.** **Note the 1994 GNU was required by the interim Constitution; this one is a political agreement.**

**A threshold for coalition participation** — ending one-seat mayoralties. **A constructive vote of no confidence** — the German model: a mayor or President may only be removed if a replacement is simultaneously elected. **Cooling-off periods** barring no-confidence motions in a term's first and last year. **Codified, enforceable coalition agreements.** **Direct election of mayors.** **Most require only ordinary legislation.** **The honest counter: stability and accountability trade off — a constructive vote makes a bad mayor harder to remove too.**

Party funding.front: Section 236, and the two public funds
Party funding.back: **"To enhance multi-party democracy, national legislation must provide for the funding of political parties participating in national and provincial legislatures on an equitable and proportional basis."** **A positive constitutional duty to fund parties publicly, and one that is unambiguously met.** **The Represented Political Parties' Fund** distributes public money to parties in the legislatures on a largely proportional formula with an equitable component; **the Multi-Party Democracy Fund** pools private donations and distributes them on the same basis. Both administered by the IEC.

In force **1 April 2021**, forced by ***My Vote Counts v Minister of Justice* (2018)**, which held PAIA invalid for failing to provide for access to information on private party funding. **Disclosure of donations above R100,000 from a single donor in a financial year, published quarterly by the IEC; a cap of R15 million per donor per party per year; donations prohibited from foreign governments and agencies, organs of state and state-owned enterprises, and from anyone in exchange for a benefit.** **Before 2021 there was no disclosure at all.**

Party funding.front: What the funding disclosures do not cover
Party funding.back: **Donations below R100,000** — R99,000 from many sources is invisible. **In-kind support**, poorly captured. **Third-party spending** by organisations that are not parties, entirely unregulated. **Campaign spending**, which has no ceiling. **Incumbency advantage** — government advertising and state communication during a campaign. **And the largest gap: internal party leadership contests, which are outside the regime entirely — and from the recall lesson, an internal leadership contest selects the country's President.**

Party funding.front: Why the disclosed totals are implausible
Party funding.back: **Disclosed donations across all parties come to a few hundred million rands per electoral cycle**, concentrated in a small number of donors — **implausibly small against observed national billboard, broadcast, transport, rally and digital campaigns across nine provinces.** **When a published figure is implausible against observable reality, ask what the measurement excludes.** Here it is known: **the threshold, in-kind support, third-party spending and internal contests.**

Who owns the press.back: **Media24 (Naspers)** — News24, City Press, Rapport, Son, Daily Sun. **Arena Holdings** — Sunday Times, Business Day, Sowetan, Financial Mail. **Independent Media** — The Star, Cape Times, The Mercury, Pretoria News, bought in 2013 with substantial Public Investment Corporation financing. **Caxton** — The Citizen and a large free-local network. **Daily Maverick** — independent, reader-funded, with Scorpio. **Mail & Guardian.** Broadcast: **the SABC** (about nineteen radio stations, including the largest-audience African-language stations), **eMedia, MultiChoice, Primedia** — and **250–300 community radio stations**, the most under-discussed part of the map.

Who owns the press.front: The Guptas' media, and Bell Pottinger
Who owns the press.back: **The New Age (2010) and ANN7 (2013)**, Gupta-owned, **funded substantially by state advertising and bulk subscriptions taken by departments and state-owned enterprises** — public money funding a private outlet aligned with the family capturing the public entities. **Bell Pottinger, a London PR firm retained in 2016, ran a campaign built on "white monopoly capital", designed to reframe the capture allegations as an attack by white business on transformation.** **Exposed, the firm was expelled from its industry body in 2017 and collapsed within weeks — and the phrase outlived it.**

Who owns the press.front: What the collapse of print means for accountability
Who owns the press.back: **Most major South African newspapers have lost half or more of their circulation since around 2010**, with many titles closed and newsroom staff sharply down. **Court reporting, council reporting and provincial legislature reporting have thinned drastically** — and **a municipality with no local newspaper has no routine external scrutiny at all.** Digital and non-profit journalism replaced it in the metros and very little anywhere else, **with the strongest investigative work increasingly behind paywalls or donor-funded while the free layer thins.**

Press freedom, and its threats.front: How the Media Appeals Tribunal was avoided
Press freedom, and its threats.back: **The ANC's 2007 and 2010 resolutions proposed a statutory Media Appeals Tribunal with power over press content, accountable to Parliament.** The print industry established **the Press Freedom Commission, chaired by former Chief Justice Pius Langa**, which in 2012 recommended **"independent co-regulation"** — a self-regulatory body with **a majority of public, non-press members** and binding rulings. **That produced the Press Council in its current form, and the tribunal was not established.** **A credible threat producing real institutional reform.**

The Constitutional Court held **RICA unconstitutional** for failing to provide **post-surveillance notification** to the subject; for **inadequate safeguards for the designated judge's independence**; for **no safeguards on bulk interception**; and specifically **for failing to protect journalists' and lawyers' communications.** The background: **an investigative journalist's communications had been intercepted, which emerged years later.** **A journalist who cannot protect a source cannot do investigative work.**

**The Protection of State Information Bill** — broad classification powers, severe penalties for possession and publication, no adequate public interest defence — was introduced in 2010, opposed by **the Right2Know campaign**, **passed by Parliament in 2013, and has never been signed by the President.** **Passed, unassented, not law — for over a decade.** So **the apartheid-era secrecy statutes remain partly in force**, the reform did not happen either, **and the Bill remains available to be signed.**

The Constitutional Court held that **abuse of process may be raised as a defence** where defamation proceedings are brought not to vindicate a reputation but **to exhaust and silence a critic** — a **SLAPP suit**, Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation. **The cost of defending a defamation claim is itself the weapon, and a small outlet or an individual activist cannot carry it. The judgment gives them something to plead.**

Civil society's route through the courts.back: **Anyone may approach a court alleging a Bill of Rights infringement, acting: in their own interest; on behalf of another who cannot act in their own name; as a member of, or in the interest of, a group or class; IN THE PUBLIC INTEREST; or as an association acting in the interest of its members.** **Public interest standing is extraordinarily broad by comparative standards** — in many jurisdictions an organisation must show it is personally affected. **Here an NGO with no personal interest may litigate for people it has never met.**

Civil society's route through the courts.front: Why South African public interest litigation works
Civil society's route through the courts.back: **Broad standing (s38) + justiciable positive rights (ss26–29 with s7(2)'s duty to respect, protect, promote and fulfil) + flexible remedies (s172(1)(b): "any order that is just and equitable" — including a plan with dates and retained supervisory jurisdiction) + a judiciary that held + PAIA + donor, pro bono and Legal Aid funding.** **The result is a thirty-year record of enforceable orders against the state on housing, health, education, social security, the environment, elections and appointments.**

Civil society's route through the courts.front: The limits civil society names itself
Civil society's route through the courts.back: **A court order does not fix a pump** — litigation cannot supply engineers. **Non-compliance is routine**, which is why structural interdicts, supervisory jurisdiction and ultimately *Mwelase*'s special master emerged; each escalation answers a failure. **The separation of powers objection has force**, and the Court's answer is that it escalates only after ordinary remedies fail. **Cost and delay.** **Donor dependence**, now tightening. **And displacement: winning in court can substitute for organising politically, producing judgments without constituencies.**

Civil society's route through the courts.front: Black Sash v Minister of Social Development (2017)
Civil society's route through the courts.back: **The Constitutional Court supervised the social grant payment system through a crisis** — retaining jurisdiction, requiring reports, and ordering the contracted payment company to account for its profits. **Nineteen million people's grants depended on it.** The clearest demonstration of **section 172(1)(b)'s "just and equitable" remedial power** in practice, alongside ***Minister of Health v TAC* (2002)**, which ordered the state to provide nevirapine and is the most consequential public interest case in South African history.

Protest.front: Section 17, and where the qualifiers sit
Protest.back: **"Everyone has the right, PEACEFULLY AND UNARMED, to assemble, to demonstrate, to picket and to present petitions."** **The qualifiers are internal to the right** — a violent or armed gathering is **not protected at all**, and no section 36 limitation analysis is needed. The **Regulation of Gatherings Act 205 of 1993** requires **notice, not permission**: seven days to the municipality for a gathering over fifteen people, with prohibition only on specified grounds.
