***SATAWU v Garvas* (2012)** upheld **section 11 liability — the convenor and the organisation can be held liable for damage caused by a gathering**, subject to a defence. ***Mlungwana v S* (2018)** **struck down section 12(1)(a), which criminalised convening a gathering without notice**, as an unjustifiable limitation of section 17. **Together: the organiser bears civil liability for damage and is not criminally liable merely for failing to notify** — more protective than most comparable systems.

Protest.front: What the protest numbers show, and do not
Protest.back: **SAPS records on the order of ten to fifteen thousand crowd management incidents a year, the large majority recorded as peaceful.** **The "protest capital of the world" claim is overstated as usually made** — there is no comparable global dataset — **but the per-capita rate is genuinely high.** Causes: **water first, then electricity, housing, roads, jobs — and frequently local political disputes over a ward councillor's selection or conduct.** **So protest is not a clean signal of public opinion: some of it is mobilised within internal party contests.**

**Andries Tatane was killed by police on camera at a service delivery protest in Ficksburg in 2011; the officers were acquitted.** **Abahlali baseMjondolo, the Durban shack dwellers' movement, has had more than twenty leaders and members assassinated since 2018.** **Political killings of councillors, candidates and officials in KwaZulu-Natal are a sustained pattern.** **Babita Deokaran, a senior Gauteng health official who had flagged irregular payments, was assassinated in 2021.** **This is stage 8's impunity finding in its most serious form, and the failure is the detective service.**

Migration politics.front: The migration numbers, and the claims
Migration politics.back: **Census 2022 counted roughly 2.4 million foreign-born residents — about 4% of the population.** Allowing for undercount, **a credible range is roughly 2 to 4 million.** **Public debate frequently claims 10 to 15 million, which rests on nothing traceable** — Africa Check has repeatedly traced such figures to assertion or misread Home Affairs data. **15 million would mean one in four people is foreign-born, which no census, school enrolment or mortality statistic supports.** **Local pressure in specific neighbourhoods is still real; a national policy built on 15 million is not.**

**The Refugees Act 130 of 1998 is strong on paper** — non-refoulement, the right to work and study while a claim is pending. **The 2017 Amendment, in force 2020, restricted the automatic right to work and allowed claims to be deemed abandoned.** **The appeal backlog has run into the hundreds of thousands, with waits of many years** — so **a person with a pending claim for a decade cannot work formally and cannot be deported.** **The Zimbabwean Exemption Permit termination (about 178,000 permits) was declared unlawful by the Gauteng High Court in 2023 for procedural unfairness.**

Migration politics.front: Where both sides of the migration argument converge
Migration politics.back: **Enforcement case:** a state that cannot control entry cannot plan services; local pressure is real; undocumented status enables exploitation that undercuts local workers. **Against:** the numbers are a fraction of what is claimed; the employment evidence mostly finds migrant workers neutral or net job-creating; street-level document checks catch South Africans without ID and have been found unlawful; the violence is lethal and rhetoric is implicated. **Both columns end at Home Affairs' capacity** — a system that decides claims in months is what both sides' strongest arguments require.

Migration politics.front: Centre for Child Law v Minister of Basic Education (2020)
Migration politics.back: Held that **undocumented children may not be excluded from schools** — **section 29's right to basic education, read with section 28, attaches to the child and not to the parent's documentation.** Alongside ***Khosa v Minister of Social Development* (2004)**, which held **permanent residents could not be excluded from social grants** because section 27 says "everyone". **Two judgments establishing that some rights do not depend on immigration status.**

What the party system is becoming.front: The three scenarios, with their tests
What the party system is becoming.back: **1 Consolidation into two or three blocs** — coalition becomes routine and small parties are squeezed. **Test: do small parties' shares fall in 2026 and 2029, and do GNU parties campaign as a bloc?** **2 Continued fragmentation and paralysis** — no threshold, low entry barriers, 26 million non-voters as a grievance base. **Test: MK's and ActionSA's 2026 local results, and whether a new party polls above 5%.** **3 Realignment around the constitutional question** — the dividing line becomes acceptance of the 1996 settlement. **Test: whether MK's and the EFF's combined share rises and their constitutional positions become more central.**

**The Electoral Task Team recommended a mixed system — multi-member constituencies plus a compensatory national list — keeping proportionality while giving every voter a named representative.** **It was shelved and has been revived in every reform discussion since, including by the Zondo Commission.** **Crucially, it needs only an amendment to the Electoral Act**, because section 46 requires proportionality and a mixed-member proportional system satisfies that. **So does a threshold, coalition stability legislation, and open lists.**

What the party system is becoming.front: The seven things to watch in a South African election
What the party system is becoming.back: **1 Turnout** — 46% at the 2021 local elections is the benchmark. **2 MK's local result against its 14.58%** — does a party built in eight months have ward structures? **3 The ANC's floor** — 45% locally in 2021, 40% nationally in 2024: which is the trend? **4 The DA's ceiling** — three elections at 21–22%. **5 Whether the SACP contests independently**, which would end the alliance as constituted since 1990. **6 Hung councils against 2021's 60–70.** **7 Independents winning wards** — the one ballot where a voter chooses a person.

How to read the last thirty years.front: The four arguments about 1994 to now
How to read the last thirty years.back: **1 Was 1994 a revolution or a transfer of political power only?** The achievement view against the incomplete-revolution view, both citing the same data. **2 Is the decline about one man or the organisation?** The Zuma-centred account against the structural one — and the arms deal predates him by a decade. **3 Was the economic decline policy failure or capacity failure?** Stage 9's five explanations. **4 Did the Constitution constrain or enable?** It held in the courts; it could not supply detectives.

How to read the last thirty years.front: Five rules for reading recent South African history
How to read the last thirty years.back: **1 Date everything** — a claim true of 2015 may be false of 2010; the capture project accelerated sharply after 2014. **2 Separate the finding from the allegation** — a commission's finding, a judgment, a report and a politician's claim are four evidentiary classes. **3 Name the source's position** — almost every account is by a participant or an opponent. **4 Check whether a number was ever substantiated.** **5 Watch for the achievement that gets forgotten** — the HIV programme, electrification, water and the grants are the largest measurable changes and feature in almost no political account.

The Mandela presidency, 1994-1999.back: **Eleven separate administrations to merge** — the central state, four provinces, and the homelands — with incompatible systems. **A civil service guaranteed in post by the sunset clauses.** **High inherited debt, honoured.** **Roughly a third of households without electricity**, millions without piped water, a housing backlog in the millions. **Nineteen racially separate education departments.** **And the KwaZulu-Natal and Reef violence had not fully stopped.** **All while writing the final Constitution, which was certified in 1996.**

**The institutions of stages 7 and 8 all date from it:** the Constitutional Court (1995), the Public Protector, the SAHRC, the IEC, the Land Claims Court, the CCMA and Labour Court, the Gender Commission. **The labour statutes:** LRA 1995, BCEA 1997, Employment Equity Act 1998. **Delivery:** mass electrification, piped water, RDP housing, free health care for pregnant women and children under six, one education system, school feeding. **And the TRC.** **An extraordinary volume of institution-building in five years.**

The Mandela presidency, 1994-1999.front: Three things about Mandela's presidency usually left out
The Mandela presidency, 1994-1999.back: **He served one term by choice**, setting a precedent that has held. **He delegated domestic administration substantially to Deputy President Mbeki**, so much of the "Mandela-era" policy record is Mbeki's work. **And the foreign policy was more contested than the hagiography allows** — the recognition switch from Taiwan to China, arms sales to questionable buyers, the failed Nigerian intervention over Ken Saro-Wiwa in 1995, and the 1998 Lesotho intervention.

The arms deal.back: Approved **1999**: **four frigates and three submarines from German consortia; 24 Hawk trainers and 26 Gripen fighters from BAE Systems and Saab; 30 light helicopters from Agusta.** **Announced at about R30 billion; eventual cost estimates run to R70 billion and above.** **A country with a massive service backlog, a debt problem and no external military threat, buying fighter jets** — and from the SANDF lesson, **the equipment cannot now be operated for lack of operating budget.**

Established **2011** to investigate the arms deal; **two of its own senior staff resigned alleging a "second agenda" to protect those implicated**; its **2016 report found no evidence of corruption by anybody.** **In August 2019 the High Court set its findings aside in full**, holding it had failed to inquire fully and comprehensively, had not tested evidence, and had not confronted witnesses with contradictory material. **And then nothing — no new commission was appointed.** **Compare Zondo, whose findings have not been set aside.**

The arms deal.front: Why the arms deal is the template
The arms deal.back: **A very large procurement few can evaluate; intermediaries and "advisers" taking fees; offsets promised and never audited to a conclusion; an investigation whose draft report was altered; a commission that found nothing and was set aside; prosecutions of intermediaries, not principals** — Shaik and Yengeni convicted, no senior decision-maker; **and foreign prosecutors doing the work South African ones did not**, with BAE settling with the US Department of Justice. **Every one of those features recurs in state capture.**

Mbeki: the technocratic presidency.back: **Growth averaged above 4% from 1999 to 2008, exceeding 5% in the boom years; the deficit was eliminated and a surplus achieved by 2006–07; debt fell toward 26% of GDP.** The grant system expanded very substantially — **the Child Support Grant, introduced 1998, grew to cover millions.** Institutions built: **the Scorpions (1999), SARS's modernisation, inflation targeting (2000), the PFMA framework (1999).** **The strongest growth and fiscal record of the post-1994 period — which is why what followed is called the lost decade.**

**Engagement with the Zimbabwean government rather than condemnation or sanctions, through SADC mediation.** **For:** no good instruments existed; sanctions would have hit Zimbabwean workers; public condemnation would have forfeited the mediating role; **and the mediation produced the 2008 Global Political Agreement.** **Against:** the 2002 and 2008 elections were not free, the agricultural economy was destroyed, hyperinflation had no modern parallel, **and millions of Zimbabweans came to South Africa.** **The sharpest episode: a South African court restrained the *An Yue Jiang* arms shipment the executive had cleared.**

**The African Renaissance** as the framing idea. **The AU replaced the OAU in 2002**, with heavy South African drafting input and a Constitutive Act permitting intervention in grave circumstances. **NEPAD (2001)** traded governance reform for investment and aid, with **the African Peer Review Mechanism** as its accountability device — **which never acquired teeth.** **The DRC and Burundi mediations were central and substantially successful** — the strongest part of the record.

AIDS denialism.back: **A 2008 Harvard School of Public Health analysis estimated on the order of 330,000 excess deaths and 35,000 avoidable infant infections** from the delayed antiretroviral rollout and the refusal of mother-to-child prophylaxis. **It is a modelled counterfactual and the figure depends on the assumed feasible rollout rate — the order of magnitude, hundreds of thousands, is not seriously disputed.** Meanwhile **life expectancy fell from the low 60s in 1990 to about 53 by the mid-2000s** — a decade lost in peacetime.

**That HIV does not cause AIDS or the link is unproven; that antiretrovirals are toxic; that the real causes are poverty and malnutrition.** **1997: Virodene, an industrial solvent promoted as a cure.** **2000: the Presidential AIDS Advisory Panel, convened with AIDS dissidents as members.** **July 2000: the Durban conference address that did not attribute AIDS to HIV, prompting the Durban Declaration signed by over 5,000 scientists.** The Health Minister advocated garlic, beetroot and olive oil. **And the state refused to provide ARVs in the public sector.**

**Founded in 1998 by Zackie Achmat and others — a mass-membership movement of people living with HIV, combining street mobilisation, scientific literacy and litigation.** **In 2001 it joined as amicus the case in which 39 pharmaceutical companies sued the South African government over the Medicines Act's parallel importation and generic substitution provisions — the companies withdrew, in a global turning point on access to medicines.** **In 2002 it won the nevirapine case in the Constitutional Court.** **Cabinet approved the treatment plan in 2003 and the rollout began in 2004** — the most consequential public interest litigation in South African history.

AIDS denialism.front: Hold both halves of the AIDS story
AIDS denialism.back: **The same state caused hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths through denialism and then built the largest HIV treatment programme in the world** — **on the order of 5.5 million people on antiretrovirals, with life expectancy recovering from about 53 to the mid-60s, and mother-to-child transmission down to very low single digits.** **Stage 8's thesis — that outcomes turn on specific decisions and appointments rather than on design — has no better illustration.**

The health system, and NHI.back: **Roughly 16% of the population — about 9 to 10 million people on medical schemes — accounts for roughly half of all health spending; the remaining 84% uses the public system.** Total health spending is around 8 to 9% of GDP. **And the Competition Commission's Health Market Inquiry (2019) found the private sector highly concentrated, with weak competition, opaque pricing and no effective regulator of prices or outcomes — so the private half is not a well-functioning market either.**

**HIV and TB** — the world's largest ART programme, and among the highest TB incidence rates globally. **Maternal, newborn and child mortality** — substantially improved since 2009. **Non-communicable disease** — hypertension, diabetes, obesity and cancers rising sharply, **in a system built for infectious disease.** **Injury and violence** — trauma units carrying the load of the murder, assault and road death rates. **Four epidemics at once, which no single health system design is optimised for.**

**For:** the two-tier system is indefensible and incremental reform has not changed it in thirty years; a single purchaser has the buying power that is the only answer to the Health Market Inquiry's concentration finding; section 27 obliges progressive realisation. **Against:** a single fund needs state administrative capacity that stage 8 gives reason to doubt; restricting medical schemes removes 10 million people's exit option and their funding; the fiscal space does not exist. **Almost nobody defends the current system — the dispute is about the vehicle and the sequence.**

Crime since 1994.back: **About 67 per 100,000 in 1994–95; about 47 in 2002–03; about 30 in 2011–12 — the low point; about 45 by 2023–24.** In absolute terms roughly **26,000 murders in the mid-1990s, 15,600 in 2011–12, and above 27,000 by the mid-2020s.** **A halving and then a two-thirds increase — and the two movements have different explanations**, which is why this is the most informative crime statistic in the country.

Crime since 1994.front: Why the murder rate fell and then rose
Crime since 1994.back: **Fell:** political violence ended; **the Firearms Control Act (2000, in force 2004)** tightened licensing, with a measurable decline in firearm homicide; economic growth; **real increases in police, detective and forensic capacity in the 2000s**; demography. **Rose:** **police capacity collapse** — detectives, forensics, crime intelligence; **illegal firearms, including thousands of confiscated guns sold by a senior police officer to Cape gangs**; extortion economies; gang economies; stagnation; **and impunity — a murder that will not be solved deters nobody.**

**Roughly 180,000 to 190,000 police, against on the order of 2.5 million registered private security officers with several hundred thousand actively employed** — one of the largest such ratios in the world. **So personal security in South Africa is substantially a purchased private good, which means its distribution follows income** — the people in the highest-crime areas have the least protection. **And the Equality Court held that police human resource allocation unfairly discriminated on race and poverty**, following the Khayelitsha Commission (2014).

Education since 1994.front: What the education system achieved, and did not
Education since 1994.back: **Achieved: one system from nineteen; per-learner spending equalised and then reversed in favour of poorer schools; near-universal enrolment for ages 7–15 and near-universal Grade R; no-fee schooling for 75–80% of schools; a meal a day to 9–10 million learners; higher education enrolment roughly doubled — all on education spending of about 6% of GDP, among the world's highest.** **Not achieved: outcomes. PIRLS 2021 found about 81% of Grade 4s could not read for meaning in any language, the lowest of all participants.** **Access was solved.**

Education since 1994.front: Why the matric pass rate misleads
Education since 1994.back: **The NSC pass rate rose from around 60% in the late 2000s to the high 80s — and it is calculated on those who write.** **Of roughly 1.2 million who start Grade 1, on the order of 700,000 write matric**, so a rising pass rate with falling throughput can mean the weakest were not entered. **The pass requirement is 30% in some subjects and 40% in others.** **Use instead: bachelor passes as a share of the original Grade 1 cohort — on the order of 15% or less.**

**The Ministerial Task Team report of 2016 found the sale of teaching and principal posts in six provinces**, involving union and departmental officials. **Stage 8's appointment thesis, in schools.** Alongside the other diagnosis items: **early grade reading instruction** (the consensus cause), **teacher subject knowledge** after the teacher training colleges closed, **measured teaching time below the curriculum's requirement**, **pit latrines and the *Komape* litigation**, and **the Grade 4 transition to English**.

Gender, and gender-based violence.back: **Women are roughly 45 to 46% of the National Assembly — among the highest shares in the world — achieved through party list quotas rather than statute.** The law is extensive: section 9's prohibited grounds, reproductive autonomy under s12(2)(a), the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act, *Bhe*, the Recognition of Customary Marriages Act, same-sex marriage from 2006. **And the rate at which women are killed is roughly five times the global average.** **Formal equality is extensive and well-enforced; the violence is among the worst measured anywhere.**

**On the order of 40,000 to 55,000 sexual offences are reported a year, and the Victims of Crime Survey indicates only a small fraction of offences are reported at all.** **The published research on rape case attrition found a conviction in well under a tenth of reported cases**, with cases lost at every stage from docket to court. **This is not a gap in the law** — the binding constraints are **detective capacity, the DNA backlog, withdrawal under pressure, and secondary victimisation in the process itself.**

***Carmichele v Minister of Safety and Security* (2001)** — **the state can be liable in delict for failing to protect a woman from a known violent offender**; police and prosecutors had not opposed bail for a man with a history. **A foundational judgment on the state's positive duty under section 12.** ***Tshabalala v S* (2020)** — **the common purpose doctrine applies to rape**, so a participant in a group attack is liable for rapes committed by others without having perpetrated the act personally.

**The #TotalShutdown marches of August 2018, then the first Presidential Summit on GBVF in November 2018 and its declaration; the National Strategic Plan on GBVF (2020) with six pillars; three Acts signed in January 2022** — **the Domestic Violence Amendment Act, the Criminal and Related Matters Amendment Act and the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act** — **and the National Council on GBVF Act (2024).** Plus **about 60 Thuthuzela Care Centres** and dedicated sexual offences courts. **The architecture is now extensive and the conviction rate has not moved correspondingly.**

The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018.back: **2005: dismissed as Deputy President after Shaik's conviction, and charged. 2006: acquitted in a rape trial. December 2007: defeated Mbeki at Polokwane. September 2008: a High Court judgment suggesting interference triggered Mbeki's recall — and was later overturned on appeal. April 2009: the NDPP withdrew the charges, citing the "spy tapes".** **The High Court set that withdrawal aside as irrational and the SCA upheld it, so the charges were reinstated in 2018.** **The charges were withdrawn weeks before he became President, and the withdrawal was later held irrational.**

The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018.front: What the courts stopped between 2009 and 2018
The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018.back: ***Earthlife Africa v Minister of Energy* (2017)** — **the Western Cape High Court set aside the 9,600 MW nuclear determination and the intergovernmental agreements as unlawful**, for want of proper public participation and NERSA concurrence. **A procurement potentially running to a trillion rand, stopped by two NGOs in a high court.** Also **the SCA's 2016 Al-Bashir judgment** and **the spy tapes decisions.** **Stage 8's finding that the judiciary held — this is the evidence.**

The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018.front: The Zuma-era record that is not negative
The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018.back: **The largest HIV treatment expansion in the world happened in this period, and life expectancy rose by roughly a decade.** **Grant coverage and value expanded substantially.** **Free higher education was announced in December 2017.** **NHI policy was developed.** **South Africa joined BRICS in 2010.** **The 2010 World Cup was delivered.** **And the renewable energy bid windows of 2011–2015 were among the most successful public procurements in South African history — and the same administration then refused to sign the resulting contracts.**

Nkandla.back: The Public Protector's report on **about R246 million of state money spent at the President's private homestead at Nkandla.** It found **the swimming pool, amphitheatre, cattle kraal, chicken run and visitors' centre were not security features**; that **he and his family had unduly benefited**; that he had **breached the Executive Ethics Code** by not stopping the escalation; and **directed that he repay a reasonable percentage as determined by Treasury.** **A 2015 ministerial report concluded the pool was a fire-fighting reservoir — the "fire pool" — and that he need not repay anything.**

***EFF v Speaker; DA v Speaker* (31 March 2016):** **the Public Protector's remedial action is binding unless set aside by a court**; **the National Assembly's resolution absolving the President was unlawful and invalid**, having no power to set the remedial action aside; and **the President had failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution** under section 83(b). **Treasury determined about R7.8 million and he paid it.** **A unanimous Court found the Assembly acted unlawfully and the President failed in his constitutional duty — which had never happened before.**

Nkandla.front: Why Nkandla mattered more than its cost
Nkandla.back: **R246 million is small against the capture-era SOE contracts, and it did more political damage than any of them — because it was legible.** A swimming pool at a private house is a fact anybody can hold; a locomotive procurement's escalation is not. **It produced the binding-remedial-action holding, which made the Public Protector's office powerful. And it gave that office the standing to issue *State of Capture* in October 2016, which produced the Zondo Commission.** **Nkandla is the causal chain's first link.** **The April 2016 impeachment motion failed.**

The Guptas, and how capture worked.front: The capture method, in seven steps
The Guptas, and how capture worked.back: **1 Place people** — allies on boards, in CEO and CFO posts and in ministries. **2 Control the procurement process.** **3 Insert an intermediary** — a company with no capability between the SOE and the real supplier, taking a fee for nothing. **4 Use the state's own money as working capital.** **5 Buy the narrative** — the media outlets and Bell Pottinger. **6 Discredit the enforcers** — SARS's "rogue unit", the attacks on Treasury, the NPA's leadership. **7 Launder and move the proceeds.** **Steps 1 and 6 are the same insight from two directions.**

**A Glencore-owned colliery supplying Eskom was put under contractual and penalty pressure, went into business rescue, and was acquired by Tegeta — a Gupta-linked company. Eskom then made a prepayment of about R659 million to Tegeta, which the Zondo Commission found was used to fund the acquisition itself.** **The state's own money as the working capital for the purchase of the state's own supplier.** Alongside **Estina (about R220m), the 1,064-locomotive escalation with over a billion rand in advisory fees, and the offer of cash and the finance ministership to Mcebisi Jonas.**

**March–April 2016: South Africa's major banks closed the Gupta companies' accounts** — a commercial decision that did more immediate damage than any state action. **May–June 2017: the #GuptaLeaks, roughly 200,000 emails leaked to amaBhungane, Scorpio and News24** — the most consequential journalism in South African history. **February 2018: the family left for Dubai.** **June 2022: two brothers arrested in the UAE. 2023: the extradition failed.** **None of the brothers has been convicted in a South African court.**

The Guptas, and how capture worked.front: "State capture" is not a synonym for corruption
The Guptas, and how capture worked.back: **The term entered South African use through the Public Protector's October 2016 report title, *State of Capture*.** **In the political science literature it means the systematic repurposing of state institutions to serve private interests — as distinct from episodic bribery.** **That distinction is what stage 8's institutional analysis rests on:** episodic bribery costs money; capture costs the institution's capacity, which is a multiple of the money.

The Zondo Commission.back: **October 2016: the Public Protector's *State of Capture* directed the President to appoint a commission headed by a judge selected by the Chief Justice.** **He litigated against it and lost in the High Court in December 2017.** **January 2018: the commission was established by proclamation**, chaired by Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo. **A Chapter 9 institution compelled the President to appoint a commission, through a court, against his resistance** — the binding-remedial-action holding doing work.

**Hearings from August 2018 to mid-2021 — on the order of 300 days, broadcast live; about 300 oral witnesses and several hundred more affidavits; on the order of 1.7 million pages of evidence; a cost of about a billion rand; and roughly 5,500 pages of report delivered in five parts between January and June 2022.** **Part One: SAA, SARS, the New Age and government advertising. Two: Transnet and Denel. Three: Bosasa and Transnet. Four: Eskom. Five: the SSA, Parliament, cadre deployment, the ANC, and the recommendations.**

**Achieved: the record — 5,500 pages of tested, free, publicly available evidence, which is why findings can be cited rather than allegations; it survived, with no part set aside by a court, unlike Seriti; a coherent institutional reform agenda, parts of which were implemented (IDAC, the Public Procurement Act); and it made defiance costly.** **Did not: prosecutions, recovery, or the appointment reforms — the highest-leverage recommendations.** **A commission establishes what happened; a prosecution requires a prosecutor, an investigator and a court.**

**Zuma appeared before the Commission once, in July 2019, then refused to return despite summonses. In January 2021 the Constitutional Court ordered him to appear and answer questions; he publicly defied the order; in June 2021 the Court found him in contempt and sentenced him to fifteen months' imprisonment.** **He surrendered on 7 July 2021, and the unrest began two days later.** **There is no more direct demonstration that section 165(5) — a court order binds all persons — is enforceable.**

What Zondo found about Parliament and th.back: **It found Parliament failed in its constitutional duty to hold the executive accountable** — committees did not pursue warnings put to them, SCOPA's work was not acted on, and **the governing party's caucus acted to shield the executive**, including by adopting the Nkandla absolution resolution. **The Eskom inquiry of 2017–18 was used to show the failure was a choice, not an incapacity.** **Recommendations: a dedicated mechanism for overseeing the Presidency; committee research capacity; that oversight duty prevail over party instruction; and a constituency element in the electoral system.**

**Cadre deployment as conducted was found unlawful and unconstitutional**, because the committee's recommendations extended into appointments the law requires to be made on merit — **and the Commission obtained the committee's minutes.** **The party received money from implicated entities, including Bosasa, whose business model it found was the systematic bribery of officials.** **It recommended legislation making party involvement in state appointments unlawful, regarded the step-aside rule as insufficient, and warned that dominant-party processes selecting the state's leadership had made the capture possible.**

What Zondo found about Parliament and th.front: Why Zondo's Part Five matters most
What Zondo found about Parliament and th.back: **The transactions are history — the locomotives were bought, the money is gone. The mechanisms are current: cadre deployment, the closed list, committee under-resourcing, party funding thresholds and whistleblower exposure all still exist.** **So the implementation record is the real measure** — IDAC and the Public Procurement Act were real; **the appointment reforms, electoral reform and the whistleblower regime were not.** **And the highest-leverage recommendations are precisely the ones that reduce patronage.**

The state capture arithmetic.back: **It was used by senior officials from around 2019 and entered general circulation. What it does not have is a published method** — no document sets out what was counted, over what period, on what basis — **and the Zondo Commission did not endorse a single aggregate.** **A figure with no traceable method is not a measurement, however senior the person repeating it.** That does not mean the cost was small; **it means the number is not evidence. Use the measurable components instead.**

The state capture arithmetic.front: Where the recovery actually came from
The state capture arithmetic.back: **McKinsey repaid about a billion rand of Transnet and Eskom fees and its Africa unit later entered a US deferred prosecution agreement with a large penalty; SAP repaid hundreds of millions of rand and settled with the US DOJ and SEC; ABB settled with South African authorities for about R2.5 billion plus a very large US penalty; Bain repaid its SARS fees and was barred from UK government contracting; KPMG repaid its SARS fees.** **Plausible total recovered: on the order of ten billion rand, overwhelmingly from settlements — not from South African prosecutions.**

The state capture arithmetic.front: The theft was the mechanism; the institutional damage was the cost
The state capture arithmetic.back: **Eskom's load-shedding cost one to two percentage points of GDP growth in 2022 and 2023 — far more than the money stolen from Eskom. Transnet lost a third of its rail volume, and the foregone export revenue exceeds the contract irregularities by a wide margin. SARS's revenue shortfall ran to tens of billions a year.** **And capture's most effective self-protection was the destruction of the institutions that would have prosecuted it** — which fully explains why two commissions thirty years apart produced findings and almost no criminal consequence.

Marikana.back: **Police moved to disperse and disarm striking rock drill operators at Lonmin's platinum operations, who had struck outside the bargaining process for R12,500 a month.** **Ten people had been killed in the preceding week, including two police officers and two Lonmin security guards.** **On 16 August 34 were killed — 17 at "Scene One" in front of television cameras, and 17 more at "Scene Two" around the koppie, out of camera view, many at close range — with 78 wounded.** **About 270 arrested miners were initially charged with their colleagues' murders; the charges were withdrawn after outcry.**

**The police plan was defective and dangerous, adopted late, and unlawful in material respects.** **The police misled the commission and altered and withheld documents.** **The National Commissioner was found not fit and proper.** Lonmin was criticised for its unfulfilled living-conditions undertakings; findings were made against both unions over the preceding week. **On political responsibility it found no improper influence on the police operation, having considered Ramaphosa's "concomitant action" email and his ministerial contacts** — a contested finding. **No police officer has been convicted.**

**The constitutional mandate functioned; the commission functioned, was thorough and severe, and was not set aside; the oversight bodies functioned — IPID investigated and a board of inquiry removed the commissioner — and nobody was prosecuted.** **The design worked, the inquiry worked, and the consequence did not.** Politically: **the largest police killing since Sharpeville in 1960**, which drove AMCU's rise, the five-month 2014 platinum strike, **the EFF's founding in 2013**, and lasting damage to the ANC's standing with workers.

RhodesMustFall and FeesMustFall.back: **March 2015: #RhodesMustFall at UCT; the statue removed 9 April.** **October 2015: #FeesMustFall over a 10.5% increase at Wits, spreading nationally in days; marches on Parliament (21 Oct) and the Union Buildings (23 Oct); a 0% increase announced for 2016.** **2016: an 8% cap, renewed protests, campus closures, hundreds of millions in arson damage, mass arrests.** **November 2017: the Heher Commission recommended against free university education, proposing an income-contingent loan scheme.** **16 December 2017: fee-free higher education announced for households under R350,000 — the opposite.**

RhodesMustFall and FeesMustFall.front: What FeesMustFall changed and did not
RhodesMustFall and FeesMustFall.back: **Changed: NSFAS from single-digit billions to on the order of R50 billion, funding about a million students as a bursary rather than a loan; a large real increase in participation by poorer students; and the insourcing of cleaning and security staff at several universities.** **Did not: the missing middle — households above the threshold and unable to pay — remains unresolved; throughput and dropout rates; a severe accommodation shortage; NSFAS's own administrative failures; and the curriculum and staff-composition demands that started it.**

**It was the born-free generation's own movement — organised by people with no personal memory of apartheid, about their own conditions, led by no party.** The EFF's student command and the ANC-aligned student organisation both sought ownership and neither controlled it. **It was horizontal and social-media-organised, which made it fast and impossible to negotiate with; it split over arson and exam disruption; it won a 0% increase in three weeks and a fee-free policy in two years — and it produced no durable organisation.**

Nasrec 2017, and the turn.back: **The ANC's 54th National Conference, 16–20 December 2017. Ramaphosa 2,440; Dlamini-Zuma 2,261 — a margin of 179 votes out of roughly 4,700.** **That decided who would be President of South Africa.** **And the leadership that emerged was split: three of the six senior officials had campaigned against him, including the Secretary-General** — who from stage 10 controls membership records, branch audits and the machinery. **So the new party President did not control the party's machinery, which is the single most useful fact for understanding 2018 to 2022.**

Nasrec 2017, and the turn.front: What Nasrec 2017 resolved, and what followed
Nasrec 2017, and the turn.back: **Resolutions: expropriation of land without compensation (adopted on the floor, against the drafted position); nationalisation of the Reserve Bank's shareholding (never implemented); a state bank (never implemented); free higher education; the step-aside principle; and cadre deployment retained.** **Then in eight weeks: the Eskom board replaced, the Zondo Commission proclaimed, Zuma recalled and Ramaphosa elected President — followed by the Nugent Commission, Batohi at the NPA and Kieswetter at SARS.** **The turn was appointments and inquiries.**

Ramaphosa's first term.front: Ramaphosa's first-term record, in four parts
Ramaphosa's first term.back: **1 Appointments and inquiries** — Zondo and Nugent, the Eskom/Transnet/SAA/Denel boards, a new NDPP, SARS Commissioner, Chief Justice and Public Protector, and IDAC. **2 Structural reform** — Operation Vulindlela, the electricity licensing changes and unbundling, the 2022 spectrum auction, the logistics roadmap, the Public Procurement Act. **3 Three crises** — Covid, July 2021, and the 2022–23 energy crisis. **4 What did not move** — prosecutions, local government, the wage bill, unemployment, appointment reform, cadre deployment.

**Too slow, and it was a choice:** the prosecutions did not follow, cadre deployment continued, local government was untouched, and appointment reform needed only legislation. **That was the available pace:** the NPA had to be rebuilt first and complex cases take years; **the party's machinery was held by the opposing faction until December 2022**; a faster pace risked a split, and the 2024 result shows what a managed split cost. **The mechanism: the levers he used — appointment and regulatory reform — are the ones that need no parliamentary majority or party consensus.**

Covid-19.front: Why Covid is a constitutional lesson
Covid-19.back: **The Disaster Management Act 57 of 2002 was used — ordinary legislation, with regulations made by a minister by notice in the Gazette.** **Section 37 — a state of emergency — was not**, which would have required an Act of Parliament, a 21-day declaration unless extended by the Assembly, automatic judicial reviewability and a list of non-derogable rights. **So for two years rights of movement, assembly, trade and religion were limited by ministerial regulation.** **Section 37's safeguards exist precisely for prolonged rights limitation — and the question was answered in practice by avoiding it.**

Covid-19.front: Which Covid death figure to use
Covid-19.back: **Recorded Covid deaths: on the order of 102,000. The SAMRC's excess natural deaths series: roughly 300,000, of which it estimated 85 to 95% was Covid-attributable.** The gap is limited testing, deaths at home, and deaths from untreated other conditions. **Use the excess deaths series: a recorded cause-of-death count is a function of testing capacity; excess mortality is not.** On that measure Covid is roughly the same order of magnitude as the cumulative AIDS denialism cost.

Covid-19.front: Omicron, and the cost of transparency
Covid-19.back: **South Africa's genomic surveillance network sequenced at a scale and speed few countries matched. It identified the Beta variant in December 2020 and, with Botswana, announced Omicron in late November 2021 — and many states imposed travel bans on southern Africa within days.** **The bans were widely criticised, including by the WHO, as penalising the transparency that had identified the variant.** **The global incentive structure punished the country that did the surveillance** — a real policy problem, named as one at the time.

**Schools closed from March 2020 with rotational attendance into 2021, and studies estimate roughly a year of learning lost for primary learners** — which is substantially why the **PIRLS 2021 reading result reversed.** From the education lesson's compounding argument, **a cohort that lost a year of foundation-phase learning carries it to matric.** Meanwhile **GDP fell about 6% in 2020 and roughly two million jobs went in one quarter**, with output recovering faster than employment.

July 2021.back: **Zuma surrendered on 7 July to serve his contempt sentence. From 8–9 July the N3 — the corridor between Durban's port and Gauteng — was blockaded and trucks burned, and from 9–18 July there was widespread looting and arson across KwaZulu-Natal and parts of Gauteng.** **About 3,000 stores, some 200 malls and more than a thousand ATMs destroyed; 354 people killed; about 5,500 arrested; roughly R50 billion of GDP and R20 billion or more in direct loss.** **Sasria paid the largest claims in its history and had to be recapitalised.**

July 2021.front: What the Expert Panel found about July 2021
July 2021.back: **Chaired by Professor Sandy Africa, reporting February 2022: the state was unprepared despite available indications; there was no coherent intelligence picture and the SSA failed to provide actionable warning or its warnings were not acted on; the police were overwhelmed and in places absent, with command and control broken down; the security cluster failed to coordinate.** **And on the characterisation it was careful — it found evidence of orchestration and declined to adopt "insurrection" as the explanation, concluding the state's own failures were the proximate cause of the scale.**

July 2021.front: Phoenix, and what state absence produced
July 2021.back: **36 of the 354 deaths were in Phoenix, north of Durban**, in confrontations between residents who had set up blockades and Black people travelling through — **the great majority of those killed were Black; the area is predominantly Indian.** It opened the most serious public argument about race between Black and Indian South Africans since the 1949 Durban riots. **The point to carry: a week of state absence produced armed community defence, and armed community defence produced a racial massacre.**

Phala Phala.front: Phala Phala, and what is undisputed
Phala Phala.back: **A burglary at the President's private game farm in Limpopo in February 2020, in which a very large sum in US dollars — on the order of $580,000 — concealed inside furniture was taken.** **The theft was not reported through ordinary police channels but handled by the Presidential Protection Unit.** His account is that the money was the proceeds of a buffalo sale. **It became public in June 2022 when the former Director-General of the SSA filed an affidavit alleging money laundering, kidnapping and defeating the ends of justice.**

Phala Phala.front: The section 89 panel, and the vote
Phala Phala.back: **An independent panel appointed by the Speaker under rules that existed only because *EFF v Speaker* (2017) ordered them made, chaired by former Chief Justice Sandile Ngcobo.** Its task was **not to decide guilt but whether there was a prima facie case to answer.** **It found prima facie evidence of a serious violation and serious misconduct.** **On 13 December 2022 the National Assembly voted not to adopt the report, so no inquiry was held.** **The same closed-list discipline that removed two presidents by party decision protected one from a constitutional process.**

Phala Phala.front: Why the Phala Phala findings are not contradictory
Phala Phala.back: **A panel found a prima facie case; the Reserve Bank found no exchange control contravention; the Public Protector cleared him under the Ethics Code; and no charges were brought.** **Those are not contradictory, because they answered different questions on different standards — a prima facie case to answer is a far lower threshold than a contravention proved.** **Both results can be correct, and anybody citing only one of them is making an argument rather than reporting.**

2024, and the coalition.back: **The Constitution requires the National Assembly's first sitting within 14 days of the result's declaration, at which it must elect a President** — so the parties had under two weeks. **2 June: the result declared. 14 June: a Statement of Intent signed and Ramaphosa re-elected President. 30 June: a Cabinet with roughly a dozen posts outside the ANC, the DA taking six.** **A governing party of thirty years lost its majority and partial power transferred in sixteen days, with no institution failing and no result disputed.**

2024, and the coalition.front: What the Statement of Intent does not contain
2024, and the coalition.back: **It sets priorities — growth, jobs, poverty and the cost of living, state capability, stabilising local government — a decision rule of "sufficient consensus", and a clearing house for disputes.** **It contains no binding programme, no enforcement mechanism, and no procedure for a party's exit.** **And the 1996 precedent is the warning: the National Party walked out of the constitutionally mandated GNU with two years to run, and nothing followed.**

2024, and the coalition.front: The three questions the coalition has not answered
2024, and the coalition.back: **1 Can it make a contested decision?** It has reformed by regulation and deferred by legislation — **NHI, expropriation, BELA and the fiscal question are all live and unresolved.** **2 Does it change accountability?** **Appointment reform has not been enacted, and a coalition is in principle better placed to enact it, because the patronage is no longer one party's to protect.** **3 What does it do to the parties?** Both the ANC's and the DA's supporters are divided about it, and 2026 and 2029 are the test.

Foreign policy since 1994.front: The founding claim, and the asset
Foreign policy since 1994.back: **A 1993 article under Mandela's name declared that human rights would be "the light that guides our foreign affairs".** **And the asset nobody else has: South Africa built nuclear weapons and then dismantled them, acceding to the NPT in 1991 — the only state ever to have done so voluntarily**, which gives it standing on disarmament no other country can claim. **The pattern set in the Mandela period and unchanged since: a declared values-based policy operated alongside interest-based decisions, with the tension managed rather than resolved.**

**In June 2015 the Sudanese President, subject to an ICC arrest warrant, attended an AU summit in Johannesburg and was allowed to leave despite a court order.** **The Supreme Court of Appeal held in 2016 that the government's conduct was unlawful.** **The ICC withdrawal announced in October 2016 was declared unconstitutional by the High Court in February 2017 for want of parliamentary approval, and was revoked.** **Section 231 and the Implementation Act made the ICC obligation domestic law, so the breach was unlawful in South Africa, not merely internationally.**

**For:** a middle power gains nothing from choosing a bloc, and non-alignment is most of the Global South's position; the liberation history creates obligations; **the ICJ case applies the Genocide Convention through the proper institution, which is what a rules-based order requires**; and the AfCFTA and continental project are the long-term interest. **Against:** **the economic exposure is asymmetric** — the US and EU are far larger markets than Russia is for anything; the consistency is contested (Myanmar, the Dalai Lama, Zimbabwe, Al-Bashir); and the continental institutions have not delivered.

**South Africa instituted proceedings against Israel under the Genocide Convention on 29 December 2023, and the International Court of Justice ordered provisional measures in January, March and May 2024, with the merits pending.** **The most consequential foreign policy action South Africa has taken since 1994** — defended as the direct application of the founding values claim, and criticised as selective. **Alongside the Russia–Ukraine abstentions, the June 2023 African Peace Initiative, and the *Lady R* inquiry, which found no evidence that weapons were loaded.**

The SANDF, and the regional deployments.back: **"Only the President, as head of the national executive, may authorise the employment of the defence force"** — in co-operation with the police, in defence of the Republic, or **in fulfilment of an international obligation**; and **201(3) requires the President to inform Parliament promptly of the reasons, the place, the numbers and the period.** **The third ground is the basis of every South African deployment since 1994.** Section 200(2) makes the primary object **defence of the Republic, its territorial integrity and its people.**

**From on the order of 4% of GDP in the late 1980s to about 0.7% now** — among the steepest peacetime reductions anywhere, and **the peace dividend was real and deliberately taken; the money went to the social wage.** **The 2015 Defence Review found the force in "a critical state of decline", set a recovery trajectory, and was never funded.** **The irony: the Gripens, frigates and submarines bought in the 1999 arms deal cannot be operated for lack of operating budget** — capability the country was told it did not need, and now cannot use.

The SANDF, and the regional deployments.front: The SANDF's integration, and its deployments
The SANDF, and the regional deployments.back: **In 1994 the SANDF was formed by integrating the SADF, Umkhonto we Sizwe, APLA and four homeland forces — a conventional army and two guerrilla armies that had been fighting each other.** **It held: no coup, no mutiny of consequence, civilian control throughout** — which was not the expected outcome. **Deployments: Burundi from 2001 (successful); the DRC from 2013; Bangui in 2013 where 13–15 soldiers were killed; SAMIM in Mozambique 2021–24; SAMIDRC from December 2023, where 14 soldiers were killed near Goma in January 2025.**

Where it stands: a dated scorecard.front: The thirty-year scorecard, in two columns
Where it stands: a dated scorecard.back: **Unambiguously improved since 1994:** political rights and the rule-of-law institutions; electrification, water and sanitation access; the grant system's reach; life expectancy and HIV treatment; school access and higher education funding; the courts' and the AG's strength; press freedom and civil society's legal reach. **Unambiguously worse since about 2009:** GDP per capita; unemployment; the murder rate; municipal service delivery; educational outcomes; state capacity in policing, prosecution and local government; public debt and debt service.

Where it stands: a dated scorecard.front: Why the scorecard's two columns prove the capacity thesis
Where it stands: a dated scorecard.back: **The improved column is overwhelmingly things the state delivered by spending money and extending access. The worsened column is overwhelmingly things that require the state to work well.** **That is stage 8's and stage 9's capacity thesis, stated as a thirty-year result** — and it is the strongest single reason the institutions and economy stages come before the narrative one. **And the dating discipline: every figure will be wrong within a year. The point is the habit of finding them, dating them, and noticing the direction.**

How to hold a live argument.front: The five parts of a live argument
How to hold a live argument.back: **1 State the question precisely** — most disagreements dissolve or narrow here. **2 State what is agreed** — almost always more than the participants admit. **3 The strongest form of each side**, as its own best advocate would put it; **if you cannot state it in terms its holders would accept, you do not understand it yet.** **4 What evidence would settle it** — named and findable; "more research" is not an answer. **5 What each side would have to concede** — the rarest part. **A position that cannot name a fact that would damage it is not an analysis.**

How to hold a live argument.front: Four failure modes in political argument
How to hold a live argument.back: **Using a number without its definition** — the Gini, the unemployment rate, the 72% land figure, BEE ownership. **Arguing a counterfactual as if it were observable** — "BEE cost the economy X", "a different transition was available in 1994". **Treating an allegation as a finding** — the SARS "rogue unit", the R500 billion, the migration figures. **And attributing a position to a whole group** — "black South Africans believe", "business wants" — **which conceals that the disagreement usually runs within each group more sharply than between them.**

Land: expropriation.front: What the land argument has already settled
Land: expropriation.back: **Ownership is racially skewed — not disputed.** **Section 25(3) does not require market value**; "willing buyer, willing seller" was a policy choice. **The Expropriation Act 13 of 2024 expressly provides for nil compensation in defined circumstances** — abandoned or purely speculative land, land where state investment exceeds market value, land already occupied by beneficiaries. **The 2021 constitutional amendment failed at two-thirds.** **And two official panels found section 25 was not the constraint** — budget, corruption, elite capture, post-settlement support and capacity were.

Land: expropriation.front: The test that is now available on land
Land: expropriation.back: **The Expropriation Act is signed. If the state expropriates at nil compensation several times, measure hectares transferred per rand of budget against the previous decade.** **If the transfer rate does not rise, the constraint was never compensation — and the two panels were right.** Conversely, **if agricultural capital formation and bank lending secured on farmland do not fall materially after commencement, the policy-uncertainty argument was overstated.** **Both claims are directly testable and the test has begun.**

Land: communal tenure.front: The land question affecting the most people
Land: communal tenure.back: **About 13% of South Africa, with 17 to 18 million people living on it, is formally held in trust by the state and administered through traditional councils** — and **section 25(6) entitles residents to "legally secure tenure or comparable redress", which has not been delivered in thirty-two years.** **The Communal Land Rights Act fell in *Tongoane* (2010) and the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act in *Mogale* (2023), both on process grounds, with no replacement in force.**

Land: communal tenure.front: What communal area residents say they want
Land: communal tenure.back: **Surveyed repeatedly, with the consistent finding that residents want secure, inheritable, individually held rights and do not want the land alienable to outsiders** — **which matches none of the three pure positions** (individual title, communal title, traditional council administration) **and matches the hybrid that has been drafted several times and never enacted: statutorily recognised, individually held, transferable use rights within a communally held title, with the allocation function regulated and appealable.**

The fiscal question.front: What both sides of the fiscal argument agree on
The fiscal question.back: **The numbers** (debt 75–77% of GDP from 26% in 2008; debt service among the largest spending items; a primary surplus achieved). **Where the debt came from** — the post-2008 revenue collapse, the wage bill, SOE bailouts, slow growth, the downgrades — **and not principally social grants.** **The sustainability condition** — nominal growth above the effective interest rate, with a primary surplus. **And the composition critique: the consolidation fell on capital and maintenance rather than the wage bill, which both sides agree was wrong.**

The fiscal question.front: The natural experiment in the fiscal argument
The fiscal question.back: **Load-shedding has largely stopped since 2024 without a fiscal expansion.** **If growth recovers materially, the binding constraint was electricity rather than the fiscal stance. If it does not, the expansion case strengthens considerably.** **And the operative question both sides avoid is the wage bill** — the expansion case asks for borrowing to fund a line item that grew through pay rather than staff, and the consolidation case protected it. **That is a narrower argument than the public one.**

A basic income grant.front: What is settled about an income grant
A basic income grant.back: **The SRD grant exists, reaching 8 to 9 million people, below the food poverty line, on an annually renewed budget line — and it cannot be withdrawn politically.** **The transfer system works: SASSA pays about 19 million regular grants monthly with low leakage.** **And the labour supply objection is not supported by the evidence** — grant receipt is associated with **more** job search, because a grant pays the transport fare. **Cost is arithmetic: it depends entirely on the level and the means test, and both sides use the same spreadsheet.**

A basic income grant.front: The unused evidence on income grants
A basic income grant.back: **The SRD is a five-year natural experiment covering 8 to 9 million people.** **Comparing labour force participation and job search among recipients and non-recipients, controlling for selection, would settle the central empirical question — and the linked QLFS and SASSA analysis has not been done at scale.** Also unresolved: **the Living Conditions Survey, which measures poverty, is run roughly once a decade** — running it more often is itself a recommendation.

NHI.front: Where the NHI argument actually is
NHI.back: **Agreed: the two-tier system is indefensible (16% of the population, roughly half the health spending); universal coverage is the right objective; section 27 obliges progressive realisation; the private sector is not a well-functioning market (the Health Market Inquiry's concentration findings); public facility quality is the binding constraint; and incremental reform has not changed the split in thirty years.** **The dispute is about the vehicle and the sequence — between people who agree on the objective.** It is presented as universal coverage against private medicine, and it is not.

NHI.front: The two tests that would settle NHI
NHI.back: **1 How is the Fund's board appointed?** Stage 8's appointment correlation is the thing to apply: **a commission-type process, or a minister appointing the board of the largest procurement entity in the country.** **2 Where is the costing?** **Treasury's full public costing has been requested repeatedly and not published — and that absence is the most telling fact in the argument.** Then watch the Fund's procurement, audit outcomes and accreditation capacity in its first three years.

BEE's future.front: The single best indicator in the BEE argument
BEE's future.back: **The Commission for Employment Equity's top-management series, published annually, which every designated employer files into.** **African South Africans remain a small minority of top management against roughly 80% of the economically active population, while lower and middle management have changed substantially.** **The trend over the next five years, under the 2022 amendment's sectoral targets, is the answer** — and if it does not move, procurement leverage will have been tried and failed.

BEE's future.front: The untested alternative to race-based redress
BEE's future.back: **A class or disadvantage criterion in place of a race criterion is proposed across the political spectrum and has never been piloted at scale.** **A sectoral or provincial pilot with published outcomes would settle more than a decade of argument.** **Also unmeasured: any credible aggregate cost of the BEE system (no published method exists); the counterfactual (unobservable); and ownership reported with direct and mandated holdings separated consistently year on year.**

The labour market.front: Where labour regulation ranks among unemployment's causes
The labour market.back: **Sixth of eight**, in stage 9's ordering: **schooling; spatial geography; demand and growth; capital-intensive production; the small informal sector; wages and regulation; market concentration; and grants (eighth and weakest).** **So regulation is a real factor and not the largest** — which both sides tend to misstate. **And the national minimum wage's measured effects went against the predicted large job losses**, which should discount the confidence of the broader regulation case.

**The Minister may extend a bargaining council agreement to non-parties, binding firms that were not represented** — and **exemption applications are administered by the bargaining council itself, which is the interested party.** **That conflict is indefensible on any view of the wider argument**, and it is the narrowest, most actionable item in the labour debate. **The Newcastle clothing cases are the concrete evidence, and both sides read them as proving their point.**

Electricity: who owns the grid.front: The single number to watch in electricity policy
Electricity: who owns the grid.back: **The transmission build programme's delivery against its published kilometre targets.** **The generation reform worked — the licensing threshold went to 100 MW in 2021 and then away, a large private build-out followed, and load-shedding has been largely suspended since 2024. Transmission is now the binding constraint:** the best wind and solar resource is in the Cape, the grid capacity is in Mpumalanga, and new lines take years and very large capital. **If the build misses its targets for three years, the funding constraint is real.**

**Municipal electricity distribution is in worse trouble than transmission and gets a fraction of the attention, because it is municipal.** Municipalities depend on the electricity surplus, face defection by their best customers, and carry a maintenance backlog in the tens of billions. **The reform in progress is ring-fencing electricity and water as separate trading entities with licensing conditions, so the surplus cannot fund general expenses and the maintenance budget is protected.**

The Reserve Bank's mandate.front: The strongest point the Reserve Bank's critics have
The Reserve Bank's mandate.back: **The Bank has undershot the 3–6% target band's midpoint in several recent periods.** **"The mandate is price stability" does not answer whether the target itself is set correctly** — which is where the real argument is, and it is the most tractable part: **both Treasury and the Bank have publicly engaged with lowering the target toward 3%.** **And the shareholding question is a distraction: shareholders have no monetary policy role, so raising it weakens the serious argument.**

Electoral reform.front: Why electoral reform needs no amendment
Electoral reform.back: **Section 46 requires only that the system "results, in general, in proportional representation" — closed lists are in the Electoral Act.** **So a mixed-member proportional system, a threshold and open lists are all available by ordinary legislation.** **Recommended by the Van Zyl Slabbert Electoral Task Team in 2003 and by the Zondo Commission in 2022, twenty years apart, and never done** — **because every party in Parliament benefits from the current system. That is the explanation, and it should be stated.**

Electoral reform.front: Open lists, the reform nobody proposes
Electoral reform.back: **Voters rank or select candidates within their chosen party's list.** **It keeps full proportionality, needs no boundary authority, no by-elections and no new institutions, and gives every MP a personal mandate** — which removes the delisting threat that stage 10's seven-step recall chain depends on. **The accountability gain people want from constituencies comes from removing that threat rather than from constituencies as such, which makes open lists the cheapest available fix.**

Coalition durability.back: **A constructive vote of no confidence: a mayor or President may be removed only if a replacement is elected in the same vote** — the German model, with a long comparative record in Germany and Spain. **It directly addresses the municipal mayoral churn that stage 8 names as a leading cause of local government failure, and it requires only ordinary legislation.** **It has not been introduced.** **The honest objection: stability and accountability trade off — it makes a bad mayor harder to remove too.**

Coalition durability.front: The four dated tests of the coalition
Coalition durability.back: **NHI's implementation, the Expropriation Act's commencement, the BELA Act's sections 4 and 5 on language and admissions, and the next budget's revenue measures.** **Each is an observable test of whether a coalition can make a contested decision, as against deferring it.** **So far the record is reform by regulation and deferral by legislation.** And the broader test: **whether the coalition parties campaign against each other locally while governing together nationally** — the hardest test of a coalition anywhere.

Devolution.front: Devolution needs a minister, not an amendment
Devolution.back: **Section 99 permits a national minister to assign a function to a province; section 156(4) requires assignment to a municipality of a Schedule 4A or 5A matter that necessarily relates to local government, where the municipality has the capacity and it would be more effectively administered locally.** **So the main route is a decision, not a constitutional change** — and section 44(2) preserves a national override for national security, economic unity and essential national standards. **The constitutional argument is largely unnecessary.**

Devolution.front: Why devolution must be argued function by function
Devolution.back: **Commuter rail devolves cleanly — it serves one city's commuters and has no national dimension, and PRASA's collapse from hundreds of millions of journeys to a fraction is the evidence. Serious and organised crime investigation does not — it fragments badly, and investigative capacity is already the binding constraint. Ports are in between.** **Arguing about "devolution" in the abstract is arguing about nothing.** **And what devolutionists are actually proposing is asymmetric devolution, which they should say, because it entrenches the inter-provincial inequality it responds to.**

The Constitution itself.front: The strongest answer to parliamentary sovereignty
The Constitution itself.back: **Apartheid was built under parliamentary sovereignty, by a Parliament that amended its own constitution to remove the coloured franchise and packed the Senate to do it.** **The Constitution's drafters knew exactly what they were guarding against — stage 5 is the evidence.** **It is not conclusive, and it is the strongest argument available, and the position has to answer it.** The other half: **every institutional gain since 1994 came from justiciable rights and binding judgments** — Nkandla, *Glenister*, *Corruption Watch*, the socio-economic rights cases.

The Constitution itself.front: What the Constitution did and did not do
The Constitution itself.back: **It constrained**: the nuclear procurement set aside, the Al-Bashir warrant, the NDPP appointments, Nkandla, the grant payment supervision, the HIV treatment order. **It could not supply capacity**: two commissions, almost no prosecutions — **a document cannot supply detectives.** **And on redress, the constitutional constraints are weaker than claimed and the administrative constraints stronger** — the two land panels, the fiscal incidence studies, and stage 9's BEE evidence all point the same way.

Crime and policing.front: Why crime is the argument least in need of being had
Crime and policing.back: **The diagnosis is not contested: the number of police is not the problem; investigative capacity is; impunity is the mechanism; resource allocation is skewed (the Equality Court so held); the National Commissioner is appointed by the President alone; and the firearms stock matters.** **The remedies are known, mostly technical and budgetable, and have not been done.** **That is a consequence-management and appointment problem, not a knowledge problem** — and of everything in stage 12, this is the argument most in need of being acted on.

Crime and policing.front: The crime data that is not published
Crime and policing.back: **The murder detection rate against the murder rate, by province and by station, over time — SAPS holds this and publishes little of it, which is itself the finding.** Also directly measurable and unpublished: **conviction rates in cases where DNA evidence was and was not available in time**, which the forensic laboratories' own data would show. **And the Equality Court's police allocation order has a compliance timetable: watch whether allocation shifts and whether murder rates in the reallocated areas move.**

Migration.front: The one migration intervention nobody campaigns on
Migration.back: **Both require a functioning Home Affairs: asylum claims decided in months rather than a decade, permits processed reliably, a working population register, and documentation of who is here.** **The enforcement case needs it because you cannot deport people whose claims are undecided or plan services without knowing the numbers. The regularisation case needs it because a person with papers can work legally, be inspected and pay tax.** **It is the one intervention both sides' strongest arguments require, and nobody campaigns on it.**

Foreign policy: non-alignment's cost.back: **Testing whether South Africa applies international law consistently is a straightforwardly checkable exercise that almost nobody does: pick five comparable situations since 1994 and record the position taken in each.** The cases usually cited against consistency are **the 2007 Myanmar Security Council vote, the Dalai Lama visa refusals, Zimbabwe's elections, and the Al-Bashir breach that the SCA held unlawful in 2016** — against **the ICJ case of 2023–24**, which is the clearest case of using the proper institution to enforce a treaty obligation.

Foreign policy: non-alignment's cost.front: The asymmetry in the non-alignment argument
Foreign policy: non-alignment's cost.back: **China is South Africa's largest single trading partner; the United States and the European Union are the largest markets for its manufactured and agricultural exports.** **That asymmetry is the whole economic argument, and the 2025 tariff and preference changes are a natural experiment whose results the trade data will show within two years.** **And both sides concede the same thing: the instruments have decayed** — the SANDF cannot sustain the deployments the policy commits to, which is stage 8's problem again.

How to keep this current.back: **1 Date every figure you write down** — an undated number is a memory, not evidence. **2 Name the base** — of the Gini, the unemployment rate, the land percentage, the ownership figure. **3 Separate the inherited from the current** — structure, geography and schooling are slow; appointment, procurement, electricity and logistics are fast. **4 Read something you expect to disagree with, monthly, and state its argument before rejecting it.** **5 Ask whether the thing you are angry about is a design failure or a capacity failure — it is almost always the second, and the remedy is completely different.**

**Quarterly: four numbers — the absorption rate (StatsSA QLFS), the murder rate (SAPS), Eskom's energy availability factor, and debt service (Budget Review). Write the date.** **Annually: the whole stage 11 scorecard, noting which rows moved against the direction you expected — and write down why you were wrong before looking for a reason you were right.** **After each election: stage 10's seven things to watch, with your prediction written down beforehand.**

How to keep this current.front: Why the curriculum is ordered as it is
How to keep this current.back: **Stage 1 is first because a reader who cannot place a source reads a committed account as a neutral one. Stages 2 to 6 are the history, because the present is unintelligible without it. Stage 7 is the document. Stages 8 to 10 are the machinery — institutions, economy, parties — because the machinery is more durable and more useful than the events. Stage 11 is the events. Stage 12 is the arguments.** **The events change constantly, the machinery changes slowly, and the method does not change at all.**
